## 1 Introduction

In this paper we study various problems related to sparse pattern matching, such as Sparse Convolution, Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances, and the Constellation problem (their definitions will be given later in this introduction).

Many of these problems take sparse integer sets as input, and it is often useful to first reduce them to dense instances which are easier to handle. In our cases, a common tool to implement this sparse-to-dense reduction is the simple mod-prime hash. That is, we pick a random prime $p$ from $[Q/2,Q]$ for some parameter $Q$ , and map each input integer $x$ (coming from a large universe $[N]$ 11 1 We use $[N]$ to denote $\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}$ . ) to $h(x):=x\bmod{p}$ . One major benefit of this hash function is that it is perfectly linear, i.e., $h(x)+h(y)\equiv h(x+y)\pmod{p}$ for any $x,y$ . This feature makes it useful in convolution and pattern matching scenarios, where we want to compress the input universe while preserving the additive structure. However, this mod-prime hash family has two main drawbacks:

- • For any $x\neq y\in[N]$ , the probability that $h(x)=h(y)$ is $O(\frac{\log N}{Q})$ .22 2 $h(x)=h(y)$ if and only if $p$ divides $x-y$ . The number of prime divisors of $x-y$ from $[Q/2,Q]$ is at most $\log_{Q/2}|x-y|=O(\log N/\log Q)$ , so a random prime from $[Q/2,Q]$ is among them with probability $O\big(\frac{\log N/\log Q}{\#\text{primes in }[Q/2,Q]}\big)=O\big(\frac{\log N/\log Q}{Q/\log Q}\big)=O\big(\frac{\log N}{Q}\big)$ by the prime number theorem. In contrast, the optimal collision probability is $\frac{1}{Q}$ by a uniformly random hash function. This means that the hash family may have bad load-balancing that leads to logarithmic factor loss in the running times of the algorithms. An alternative is to use almost linear hash functions (such as Dietzfelbinger’s hash function [36] or the classic textbook hash function $h(x)=((ax+b)\bmod{p})\bmod{m}$ ), which have optimal (up to constant factor) collision probability. However, these hash families do not perfectly achieve the linearity condition, but rather achieve it with small errors. These hard-to-predict errors often pose serious challenges in algorithm design (e.g., [20, 21]).

- • This hash family is not easily applicable to deterministic algorithms, since it is hard to derandomize the choice of the prime $p$ . The naive way that tries all primes in the given range is too slow. A smarter way of derandomization used in [29, 27, 28, 41] is to hash modulo $q=p_{1}\cdots p_{k}$ , where each factor $p_{i}$ is small and is deterministically chosen by brute force. However, this multi-level approach leads to super-logarithmic overhead [29]. (Some recent deterministic algorithms [21, 43] removed this super-logarithmic overhead by using algebraic techniques instead of hashing, but these algebraic techniques were tailored towards the specific applications, and it is not clear whether they are as widely applicable as hashing-based techniques.)

In this paper, we partially overcome these two drawbacks in certain scenarios. Our main tool is the large sieve inequality (and its variants) from analytic number theory (described in more detail in Section 2.3). We use this tool to analyze the mod-prime hash function and obtain better bounds. This leads to improved hashing-based algorithms for many sparse convolution and pattern matching problems. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to apply this number-theoretic tool in the context of algorithm design.

Before discussing this number-theoretic tool, we first introduce the problems we consider in this paper, known results, and our improved results. We use the standard word RAM model of computation throughout this paper (see formal definitions in Section 2.2).

#### Sparse Convolution

Computing the convolution $A\star B$ of two integer vectors $A,B$ , defined as $(A\star B)_{k}=\sum_{i+j=k}A_{i}\cdot B_{j}$ , is a fundamental task in computer science. It is useful in various fields of engineering: signal processing, computer vision, symbolic computation, discrete algorithm design, computational complexity theory, and so on. In most scenarios of discrete algorithm design, we care about nonnegative convolution where $A,B$ are nonnegative vectors (sometimes even Boolean convolution suffices). Applications include $k$ SUM [29], Subset Sum [25, 63, 22, 24], Knapsack [19] and pattern matching problems [40, 52].

It is well-known that convolution of two length- $N$ vectors can be computed in deterministic $O(N\log N)$ time using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). This running time is widely conjectured to be optimal, and there is some partial evidence in favor of the conjecture [5, 3].

In many algorithmic applications, the input and output vectors are often sparse (e.g., [26, 32, 7, 29, 22, 23, 56, 1, 30, 19, 31]), so it is important to have algorithms that can exploit the sparsity of the input and output. Motivated by this, there has been a long line of work studying the Sparse Convolution problem [72, 32, 77, 67, 82, 29, 8, 78, 73, 48, 20, 21]. A major open question is whether we can solve Sparse Convolution as fast as dense convolution [20].

One interesting case of Sparse Convolution which is particularly useful for algorithmic applications is when the input integers are all nonnegative. This is known as the Sparse Nonnegative Convolution problem. More formally, let $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ be two input vectors. We denote the sparsity by $t=\max\{\|A\|_{0},\|B\|_{0},\|A\star B\|_{0}\}$ . When $A,B$ are nonnegative vectors, $t=\|A\star B\|_{0}$ . The Sparse Nonnegative Convolution problem asks to compute $A\star B$ , and preferably the running time should mainly depend on the sparsity $t$ instead of the length $N$ .

Previously, the fastest algorithm for Sparse Nonnegative Convolution was given by Bringmann, Fischer and Nakos [20]. Their algorithm runs in $O(t\log t+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta))$ time where $\Delta=\max\{\|A\|_{\infty},\|B\|_{\infty}\}$ denotes the maximum entry size, is Monte Carlo randomized, and has error probability $2^{-\sqrt{\log t}}$ . When $N\Delta$ is reasonably small, their running time is $O(t\log t)$ , matching the running time of dense convolution.

However, compared to dense convolution (which has a deterministic algorithm), one weakness of [20]’s result is that the success probability is only $1-2^{-\sqrt{\log t}}$ . In algorithm design, it is often desirable to achieve $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ error probability, which is typically called “with high probability” in algorithmic literature.

Resolving this issue was explicitly asked as the first open question in [20]:

[20]: Can Sparse Nonnegative Convolution be solved by a randomized algorithm in $O(t\log t)$ time with $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ success probability?

This issue also motivated the authors of [20] to study Las Vegas and deterministic algorithms for Sparse Nonnegative Convolution in a follow-up work [21].33 3 See the last paragraph on page 2 of [21]. However, [21] only obtained an $O(t\log t\log\log t)$ time Las Vegas algorithm, and a much slower $O(t\log^{5}(N\Delta)\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log(N\Delta))$ time deterministic algorithm. [21] raised the following open question:

[21]: Can Sparse Nonnegative Convolution be solved by a Las Vegas randomized algorithm in $O(t\log t)$ expected time?

In this paper, we resolve both open questions in the affirmative. In fact, we get the best of both worlds: We obtain a Las Vegas algorithm that achieves $O(t\log t)$ running time with high probability.

#### Theorem 1.1 (Las Vegas Sparse Nonnegative Convolution w.h.p.).

Given two vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ , one can compute $A\star B$ by a Las Vegas algorithm that terminates in $O(t\log t)$ time with at least $1-1/t$ probability, where $t=\|A\star B\|_{0}$ .

Theorem 1.1 also affirmatively resolves a secondary open question asked in [20] on whether the $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ term in their $O(t\log t+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta))$ -time Monte Carlo algorithm can be removed (see Footnote 8).

As a straightforward application, we improve the best known Las Vegas algorithm for the Constellation problem, which was recently considered by Fischer [43] as a representative problem for a rich class of sparse pattern matching problems (with applications in computational geometry). In this problem, we are given two integer sets $A,B\subseteq[N]$ of size $|A|,|B|\leq n$ , and we need to output all shifts $s$ such that $A+s\subseteq B$ . The best Monte Carlo algorithm for this problem runs in $O(n\log n)$ time [26], and the best Las Vegas algorithm runs in $O(n\log^{2}N)$ time [32]. Fischer [43] gave an $O(n\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log N)$ time deterministic algorithm, improving an $n\cdot 2^{O(\sqrt{\log n\log\log N})}$ time algorithm by Chan and Lewenstein [29].

Our algorithm is a straightforward combination of the Monte Carlo algorithm by Cardoze and Schulman [26] and our Las Vegas Sparse Nonnegative Convolution algorithm.44 4 In fact, our method shows that the previous $O(t\log t\log\log t)$ time Las Vegas Sparse Nonnegative Convolution algorithm [21] would already imply an $O(n\log n\log\log n)$ time Las Vegas algorithm for the Constellation problem, which is faster than the previously known $O(n\log^{2}N)$ time Las Vegas algorithm [32].

#### Theorem 1.2 (Constellation).

Given two sets $A,B\subseteq[N]$ of size $|A|,|B|\leq n$ , one can output all shifts $s$ such that $A+s\subseteq B$ by a Las Vegas algorithm that terminates in $O(n\log n)$ time with at least $1-1/n$ probability.

We prove Theorem 1.2 in Section 8.

#### Sparse General Convolution.

Our Theorem 1.1, as well as the previous works [32, 8, 20, 21], crucially requires that the input vectors are nonnegative. For Sparse General Convolution (with input vectors from $\mathbb{Z}^{N}$ rather than $\mathbb{N}^{N}$ ), various previous techniques are all stuck at $O(t\log^{2}N)$ (see [20, Section 3.3]55 5 When referencing the theorems and lemmas in the previous works by Bringmann, Fischer, and Nakos [20, 21], we always refer to their long versions appearing on arXiv. and [42, Section 2.2.2] for related discussions). Getting faster algorithms for Sparse General Convolution is explicitly mentioned in [20] as an open problem:

[20]: Can Sparse General Convolution be solved in $O(t\log t+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta))$ time?

In this paper, we give a partial answer to this question: For the special case of $N\leq t^{1.99}$ and $\Delta\leq 2^{2^{\log t/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log t}}$ , we obtain an $O(t\log t)$ -time Monte Carlo randomized algorithm for general convolution.

#### Theorem 1.3 (Sparse General Convolution for short vectors).

Let $\varepsilon>0$ be a fixed constant. Given two vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{N}$ with the promise that $N<t^{2-\varepsilon}$ , where $t=\max\{\|A\|_{0},\|B\|_{0},\|A\star B\|_{0}\}$ , one can compute $A\star B$ in $O(t\log t+t(\log\log t)^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log\Delta)$ expected time by a Monte Carlo algorithm with $0.9$ success probability, where $\Delta=\max\{\|A\|_{\infty},\|B\|_{\infty}\}$ .

The upper bound $2^{2^{\log t/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log t}}$ on $\Delta$ is much higher than $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ , which is the interesting case for most algorithmic applications. The constraint $N\leq t^{1.99}$ is more restricted. In [20], they actually reduced Sparse Nonnegative Convolution with general $N$ to Sparse Nonnegative Convolution with a similar constraint $N\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ . Unfortunately, their reduction does not work for Sparse General Convolution. If one could design a similar reduction that works for Sparse General Convolution, then Theorem 1.3 would extend to general values of $N$ . In light of such reductions, we hope Theorem 1.3 can eventually lead to an $O(t\log t)$ time algorithm for Sparse General Convolution.

Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.3 assume the word RAM model with word length $w=\Omega(\log t+\log(N\Delta))$ (see more details in Section 2.2). An alternative choice is to consider the bit complexity (which is the focus of papers in symbolic computation such as [48, 47]), which would be more realistic in the scenario where $\log(N\Delta)$ can be much larger than $t$ . By taking into account the bit complexity of arithmetic operations on $\log t+\log(N\Delta)$ -bit integers, we see that both Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.3 have bit complexity $O(t\log t\log(N\Delta)\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log(N\Delta))$ . In comparison, [48] gave a Monte Carlo algorithm for Sparse General Convolution in bit complexity $O(t\log(N\Delta)\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(\log t,\log\log(N\Delta)))$ with unspecified number of polylogarithmic factors. Our algorithms achieve better dependency on $t$ , but only apply to more restrictive scenarios than [48].

#### Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances.

In the classic Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances problem, we are given a pattern $P$ of length $m$ and a text $T$ of length $n$ , both over a polynomial-size alphabet, and we need to compute the Hamming distance between $P$ and $T[i\mathinner{.\,.}i+m-1]$ for every shift $i$ .

For a long time, the fastest algorithm for this problem had $O(n\sqrt{m\log m})$ deterministic time by Abrahamson [2]. Very recently, Chan, Jin, Vassilevska Williams and Xu [28] gave a Las Vegas algorithm achieving improved $O(n\sqrt{m})$ running time with high probability. Although Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances a priori is not a sparse problem, the improvement of [28] crucially used hashing-based techniques similar to those used in Sparse Convolution and sparse recovery. Thus, it is difficult to derandomize their hashing-based algorithms with small overhead. Using a derandomization technique by Chan and Lewenstein [29] (mentioned in the beginning of this introduction), they obtained a slower deterministic algorithm in $O(n\sqrt{m}(\log m\log\log m)^{1/4})$ time.

In this work, we obtain an improved deterministic algorithm for the Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances problem, matching the state-of-the-art randomized algorithms [28] up to a $\sqrt{\log\log m}$ factor.

#### Theorem 1.4.

The Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances problem can be solved by a deterministic algorithm in $O(n\sqrt{m\log\log m})$ time.

We also obtain a similar improvement for the Text-to-Pattern Dominance Matching problem (see definition in Section 7).

The main technical component behind Theorem 1.4, which may be of independent interest, is a variant of a lemma that computes the convolution between two nonnegative vectors that appeared in [28], which they call the $X+Y$ lemma.

#### Theorem 1.5 (Deterministic $X+Y$ lemma).

Given two nonnegative vectors $X,Y\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ with $\|X\|_{1},\|Y\|_{1}\leq s$ for some $s\geq\sqrt{2N}$ , there is a nonuniform deterministic algorithm that can compute $X\star Y$ in $O(N\log(s^{2}/N)+N\log\log N)$ time.

The advice (a.k.a. non-uniformity) of the algorithm only depends on $N$ and has $O(\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log N)$ bits. Moreover, this advice can be computed in $O(N^{1.01})$ time deterministically.

We can compare this result with [28] who gave two algorithms for the $X+Y$ lemma. Their Las Vegas algorithm runs in $O(N\log(s^{2}/N))$ expected time, and their deterministic algorithm runs in $O(N\log(s^{2}/N)+N\sqrt{\log s\log\log N})$ time. Their deterministic running time is about a $\sqrt{\log s}=\Omega(\sqrt{\log N})$ factor higher than ours. Although our algorithm additionally requires a small $O(N^{1.01})$ preprocessing time to compute the advice, it becomes negligible in applications where we need to apply the $X+Y$ lemma many times (such as the Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances problem).

### 1.1 Technical overview

#### Mod-prime hash and large sieve inequality.

Suppose the input sparse vectors are from $\mathbb{Z}^{N}$ . Let $p$ be a random prime from $[Q/2,Q]$ . The mod-prime hash is defined as $h(a):=a\bmod{p}$ for $a\in[N]$ . In many applications of the mod-prime hash, one is interested in the probability that two hashes collide, i.e., $h(a)=h(b)$ for $a\neq b\in[N]$ . Note that the number of prime factors in $[Q/2,Q]$ of $a-b$ is upper bounded by $O(\frac{\log N}{\log Q})$ , and the total number of primes in $[Q/2,Q]$ is $\Theta(\frac{Q}{\log Q})$ , so the probability that a random prime can cause $h(a)=h(b)$ , which is equivalent to $p\mid a-b$ , is $O(\frac{\log N}{Q})$ .

This $O(\frac{\log N}{Q})$ probability is affected by the number of prime factors of $a-b$ in $[Q/2,Q]$ . In the worst-case, it is certainly possible that $a-b$ has $\Theta(\frac{\log N}{\log Q})$ prime factors in the range. However, on average, each number in $[N]$ only has $O(1/\log Q)$ prime factors from $[Q/2,Q]$ .66 6 This is because each prime $p\in[Q/2,Q]$ is the divisor of only $O(N/Q)$ numbers in $[N]$ , so on average, each number in $[N]$ has $O(\frac{1}{N}\cdot\frac{N}{Q}\cdot\frac{Q}{\log Q})=O(1/\log Q)$ prime divisors from the range. This suggests that, when $a-b$ is not selected in a worst-case way, it could potentially be possible to improve the $O(\frac{\log N}{Q})$ collision probability.

In fact, when applying the mod-prime hash to a subset of numbers $A\subseteq[N]$ , we are interested in the number of pairs $(a,b)\in A\times A$ such that $p\mid(a-b)$ . If we apply mod-prime hashing naively, we get an $O(|A|^{2}\cdot(\frac{\log N}{Q})+|A|)=O(|A|\cdot(\frac{|A|\log N}{Q}+1))$ upper bound (the $+|A|$ accounts for the fact that $a\in A$ always collides with itself). However, intuitively, it is difficult to construct $A$ , so that most numbers $a-b$ where $(a,b)\in A\times A$ have the largest possible $\Theta(\frac{\log N}{\log Q})$ number of prime factors from $[Q/2,Q]$ .

This is where the large sieve inequality plays a role in our paper. In number theory, the large sieve inequality has been used to prove arithmetic properties about sumsets [10, 76, 11]; this is somewhat similar to our goal of understanding the prime factors of elements in the difference set $A-A$ . A standard application of a version of the large sieve inequality [84] formalizes the above intuition for a certain regime of parameters. More specifically, it can be shown that, as long as $10\leq Q\leq N\leq Q^{1.99}$ , the expected number of pairs $a,b\in A$ such that $h(a)=h(b)$ can be bounded by $O\left(|A|\cdot\left(\frac{|A|}{Q}+\log\log N\right)\right)$ . In the natural $Q=\Theta(|A|)$ setting, this bound achieves an $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ improvement over the naive $O(|A|\cdot(\frac{|A|\log N}{Q}+1))$ bound. In fact, we can even decrease $Q$ to $|A|/\log\log N$ , while maintaining the same bound, and in this case, the $O\left(|A|\log\log N\right)$ bound matches the bound achieved by the fully random hash function. Thus, for each $i\in[p]$ (we typically call such $i$ a bucket), if we count how many $a\in A$ are mapped to $i$ , we should expect to see $O(\log\log N)$ of them, at least for most buckets. This improvement lies at the heart of our $O(t\log t)$ -time Sparse Nonnegative Convolution and Sparse General Convolution algorithms.77 7 This improvement alone leads to $O(t\log t)$ expected time Las Vegas algorithm. The high success probability of Theorem 1.1 is made possible by other techniques, which will be explained later.

The statements of the large sieve inequality and the formal version of the above bound can be found in Section 2.3.

#### Sparse General Convolution.

For the Sparse Convolution problem, we follow a series of previous works (e.g., [73, 20, 21]) which used the iterative peeling algorithm (similar to techniques used in the sparse recovery literature) combined with linear hashing. Roughly speaking, given input vectors $A,B$ , we maintain an approximate answer $C$ , and gradually decrease the number of errors, $\|A\star B-C\|_{0}$ . In each round, hash the non-zero entries of the difference vector $A\star B-C$ into buckets (where the number of buckets is comparable to the support size $\|A\star B-C\|_{0}$ ), and try to recover the entries in light buckets. Here it is important that the hash function is linear, i.e., $h(x)+h(y)=h(x+y)$ , so that it respects the convolution operator $\star$ . In this way, each round becomes a dense convolution problem with length comparable to $\|A\star B-C\|_{0}$ , and can be solved via FFT. This is a common technique in designing algorithms for additive problems.

A common choice for the hash function is the mod-prime hash function, which satisfies perfect linearity $h(x)+h(y)\equiv h(x+y)\pmod{p}$ . It suffers from an extra logarithmic factor in the collision probability, so using it in the iterative peeling algorithm only led to an $O(t\log^{2}N)$ algorithm. See [42, Section 2.2.2] for a detailed exposition of this algorithm; see also [73]. Another choice is to use almost linear hash families, which have smaller collision probability. However, the unpredictability of the error of the hash function led to difficulties when implementing the iterative peeling algorithm, namely we do not know where to subtract the $C$ entries. See [20, page 8] for a discussion of this challenge. In [20], they overcame this challenge for Sparse Nonnegative Convolution, but their techniques completely break down when the input vectors have possibly negative entries that might lead to cancellation, due to the errors in almost linear hashing; see discussion in [20, Section 3.3].

Now we explain how we use mod-prime hashing to obtain a faster algorithm for Sparse General Convolution in certain regimes.

Recall that in our algorithm for Sparse General Convolution, we assume the input vectors have length $N\leq t^{1.99}$ , that is, the size of the universe is sub-quadratically smaller than the number of elements we apply hash to. This perfectly meets the condition for applying the results from the large sieve inequality (i.e., $N\leq Q^{1.99}$ ). Therefore, if we pick the prime $p$ for the mod-prime hash from the range $p=\Theta(t/\log\log N)$ , we expect most buckets to have size $O(\log\log N)$ .

Then the high-level idea is to use Prony’s method [35], to recover all numbers in each bucket. This was suggested before in [20]; however, without the improved bounds for mod-prime hashing from the large sieve inequality, this idea would be too slow. Prony’s method is a way to recover a sparse polynomial with $s$ nonzero terms from $2s$ evaluations and its running time is roughly $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)$ given the evaluation results. Now the idea is to view each bucket as a sparse polynomial, and use Prony’s method to recover each bucket and we can set $s=O(\log\log N)$ .

We can compute these $2s$ evaluations for all buckets simultaneously, and each evaluation uses an FFT on array of size $O(p)$ . Overall, these evaluations take $O(sp\log p)=O(t\log t)$ time. Running Prony’s method for every bucket would roughly take time $O(t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log t)$ , so the overall running time would be $O(t\log t)$ .

The above intuition ignores some details about the running time of Prony’s method. As it turns out, the current best algorithm for Prony’s method over finite fields is only fast enough over fields with relatively small characteristic. Therefore, we will choose some finite field with small characteristic to run Prony’s method; this will make some nonzero entries in the output vector vanish, i.e., equivalent to $0$ in the finite field, but most entries will remain. Running Prony’s method over such finite fields gives a large fraction of the support of the output vector, but does not give the exact values of the coefficients. Therefore, we need to add an additional step to recover the coefficients over a large prime field $\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ where $p_{b}=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(N\Delta)$ .88 8 To generate such a prime $p_{b}=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(N\Delta)$ , the fastest known way (allowing randomization) takes $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ time, which may become a bottleneck in extreme cases where $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ is much larger than $t$ (this is the same reason why the previous work of [20] incurred extra $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ time complexity). In the main text of this paper, to simplify the presentation, we still work over $\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ and incur this extra $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ time. In Appendix A, we describe how to avoid spending $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ time by working over $\mathbb{C}$ instead.

#### Las Vegas Sparse Nonnegative Convolution.

We can adapt the above idea for Sparse General Convolution to also work for Las Vegas Sparse Nonnegative Convolution that terminates in $O(t\log t)$ time with constant probability. We briefly mention the main differences in the following.

The first difference is that, since now we are working with Sparse Nonnegative Convolution, we can apply the length reduction steps in [20]. As a result, this algorithm does not have the restriction that $N\leq t^{2-\varepsilon}$ any more.

Secondly, we use a sparsity test that can verify whether a bucket indeed has at most $s$ terms. [21] used this sparsity test in the case $s=1$ , and they suggested to use it for larger $s$ . The sparsity test uses the following result: For a nonnegative vector $V$ , $\|V\|_{0}\geq s$ if and only if the $s\times s$ matrix $A$ defined as $A_{i,j}=\sum_{k}k^{i+j}V_{k}$ is nonsingular [60]. As this result only works for nonnegative vectors, it could not be applied to Sparse General Convolution. Furthermore, via a folklore result, two distinct $s$ -sparse vectors cannot lead to the same matrix defined above. This enables us to verify whether we have correctly recovered all terms in a bucket, and make our algorithm Las Vegas.

One technicality in using this sparsity test is that the entries in the matrix $A$ become too large (cannot fit into one word) due to the $k^{i+j}$ factor when $i+j\in[2s]$ is super-constant, since $k$ can be as large as $N\leq t^{2-\varepsilon}$ and $s=O(\log\log N)$ . To resolve this issue, we need to make $k$ smaller. This is made possible by first reducing $N$ down to $t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ (in a similar way as [20], but they did this for a different purpose), and then observing that the items hashed to the $r$ -th bucket ( $r\in[p]$ ) can only belong to $\{k\in[N]:k\equiv r\pmod{p}\}$ , which allows us to treat $k$ as effectively coming from the range $[N/p]=[\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)]$ instead of from $[N]$ .

#### Sparse Nonnegative Convolution with high success probability.

To improve our Las Vegas algorithm from $O(t\log t)$ time in expectation to $O(t\log t)$ time with $1-1/t$ probability, we borrow techniques from [20] and combine with a few more ideas. The main techniques of this part do not rely on the large sieve inequality.

The main obstacle to achieving high success probability lies in the choice of the prime $p$ for the mod-prime hash. We already know that a random $p$ achieves the desired load-balancing properties with constant probability, and thus a sample of $O(\log t)$ primes will contain a good prime with $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ probability. However, in order to pick the good prime, the naive way would require running the whole procedure of FFT and bucket-recovery for all the $O(\log t)$ sampled primes, which would blow up the time complexity by a $O(\log t)$ factor. (A similar issue also occurs in a different step in the Las Vegas algorithm, namely the step of reducing $N$ down to $t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ by hashing modulo a prime $p\approx t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ : It is known that a random prime is good with $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ probability, so the naive way of boosting to high probability incurs $O(\log t/\log\log t)$ blow-up.) In order to avoid this blow-up, our goal is to use a cheaper way to test the load-balancing property of a mod-prime hash function.

As it turns out, in order to do this testing, it suffices to have the following subroutines given input $A,B\in\{0,1\}^{t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t}$ with $|\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)|\leq t$ : (1) a high-success-probability $O(t\log t)$ -time algorithm for computing the support of Sparse Convolution $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)$ and (2) an $O(t\log\log t)$ -time algorithm for estimating the support size $|\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)|$ to high accuracy with $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ success probability.99 9 $\star_{p}$ denotes cyclic convolution of array length $p$ . These subroutines do not need to be Las Vegas. See Section 5.1 for more formal statements. Intuitively, (1) is useful because we can prepare $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)$ at the beginning (correct with high probability) and every time we can tell whether $p$ is a good prime by directly hashing $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)$ modulo $p$ (instead of running FFT and bucket recovery). (2) is useful, because if the remaining support size of $A\star_{p}B$ is large, it means fewer hash collisions happened modulo $p$ .

To implement the above two subroutines, we use a random algebrization idea (similar to Indyk’s technique [52], which was also used in [20]): we replace the non-zero entries in $A,B$ by random elements in $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ for some small prime $q$ , and then convolve them over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , and use the support of this convolution as an estimate of $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)$ (or $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ ), which has one-sided error due to vanishing over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ . We end up setting prime $q$ to be $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ , and thus we need a version of Sparse Convolution algorithm over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ that runs in very fast $O(t\log q)=O(t\log\log t)$ time, matching the best known $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ convolution algorithm in the dense case (Theorem 2.8). See Section 5.1 for more formal statements. We design such an algorithm using techniques from [20], namely an almost 3-wise independent and almost linear hash family $h(x)=((\sigma x+\tau)\bmod p)\bmod m$ . As a main difference, [20] avoided using Prony’s method and replaced it with other techniques (which only apply to nonnegative convolution instead of our $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ case), while we still use Prony’s method, but with a more time-efficient implementation powered by a lot of bit-packing and table look-ups in word RAM. Another challenge happens in the bucket-recovery step: Since the field $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ is small, we do not have primitive roots of high enough order to let us recover the exponent of a term (which can be as high as $t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ ). We work around this by effectively seeing the exponent as from the range $[\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)]$ (similar to how we reduced $k$ in the Las Vegas algorithm, but it is more complicated here because of the hash family $h(x)$ ), but this requires some technicalities dealing with the errors of almost-linear hash functions.

#### Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances.

Now we very briefly describe the ideas behind the new deterministic $X+Y$ lemma (Theorem 1.5), which implies our improved deterministic Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances algorithm by the same reduction as [28].

[28] proved their slower deterministic $X+Y$ lemma using hashing based techniques, which required them to deterministically find a modulus $q$ so that the mod- $q$ hash function achieves good load-balancing property (we know that a random $q$ will have good load-balancing). To achieve this, they used the derandomized hashing idea from [29] of constructing $q$ as the product of super-constant many small prime factors, which led to large overhead.

In our work, we achieve this desired derandomization with smaller overhead than [29, 28] in the regime of interest. At a high level, we show that in our scenario there exists a small subset $\mathcal{P}$ of candidate primes in some interval $[T/2,T]$ , such that sampling a random prime from $\mathcal{P}$ achieves almost as good load-balancing as sampling a prime from the full interval $[T/2,T]$ . Hence, for fast derandomization, we only need to deterministically check all candidates in the small set $\mathcal{P}$ , instead of all primes in the interval $[T/2,T]$ .

The existence of such a small set $\mathcal{P}$ is highly nontrivial (the set $\mathcal{P}$ only depends on the input size, not the input instance itself). The load-balancing quality of set $\mathcal{P}$ for this purpose is analyzed using the large sieve inequality: Set $\mathcal{P}$ is good if the Farey fractions with denominator from $\mathcal{P}$ are well-spaced. Then, the existence of good $\mathcal{P}$ follows from the probabilistic method; this already yields a (non-uniform) deterministic algorithm with small advice. To further remove the advice, we use the method of conditional expectation to deterministically compute the advice as a preprocessing stage. For technical reasons, we need to use a composite modulus (product of constant many small primes) instead of mod prime to further speed up the running time of this preprocessing stage.

### 1.2 Further related works

To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first (direct) algorithmic application of the large sieve inequality. As for indirect algorithmic applications in the literature, the large sieve inequality and its variants have been used to show a wide range of results in analytic number theory, such as the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem and Linnik’s theorem, which in turn have been used in algorithm design (mostly for the purpose of constructing finite fields of certain desired order). For example, [9, 55, 37, 13] used the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem and [15, 34, 16] used Linnik’s theorem.

Other results from analytic number theory were also used in algorithmic applications. For instance, [65, 86, 18] explored the relationship between explicit construction of RIP matrices and the exponential sum of characters.

### 1.3 Open questions

An interesting open question is whether we can relax the $N\leq t^{2-\varepsilon}$ assumption in our $O(t\log t)$ algorithm for Sparse General Convolution (Theorem 1.3). It would also be interesting to see whether our derandomization techniques can lead to better deterministic algorithms for Sparse Nonnegative Convolution [21] and Constellation [43]; currently these deterministic algorithms rely on algebraic techniques instead of hashing-based techniques, and have many logarithmic factors in the running time. Finally, it would be interesting to explore other applications of tools from analytic number theory in algorithm design.

#### Paper organization.

In Section 2 we introduce useful notations and tools, in particular the large sieve inequality.

In Section 3 we describe a Monte Carlo $O(t\log t+t(\log\log t)^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta))$ -time Sparse General Convolution algorithm for short vectors (Theorem 1.3). In Section 4, we describe a Las Vegas algorithm for Sparse Nonnegative Convolution in expected $O(t\log t+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta))$ time. In Appendix A we remove the $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ dependency from these algorithms. In Section 5 we describe how to boost the Las Vegas algorithm to succeed with high probability, fully proving Theorem 1.1.

In Section 6 and Section 7, we give an improved deterministic algorithm for the Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances problem. These two sections can be read independently from Sections 3, 4 and 5.

## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 Notations

Let $\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{N},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}$ denote the integers, the nonnegative integers, the reals, and the complex numbers, respectively. Let $[N]=\{0,1,\dots,N-1\}$ . We use $\widetilde{O}(f)$ to denote $f\cdot(\log f)^{O(1)}$ .

We sometimes use $a\equiv_{m}b$ to denote $a\equiv b\pmod{m}$ ( $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $m$ ).

In an Abelian group $G$ , the sumset of two sets $A,B\subseteq G$ is defined as $A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B\}$ .

For a vector (an array) $A$ of length $N$ and an index $i\in[N]$ , we use $A_{i}$ or $A[i]$ to refer to the $i$ -th coordinate of $A$ . The support of $A$ is denoted as $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A)=\{i\in[N]:A[i]\neq 0\}$ . Denote $\|A\|_{0}=|\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A)|$ , $\|A\|_{\infty}=\max_{i\in[N]}|A[i]|$ , and $\|A\|_{1}=\sum_{i\in[N]}|A[i]|$ . We say a vector $A$ is $s$ -sparse if $\|A\|_{0}\leq s$ .

For two vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ we write $A\leq B$ if $A[i]\leq B[i]$ for all $i\in[N]$ . We say $A$ is a nonnegative vector if $A[i]\geq 0$ for all $i\in[N]$ .

The convolution of two length- $N$ vectors $A,B$ is defined as the vector $A\star B$ of length $2N-1$ with

$$ (A\star B)[k]=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[N]\\
i+j=k\end{subarray}}A[i]\cdot B[j]. $$

The cyclic convolution $A\star_{m}B$ is the length- $m$ vector with

$$ (A\star_{m}B)[k]=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[N]\\
i+j\equiv_{m}k\end{subarray}}A[i]\cdot B[j]. $$

We also view vectors as (univariate) polynomials: A length- $N$ vector $A$ corresponds to the polynomial $a(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}A[i]x^{i}$ . In this way, the convolution $A\star B$ corresponds to polynomial multiplication $a(x)b(x)$ , and the cyclic convolution $A\star_{m}B$ corresponds to $a(x)b(x)\bmod(x^{m}-1)$ . We say a polynomial is $s$ -sparse if it has at most $s$ non-zero terms.

We will use the following (non-standard but convenient) notations borrowed from [21]: For a vector $A$ , we define vector $\partial A$ with

$$ (\partial A)[i]=i\cdot A[i], $$

and more generally define

$$ (\partial^{d}A)[i]=i^{d}\cdot A[i]. $$

Given a hash function $h\colon[N]\to[m]$ , define the length- $m$ vector $h(A)$ by

$$ h(A)[j]=\sum_{i\in[N]:h(i)=j}A[i]. $$

### 2.2 Machine model

We work in the standard word RAM model where each word is a $w$ -bit binary integer, and standard bitwise operations and arithmetic operations (including integer multiplication and division with remainders) on words take unit time, and accessing an element by its memory address also takes unit time. The word length $w$ is chosen so that each input integer fits into one machine word, and each input integer can be indexed by an address that fits into one machine word.

For the sparse convolution problem of two length- $N$ input integer vectors $A,B$ with coefficient bound $\|A\|_{\infty},\|B\|_{\infty}\leq\Delta$ and sparsity bound $\max\{\|A\|_{0},\|B\|_{0},\|A\star B\|_{0}\}\leq t$ , we assume the word length is $w=\Omega(\log t+\log(N\Delta))$ . Note that the total input and output size is $O(t\log(N\Delta))$ bits and thus $O(t)$ words.

This assumption on word length was also used in the previous works [20, 21, 42] that we build on. The most interesting regime for our results is where $\log(N\Delta)\leq O(\log t)$ , which is satisfied in almost all combinatorial applications of sparse convolution algorithms mentioned in Section 1.

In the case of large word length $w=\omega(\log t)$ , we additionally assume that the word RAM model supports usual elementary functions such as $\sin,\cos,\ln,\exp$ on $w$ -bit precision numbers in unit time. In particular, we need this assumption to justify that two arrays of $t$ words can be convolved in the word RAM model in time complexity $O(t\log t)$ without any extra $w$ -dependent factors (which is regarded as a standard fact in the algorithmic literature, including previous works [20, 21]), because the FFT algorithm needs the $t$ -th root of unity, $\exp(2\pi\sqrt{-1}/t)$ , with $O(w)$ -bit precision. Without this assumption, we need to pay an additive $O(\log w)=O(\log\log(N\Delta))$ time complexity in word RAM to compute the root of unity. (We are not aware of any alternatives to FFT that run in $O(t\log t)$ time without this assumption. For example, the Number-Theoretic Transform requires generating a suitable $O(w)$ -bit prime, which takes time complexity growing with $w$ .)

### 2.3 Large sieve inequality and its consequences

We need several versions of the large sieve inequality from analytic number theory (see e.g. the survey of Montgomery [70]).

For $x\in\mathbb{R}$ , let $e(x)=\exp(2\pi\sqrt{-1}x)$ , which only depends on $(x\bmod 1)\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ . Let $\|x\|$ denote the distance from $x$ to the nearest integer. A basic version of the large sieve inequality is as follows.

#### Theorem 2.1 (see e.g., [53, Theorem 7.7]).

Let $\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ be a set of $\delta$ -spaced numbers $(0<\delta\leq 1/2)$ , i.e., $\|\alpha-\beta\|\geq\delta$ for all distinct $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{X}$ . Let $a_{0},\dots,a_{N-1}$ be complex numbers. Then,

$$ \sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{X}}\Big\lvert\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}a_{n}\,e(n\alpha)\Big\rvert^{2}\leq(\delta^{-1}+N)\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|a_{n}|^{2}. $$

The best possible factor on the right hand side is $(\delta^{-1}+N-1)$ [68]. For our application it is sufficient to use estimates with $C(\delta^{-1}+N)$ for a constant $C$ ; such estimates were first shown in [33].

Specializing Theorem 2.1 to the Farey fractions $\mathcal{X}=\{h/q:1\leq h\leq q\leq Q,\gcd(h,q)=1\}$ , which have spacing $\|h/q-h^{\prime}/q^{\prime}\|=\big\|\frac{hq^{\prime}-h^{\prime}q}{qq^{\prime}}\big\|\geq(qq^{\prime})^{-1}\geq Q^{-2}$ , yields the following well-known estimate (see e.g., [53, Theorem 7.11]):

$$ \sum_{1\leq q\leq Q}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq h\leq q,\\
\gcd(h,q)=1\end{subarray}}\Big\lvert\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}a_{n}\,e(nh/q)\Big\rvert^{2}\leq(Q^{2}+N)\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|a_{n}|^{2}. $$

However, Eq. 1 is not sufficient for our applications in Sections 3, 4 and 5. Instead, we need a more refined version of Eq. 1 which restricts to prime denominators, proved by Wolke [85, 84].

#### Theorem 2.2 ([84]).

Let $Q\geq 10,0<\varepsilon<1,N\leq Q^{2-\varepsilon}$ . Let $a_{0},\dots,a_{N-1}$ be complex numbers. Then,

$$ \sum_{\text{prime $p\leq Q$}}\sum_{h=1}^{p-1}\Big\lvert\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}a_{n}\,e(nh/p)\Big\rvert^{2}\leq\frac{C}{\varepsilon}\frac{Q^{2}\ln\ln Q}{\ln Q}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|a_{n}|^{2}, $$

for some absolute constant $C$ .

By restricting to prime denominators $p\leq Q$ , Eq. 2 improves over Eq. 1 by an order of $\frac{\ln\ln Q}{\ln Q}$ , which is crucial for our applications in Sections 3, 4 and 5. It is conjectured by Elliott [38] that this factor in Eq. 2 can be further improved to $\frac{1}{\ln Q}$ , matching the density of primes $p\leq Q$ . This conjecture remains open; see recent partial results by Iwaniec [54]. Balog, Rivat, and Sárközy [11] obtained a better estimate than Eq. 2 when $N\leq Q^{1+o(1)}$ .

Our derandomization result in Sections 6 and 7 is based on the following immediate corollary of Theorem 2.1. See also [69, Theorem 2.1] for a stronger statement.

#### Corollary 2.3.

Let $\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ be a finite set of real numbers. Suppose there are $0<\delta\leq\frac{1}{2}$ and $K\geq 1$ such that for all $\alpha\in\mathcal{X}$ it holds that $|\{\beta\in\mathcal{X}:\|\alpha-\beta\|<\delta\}|\leq K$ . Then,

$$ \sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{X}}\Big\lvert\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}a_{n}\,e(n\alpha)\Big\rvert^{2}\leq K(\delta^{-1}+N)\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|a_{n}|^{2}. $$

Corollary 2.3 is easily derived from Theorem 2.1 by greedily decomposing $\mathcal{X}$ into $\delta$ -spaced sets $\mathcal{X}_{1},\mathcal{X}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{X}_{K}$ and applying Theorem 2.1 separately.

Using Theorem 2.2, the following lemma follows from standard techniques (such as [11]).

#### Lemma 2.4.

Let $0<\varepsilon<1$ be a constant. Let $10\leq Q\leq N\leq Q^{2-\varepsilon}$ . Let $A\subseteq[N]$ . Then, over a uniform random prime $p\in[Q/2,Q]$ ,

$$ \sum_{a,b\in A}\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{p}[p\mid a-b]\leq|A|\cdot O\left(\frac{|A|}{Q}+\log\log N\right). $$

#### Proof.

Apply Theorem 2.2 with $a_{n}=\begin{cases}1&n\in A\\ 0&n\notin A\end{cases}$ . Then $\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|a_{n}|^{2}=|A|$ . Denote $S(\alpha)=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}a_{n}\,e(n\alpha)=\sum_{a\in A}e(a\alpha)$ , and note that $S(0)=|A|$ .

Let $\mathcal{P}$ denote the set of primes in $[Q/2,Q]$ , with size $|\mathcal{P}|=\Omega(Q/\log Q)$ by the prime number theorem.

For any integer $c$ , if $p$ does not divide $c$ , then $\{e(\frac{hc}{p})\}_{h=0}^{p-1}$ equals $\{e(\frac{i}{p})\}_{i=0}^{p-1}$ as $hc$ ranges over all values modulo $p$ . Hence $\sum_{h=0}^{p-1}e(\frac{hc}{p})=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\exp(2\pi\sqrt{-1}i/p)=0$ . If $p$ divides $c$ , then $\sum_{h=0}^{p-1}e(\frac{hc}{p})=p\cdot e(0)=p$ . In either case, we have $\mathbf{1}[p\mid c]=\frac{1}{p}\sum_{h=0}^{p-1}e(\frac{hc}{p})$ . Therefore,

$$ \sum_{a,b\in A}\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{p\in\mathcal{P}}[p\mid a-b]=\sum_{a,b\in A}\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\left[\frac{1}{p}\sum_{h=0}^{p-1}e\left(\frac{h(a-b)}{p}\right)\right]. $$

For fixed $h,p$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{a,b\in A}e\left(\frac{h(a-b)}{p}\right) \displaystyle=\sum_{a,b\in A}e\left(\frac{ha}{p}\right)e\left(-\frac{hb}{p}\right) \displaystyle=\sum_{a,b\in A}e\left(\frac{ha}{p}\right)\overline{e\left(\frac{hb}{p}\right)} \displaystyle=\left(\sum_{a\in A}e\left(\frac{ha}{p}\right)\right)\overline{\left(\sum_{a\in A}e\left(\frac{ha}{p}\right)\right)} \displaystyle=S(h/p)\overline{S(h/p)} \displaystyle=|S(h/p)|^{2}. $$

Hence, Eq. 3 can be further simplified in the following way:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{a,b\in A}\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\left[\frac{1}{p}\sum_{h=0}^{p-1}e\left(\frac{h(a-b)}{p}\right)\right] \displaystyle=\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\left[\frac{1}{p}\sum_{h=0}^{p-1}\left\lvert S(h/p)\right\rvert^{2}\right] \displaystyle\leq\frac{|A|^{2}}{Q/2}+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|Q/2}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{h=1}^{p-1}\left\lvert S\left(h/p\right)\right\rvert^{2} \displaystyle\leq\frac{|A|^{2}}{Q/2}+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|Q/2}\cdot O\Big(\frac{Q^{2}\ln\ln Q}{\ln Q}|A|\Big) \displaystyle=|A|\cdot O\left(\frac{|A|}{Q}+\ln\ln Q\right). |\mathcal{P}|=\Omega(Q/\log Q) $$

∎

#### Corollary 2.5 (Few items land in heavy buckets).

Let $m\leq N\leq m^{2-\varepsilon^{\prime}}$ , where $0<\varepsilon^{\prime}<1$ is some fixed constant, and $m$ is large enough. Let $A\subseteq[N]$ with $|A|\leq m$ . Then, for a uniformly random prime $p\in[m/\log\log m,2m/\log\log m]$ , if we define buckets $B_{k}=\{a\in A:a\equiv_{p}k\}$ for all $k\in[p]$ , then

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{p}\Big[\big|\big\{a\in A:|B_{a\bmod p}|\geq c\cdot\log\log m\big\}\big|<0.1|A|\Big]\geq 0.9, $$

where $c>0$ is some constant.

#### Proof.

We apply Lemma 2.4 with $Q:=2m/\log\log m$ , $N:=N$ and $\varepsilon:=\varepsilon^{\prime}/2$ . Assume $m$ is large enough so that $m^{2-2\varepsilon}\leq(2m/\log\log m)^{2-\varepsilon}$ , which implies $N\leq m^{2-\varepsilon^{\prime}}\leq Q^{2-\varepsilon}$ as required in Lemma 2.4. Then Lemma 2.4 states that

$$ \sum_{a,b\in A}\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{p}[p\mid a-b]\leq|A|\cdot O\left(\frac{|A|}{2m/\log\log m}+\log\log N\right)\leq O(|A|\cdot\log\log m). $$

Define a random variable $X_{a,b}$ that equals $1$ if $p\mid a-b$ and $0$ otherwise. The above equation implies that

$$ \sum_{a,b\in A}\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}[X_{a,b}]=O(|A|\cdot\log\log m). $$

By linearity of expectation, $\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}\left[\sum_{a,b\in A}X_{a,b}\right]=O(|A|\cdot\log\log m)$ . By Markov’s inequality, we know that with at least $0.9$ probability over the choice of $p$ , it holds that

$$ \sum_{a,b\in A}X_{a,b}\leq c^{\prime}\cdot|A|\cdot\log\log m $$

for some constant $c^{\prime}$ . Since the left hand side equals $\sum_{a\in A}|B_{a\bmod p}|$ , we know the number of $a\in A$ such that $|B_{a\bmod p}|\geq 10c^{\prime}\log\log m$ is at most $\frac{c^{\prime}\cdot|A|\cdot\log\log m}{10c^{\prime}\log\log m}\leq 0.1|A|$ . Hence setting $c=10c^{\prime}$ satisfies the desired statement. ∎

### 2.4 Basic algebraic tools

We will perform arithmetic operations over finite fields $\mathbb{F}_{q}=\mathbb{F}_{p^{\kappa}}$ , where an $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ element fits in a constant number of machine words. We perform such operations efficiently with the help of precomputed look-up tables. The following lemma will be applied in our sparse convolution algorithms with the parameter choice $q\leq\widetilde{O}(t^{6})$ , so that the precomputation time is sublinear in $t$ and hence not a bottleneck.

#### Lemma 2.6.

Let $q=p^{\kappa}$ where $p$ is prime and $\kappa\geq 2$ is an integer. On a machine with word length $\Omega(\log q)$ , after deterministic preprocessing in $\widetilde{O}(q^{0.04}+\kappa^{4}p^{1/2})$ time, we can perform additions, subtractions and multiplications over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ in $O(1)$ time, and multiplicative inversions in $O(\log\kappa)$ time.

#### Proof Sketch.

We need a degree- $\kappa$ monic irreducible polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ that represents $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , which can be found by a deterministic algorithm in $\widetilde{O}(\kappa^{4}p^{1/2})$ time [80].

By our machine assumption, additions, subtractions, and multiplications over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ can be done in $O(1)$ time each. If $\kappa\leq 100$ , then we can naively perform arithmetic operations on $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ -elements (viewed as $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ -polynomials of degree $<\kappa$ ) in $\kappa^{O(1)}=O(1)$ time.

Otherwise, $\kappa>100$ , and we partition each $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ -element (which we view as an $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ -polynomial of degree $<\kappa$ ) into $100$ chunks each containing $\leq\lceil\kappa/100\rceil$ terms. Each chunk has $p^{\lceil\kappa/100\rceil}\leq p^{2\kappa/100}=q^{0.02}$ possibilities. We prepare an addition table and a multiplication table for the chunks in $(q^{0.02})^{2}\cdot\kappa^{O(1)}\leq\widetilde{O}(q^{0.04})$ time. Then, addition and multiplication over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ take $O(1)$ table look-ups.

It is known that computing multiplicative inverses in $\mathbb{F}_{p^{\kappa}}$ amounts to $O(\log\kappa)$ many multiplications of degree- $\kappa$ $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ -polynomials [83, Theorem 11.10 (i)] and can hence be done in $O(\log\kappa)$ time via table look-ups (the algorithm [83, Theorem 11.10 (i)] uses recursion; in our word RAM adaptation here, once the problem size drops below a small constant fraction of $\kappa$ , we can directly look up the answers from another precomputed table instead). ∎

We need a division-free algorithm for computing the determinant:

#### Theorem 2.7 ([59]).

There is a deterministic algorithm that computes the determinant of an $n\times n$ matrix with entries from an arbitrary commutative ring in $O(n^{3}\sqrt{n}\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(n))$ ring additions, subtractions, and multiplications.

The following is a word RAM adaptation of Harvey, van der Hoeven, and Lecerf’s algorithm [49] for multiplying polynomials over small prime fields.

#### Theorem 2.8 ([28, Appendix B]).

For any prime $p$ , computing the product of two degree- $n$ polynomials from $\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$ can be solved in $O(n\log p)$ deterministic time on a machine with word length $\Omega(\log n+\log p)$ bits.

The following is an immediate corollary of Theorem 2.8 by flattening a degree- $n$ polynomial in $\mathbb{F}_{q}[x]$ to a degree- $2\kappa n$ polynomial in $\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$ .

#### Corollary 2.9.

For any $q=p^{\kappa}$ for prime $p$ , computing the product of two degree- $n$ polynomials from $\mathbb{F}_{q}[x]$ can be solved in $O(n\log q)$ deterministic time on a machine with word length $\Omega(\log n+\log q)$ bits, assuming the preprocessing in Lemma 2.6 has been performed.

#### Proof.

Given two polynomials $f,g\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[x]$ , where $f=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\sum_{j=0}^{\kappa-1}a_{i,j}x^{i}y^{j}$ and $g=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\sum_{j=0}^{\kappa-1}b_{i,j}x^{i}y^{j}$ , we create two degree- $2\kappa n$ polynomials in $\mathbb{F}_{p}[y]$ : $F=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\sum_{j=0}^{\kappa-1}a_{i,j}y^{2i\kappa+j}$ and $G=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\sum_{j=0}^{\kappa-1}b_{i,j}y^{2i\kappa+j}$ . Then we use Theorem 2.8 to compute the product $F\cdot G$ in $O(\kappa n\log p)=O(n\log q)$ time. Note that $F\cdot G$ equals

$$ \sum_{k\geq 0}\left(\sum_{i+j=k}\left(\sum_{t=0}^{\kappa-1}a_{i,t}y^{t}\right)\left(\sum_{t=0}^{\kappa-1}b_{j,t}y^{t}\right)\right)\cdot y^{2\kappa k}. $$

The $k$ -th term in the summation (ignoring the $y^{2\kappa k}$ term) modulo the monic polynomial that represents $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ is exactly the $k$ -th term in $f\cdot g$ . ∎

### 2.5 Prony’s method

We need an old algorithm for interpolating sparse polynomials, called Prony’s method [35], which was rediscovered later by Ben-Or and Tiwari [12]. See [78] for a recent survey, and expositions in [9, Section 2.7.3] and [42, Section 2.3.1]. We will need two instantiations of Prony’s method. Throughout, we use the fact that the word length of word RAM is $\Omega(\log t)$ bits, where $t$ is the input/output sparsity. Note that in our actual applications we will only apply Prony’s method with very small sparsity parameter $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ or even $O(\log\log t)$ , so the word size will be comparable to the size of the Prony instances.

In the following we first discuss the first instantiation of Prony’s method, which will be mainly used in Section 3: We work with a finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q}=\mathbb{F}_{p^{\kappa}}$ (in our applications we can assume additions and multiplications over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ take $O(1)$ time, and multiplicative inverses take $O(\log\kappa)$ time, using Lemma 2.6). We need the following algorithm for factorizing degree- $s$ polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ into distinct linear factors, which is very fast when the characteristic $p$ is much smaller than the field size $q$ . In this application, the polynomials have very small degree $s$ (think of $s=O(\log\log t)$ ), so we are less concerned about the exponent of $s^{O(1)}$ . However, it will be important that it only has $\log p$ dependency instead of $\log q$ , since in our application $q$ can be as large as $t^{O(1)}$ .

#### Lemma 2.10 ([58] or [51, Section 4.3]).

Let $q=p^{\kappa}$ . On a machine with word length $\Omega(\log q)$ , after deterministic preprocessing in $\widetilde{O}(q^{0.04}+\kappa^{4}p^{1/2})$ time: given a degree- $s$ polynomial $f\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[z]$ with $s$ distinct roots in $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , we can factorize $f$ into linear factors by a Las Vegas algorithm using expected $s^{O(1)}\cdot\log(p\kappa)$ time.

#### Proof Sketch.

The desired task can be solved by the equal degree factorization algorithm described in [51, Section 4.3], but with slight adaptation to our word RAM setting in order to achieve the claimed time complexity. We briefly describe the needed modification as follows.

[51, Proposition 3] stated that equal degree factorization on a degree- $s$ input polynomial in $\mathbb{F}_{q}[z]$ with $s$ distinct roots in $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ can be performed in expected time complexity

$$ \displaystyle O\big(\big(\mathsf{C}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}(s)\log\kappa+\mathsf{M}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}(s)\log(s\kappa p)+s\mathsf{D}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}+s\mathsf{\Phi}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}\log\kappa\big)\log s\big) \displaystyle\leq s^{O(1)}\cdot O\big(\big(\mathsf{C}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}(s)+\mathsf{M}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}(s)+\mathsf{\Phi}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}\big)\log(p\kappa)+\mathsf{D}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}\big), $$

where

- • $\mathsf{C}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}(s)$ denotes the time complexity for modular composition: compute $(f(z)\circ g(z))\bmod h(z)$ given $f,g\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[z]$ of degrees less than $s$ and monic $h\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[z]$ of degree $s$ ,

- • $\mathsf{M}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}(s)$ denotes the time complexity for multiplying two degree- $s$ polynomials in $\mathbb{F}_{q}[z]$ ,

- • $\mathsf{D}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}$ denotes the time complexity for inverting one element in $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , and

- • $\mathsf{\Phi}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}$ denotes the time complexity for evaluating the iterated Frobenius map, i.e., $a^{p^{j}}$ for given $a\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ and $0\leq j\leq\kappa$ .

In our word RAM model with word length $\Omega(\log q)$ , we assume efficient arithmetic operations over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ after the precomputation of Lemma 2.6. Then, $\mathsf{C}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}(s),\mathsf{M}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}(s)\leq s^{O(1)}$ (by brute force) and $\mathsf{D}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}=O(\log\kappa)$ (by Lemma 2.6). Thus, to establish the claimed $s^{O(1)}\cdot\log(p\kappa)$ overall time bound, it remains to show $\mathsf{\Phi}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}=O(1)$ , i.e., iterated Frobenius map can be evaluated in constant time in the word RAM after pre-computation.

To evaluate $a^{p^{j}}$ for any given $a\in\mathbb{F}_{q}=\mathbb{F}_{p^{\kappa}}$ and $0\leq j\leq\kappa$ , we write $a$ (which we view as an $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ -polynomial of degree $<\kappa$ ) into the sum of $100$ chunks each containing $\leq\lceil\kappa/100\rceil$ terms, $a=\sum_{i=1}^{100}a_{i}$ . Then, $a^{p^{j}}=\sum_{i=1}^{100}(a_{i})^{p^{j}}$ due to characteristic $p$ . Thus, after precomputing all possible values for $(a_{i})^{p^{j}}$ , we can compute $a^{p^{j}}$ using constant many table look-ups and additions, in constant total time. Since each chunk $a_{i}$ has $p^{\lceil\kappa/100\rceil}\leq p^{2\kappa/100}=q^{0.02}$ possibilities, the total time for precomputation is only $100\cdot q^{0.02}\cdot\kappa^{O(1)}\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(q)\leq O(q^{0.02+o(1)})$ , which is dominated by the precomputation time required by Lemma 2.6. ∎

A sequence $a=(a_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\in F^{\mathbb{N}}$ is called linearly recurrent (over a field $F$ ) if there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $f_{0},\dots,f_{n}\in F$ with $f_{n}\neq 0$ such that $\sum_{0\leq j\leq n}f_{j}a_{i+j}=0$ for all $i\geq 0$ , and the polynomial $f=\sum_{0\leq j\leq n}f_{j}x^{j}\in F[x]$ of degree $n$ is called a characteristic polynomial of $a$ . The minimal polynomial of $a$ is the monic polynomial of least degree that is a characteristic polynomial of $a$ , and the degree of this minimal polynomial is called the recursion order of $a$ .

#### Lemma 2.11 (Prony’s method over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ ).

Let $q=p^{\kappa}$ and let $\omega_{pm}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}$ have multiplicative order at least $d$ . Assume efficient arithmetic operations over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ after the precomputation of Lemma 2.6. The following can be done after $O(d)$ time preprocessing:

Let $f\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[x]$ be an $s$ -sparse polynomial with degree smaller than $d$ . Given the evaluation of $f(\omega_{pm}^{j})$ for all $0\leq j<2s$ , we can recover all terms of $f$ in $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)\log(p\kappa)$ expected time by a Las Vegas algorithm.

Note that this implies a zero-error algorithm (i.e., either outputs the correct answer or $\bot$ )1010 10 Throughout the paper we use $\bot$ to indicate failure. that terminates in worst case $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)\log(p\kappa)$ time (even under ill-formed input, i.e., the input evaluations do not come from an $s$ -sparse polynomial), and the probability of outputting $\bot$ under valid input is at most $2^{-\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)}$ .

#### Proof Sketch.

Here we verify that Prony’s method can be easily implemented under the claimed time budget. We refer to the exposition in [42, Section 2.3.1].

We first let $\Lambda(z)$ denote the minimal polynomial of the linear recurrence $f(\omega_{pm}^{0}),\dots,f(\omega_{pm}^{2s-1})$ , which is defined as the lowest-degree monic polynomial $\Lambda(z)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{r}\lambda_{\ell}z^{\ell}$ such that $\sum_{\ell=0}^{r}\lambda_{\ell}f(\omega_{pm}^{i+\ell})=0$ for all $0\leq i\leq 2s-1-r$ . It is known that $\Lambda(z)=\prod_{j=1}^{s^{\prime}}(z-\omega_{pm}^{e_{j}})$ if $f(x)$ has exactly $s^{\prime}$ terms and $f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{s^{\prime}}a_{j}x^{e_{j}}$ (where $a_{j}\neq 0$ , $s^{\prime}\leq s$ , and $e_{j}<d$ ).

We compute the coefficients of $\Lambda(z)$ by solving linear systems using $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)$ $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ -operations in $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)\log(\kappa)$ time. Then, we can factor $\Lambda(z)$ to obtain all roots $\omega_{pm}^{e_{j}}$ using Lemma 2.10 in $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)\cdot\log(p\kappa)$ time. We can precompute $\omega_{pm}^{i}$ for all $0\leq i<d$ in $O(d)$ time, so that we recover the support $\{e_{j}\}$ from the given $\{\omega_{pm}^{e_{j}}\}$ using table look-ups.

Finally, the equations $f(\omega_{pm}^{i})=\sum_{j=1}^{s^{\prime}}a_{j}(\omega_{pm}^{e_{j}})^{i}$ for all $0\leq i<s^{\prime}$ form a full rank linear system (a transposed Vandermonde system) with unknown coefficients $a_{1},\dots,a_{s^{\prime}}$ , which can be solved in $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s^{\prime})\log(\kappa)\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)\log(\kappa)$ time.

The algorithm described above is Las Vegas, due to the factoring step. We transform it into an algorithm with worst-case time upper bound by aborting after two times the expected running time. Then we reduce the failure probability to $2^{-\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)}$ by running $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)$ times independently. ∎

Now we state our second instantiation of Prony’s method (over small prime fields only), which will be used in Section 5. In this application we have more stringent requirement on the dependency on the sparsity $s$ . It is more complicated and more substantially relies on bit-packing and look-up tables in word RAM.

#### Lemma 2.12 (Prony’s method over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ with bit packing).

Let $t$ be a parameter. Let $\varepsilon>0$ be any small fixed constant. Let $p\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ be a prime, and $\omega\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{*}$ have multiplicative order $p-1$ . On a machine with word length $\Omega(\log t)$ bits, the following holds after $t^{0.2+o(1)}$ time preprocessing:

Let $f\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$ be an $s$ -sparse polynomial with degree smaller than $(p-1)/2$ and $p\geq s^{2}$ . Given the evaluation of $f(\omega^{j})$ for all $0\leq j<2s$ , we can recover all terms of $f$ in worst case $O\big(s\log s+(\frac{s}{\log t}+1)\cdot(\log t)^{0.1}\cdot(\log p)^{O(\sqrt{\log s})}\big)$ time by a zero-error algorithm (i.e., either outputs the correct answer or returns $\bot$ ), and the probability of outputting $\bot$ is at most $2^{-(\log t)^{0.1}}$ under valid input.

In our actual application we will choose $s=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ and $p=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ , so the second term in the running time becomes negligible. The proof of Lemma 2.12 is given in Section B.1.

### 2.6 Sparsity test

We need to test the sparsity of a polynomial given its evaluations on several points.

In [21], the authors suggested that the following lemma could be potentially useful in improving their $O(t\log t\log\log t)$ -time Las Vegas algorithm.

#### Lemma 2.13 ([60], see also [66]).

Let $V$ be a nonnegative vector. Then $\|V\|_{0}\geq s$ if and only if the following $s\times s$ matrix is non-singular: $A_{i,j}=\|\partial^{i+j}V\|_{1}$ where $0\leq i,j<s$ .

The following lemma is folklore:

#### Lemma 2.14.

Let $U,V$ be nonnegative vectors indexed on $\mathbb{N}$ where $\|U\|_{0},\|V\|_{0}<s$ . If $\|\partial^{i}U\|_{1}=\|\partial^{i}V\|_{1}$ for every $0\leq i<2(s-1)$ , then $U=V$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\{x\in\mathbb{N}:U[x]\neq 0\text{ or }V[x]\neq 0\}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}$ with $m\leq\|U\|_{0}+\|V\|_{0}\leq 2(s-1)$ . By nonnegativity of $U$ and $V$ , $\|\partial^{i}U\|_{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_{j}^{i}U[x_{j}]$ , $\|\partial^{i}V\|_{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_{j}^{i}V[x_{j}]$ , and hence $\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_{j}^{i}(U[x_{j}]-V[x_{j}])=\|\partial^{i}U\|_{1}-\|\partial^{i}V\|_{1}=0$ for all $0\leq i<m\leq 2(s-1)$ , expressed as the following linear system:

$$ \begin{bmatrix}1&1&\cdots&1\\
x_{1}&x_{2}&\cdots&x_{m}\\
&&\vdots&\\
x_{1}^{m-1}&x_{2}^{m-1}&\cdots&x_{m}^{m-1}\\
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}U[x_{1}]-V[x_{1}]\\
U[x_{2}]-V[x_{2}]\\
\vdots\\
U[x_{m}]-V[x_{m}]\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\
0\\
\vdots\\
0\end{bmatrix}. $$

The coefficient matrix is a transposed Vandermonde matrix and has nonzero determinant as $x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}$ are distinct. Hence the system is uniquely solved to get $U[x_{j}]-V[x_{j}]=0$ for all $1\leq j\leq m$ , that is, $U=V$ . ∎

### 2.7 Known lemmas for sparse convolution

#### Sumset size estimation.

We use the following lemma from [42] for estimating the sumset size up to a constant factor.

#### Lemma 2.15 (Estimating Sumset Size [42, Lemma 4.26]).

Let $\delta>0$ . There is an algorithm that, given two sets $X,Y\subseteq[N]$ computes a constant-factor approximation $t^{*}$ of $t=|X+Y|$ in time $O(t\log(\delta^{-1})+t\log\log t)$ with error probability $\delta$ . Additionally, $t^{*}\leq O(t)$ always holds.

#### Efficient error correction.

The following lemma says that, once we have a good approximation $C$ of $A\star B$ , then we can quickly correct the remaining errors and compute $A\star B$ .

#### Lemma 2.16 (see [20, Section 8]).

Let $t$ be a parameter, and $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ be a prime field for $p\leq t$ . Let $\delta\leq 1/\log t$ . Given vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{t^{2-\varepsilon}}$ and $C\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2t^{2-\varepsilon}-1}$ for $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\|A\star B-C\|_{0}\leq t/\log^{2}t$ , there is a Monte Carlo algorithm that computes $A\star B$ in time

$$ O\left((\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0}+t)\cdot\log(1/\delta)\right) $$

with error probability $\delta$ .

The same statement holds if $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ is replaced by $\mathbb{Z}$ .

A version of Lemma 2.16 over nonnegative integers was implicit in the proof from [20, Section 8]. In Section B.3 we prove Lemma 2.16 by adapting that proof to finite fields and integers.

We also need a Las Vegas version from [21].

#### Lemma 2.17 ([21, Lemma 20]).

Given vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{N}$ and $C\in\mathbb{Z}^{2N-1}$ such that $A\star B-C$ is nonnegative, and any parameter $s$ , there is a Las Vegas algorithm that runs in (worst case) time $O(\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0}+s\log s)$ and computes a vector $R$ such that for every $z\in[2N-1]$ :

- • $R[z]\leq(A\star B-C)[z]$ (always), and

- • $R[z]<(A\star B-C)[z]$ with probability at most $c\log N\cdot\frac{\|A\star B-C\|_{0}}{s}$ for some constant $c$ .

This immediately implies the following high probability version of the algorithm.

#### Corollary 2.18.

Given vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{N}$ and $C\in\mathbb{Z}^{2N-1}$ such that $A\star B-C$ is nonnegative and any parameter $m$ , there is a Las Vegas algorithm running in (worst case) time $O((\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0})\log N+m\log^{2}N(\log m+\log\log N))$ that computes a vector $R$ such that

- • $R\leq A\star B-C$ (always), and

- • when $m\geq\|A\star B-C\|_{0}$ , $R=A\star B-C$ with $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(N)$ probability.

#### Proof.

We apply Lemma 2.17 $c\log N$ times with $s=2cm\log N$ , and take the entrywise maximum of the resulting arrays.

If $m\geq\|A\star B-C\|_{0}$ , then for every $z\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B-C)$ , each invocation correctly recovers $(A\star B-C)[z]$ with probability $1-c\log N\cdot\frac{\|A\star B-C\|_{0}}{s}\geq 1/2$ . Therefore, after $O(\log N)$ invocations, all terms are recovered with high probability.

The total running time is $O(\log N\cdot((\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0})+s\log s))=O((\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0})\log N+m\log^{2}N(\log m+\log\log N))$ . ∎

#### Sparse verification.

We need the following lemma from [20] for efficiently checking whether $A\star B=C$ given sparse vectors $A,B,C$ .

#### Lemma 2.19 (Sparse Verification, slight modification of [20, Lemma 9.2]).

Given three vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{N}$ and $C\in\mathbb{Z}^{2N-1}$ with sparsity at most $t$ where $N\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ , and with $\|A\|_{\infty},\|B\|_{\infty}\leq\Delta$ , there is an $O(t+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t\log\Delta))$ time randomized algorithm checking whether $A\star B=C$ with $1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ error probability. In addition, if $A\star B=C$ , the algorithm is always correct.

#### Proof.

We follow the proof of [20, Lemma 9.2] with a slight modification. First, we verify that every entry of $C$ has absolute value at most $\Delta^{2}t$ , since otherwise $C$ cannot be equal to $A\star B$ and we can immediately reject. Pick a random prime $p\in[P,2P]$ where $P:=t(N+\log\Delta)$ , in time $O(\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log P)=O(\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t\log\Delta))$ .1111 11 This is the only difference from [20]. In [20, Lemma 9.2], the prime $p$ was from a different range, and the analysis did not rely on $p$ being random. Reduce the entries of the input vectors modulo $p$ , and view the input vectors as polynomials $A(x),B(x),C(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$ of degree lower than $2N$ . Then, pick a random $\omega\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ and evaluate $A(\omega),B(\omega),C(\omega)$ in $O(t\log_{t}N)=O(t)$ time (using bulk exponentiation [20, Lemma 4.2]), and reject if and only if $A(\omega)B(\omega)\neq C(\omega)$ .

When $A\star B-C=0$ , the algorithm always accepts, so we focus on the case where $A\star B-C\neq 0$ . Fix any entry $(A\star B-C)[i]\neq 0$ , which has absolute value bounded by $2\Delta^{2}t$ . By the same argument as in Footnote 2, the probability that $p$ divides $(A\star B-C)[i]$ is $O(\frac{\log(2\Delta^{2}t)}{P\log P})=O(1/t)$ . Thus, $A(x)B(x)-C(x)$ is a nonzero polynomial in $\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$ with $1-O(1/t)$ probability. Then, by Schwartz–Zippel lemma, $A(\omega)B(\omega)=C(\omega)$ happens with probability at most $\frac{\deg(A(x)B(x)-C(x))}{p}\leq\frac{2N}{t(N+\log\Delta)}=O(1/t)$ . The error probability can be reduced to $1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ by repeating a constant number of times. ∎

We also need a version of sparse verification over small prime fields.

#### Lemma 2.20.

Given three vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{N}$ and $C\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2N-1}$ with sparsity at most $t$ where $N\leq t^{2}$ and prime $p\leq t$ , there is an $O(t)$ time randomized algorithm checking whether $A\star B=C$ with $1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ error probability. Furthermore, if $A\star B=C$ , the algorithm is always correct.

#### Proof.

Let $\kappa$ be the smallest positive integer such that $q=p^{\kappa}\geq t^{3}$ . We work over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q}\supset\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . By Lemma 2.6, after preprocessing in $\widetilde{O}(q^{0.04}+\kappa^{4}p^{1/2})\leq\widetilde{O}((t^{3}p)^{0.04}+(\log t)^{4}p^{1/2})=o(t)$ time, we can assume additions and multiplications over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ take constant time each.

The rest of the proof is the same as the previous lemma. View vectors $A,B,C$ as polynomials $A(x),B(x),C(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]\subset\mathbb{F}_{q}[x]$ , pick a random element $\omega\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , and verify whether $A(\omega)B(\omega)=C(\omega)$ in $O(t)$ time (using bulk exponentiation [20, Lemma 4.2]). By Schwartz–Zippel lemma, the error probability is at most $2N/q=O(t^{2}/t^{3})=O(1/t)$ . The error probability can be reduced to $1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ by repeating a constant number of times. ∎

## 3 Sparse General Convolution for Short Vectors

In this section we show a Monte Carlo algorithm for Sparse General Convolution (with possibly negative coefficients) when the input vectors have short length:

See 1.3

Throughout Sections 3, 4 and 5, we make the following simplifying assumption:

#### Assumption 1.

Assume a large prime $p_{b}=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(N\Delta)$ is given.

Assumption 1 allows us to work with a large enough prime field $\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ for recovering the coefficients of $A\star B$ . We could fulfill Assumption 1 by additionally running a Las Vegas $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ -time algorithm that finds such a large prime $p_{b}$ (by rejection sampling with the AKS primality test [4]). This would add a $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ term to the claimed time complexities of the algorithms described in Sections 3, 4 and 5 (namely Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.3), which is non-negligible only when $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ is very large compared to $t$ . Later in Appendix A, we will describe how to avoid paying this extra $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ term, by modifying the algorithms described in Sections 3, 4 and 5 to work over $\mathbb{C}$ instead of over the prime field $\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ assumed in Assumption 1.

### 3.1 The algorithm

For now, we assume that we know an upper bound $t$ such that $\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|A\star B\|_{0}\leq t$ and $N<t^{2-\varepsilon}$ . Later we will relax this assumption.

Our algorithm proceeds in multiple rounds. In each round we invoke RecoveryStep with some sparsity parameter $m$ to be determined later (see pseudocode in Algorithm 1).

#### Preparation.

Let $\hat{P}_{0}=\Theta(\log^{2}t\cdot\log(t\Delta))$ , and we need the following technical definition of $P_{0}$ to get around some corner case later:

$$ P_{0}:=\begin{cases}\hat{P}_{0}&(\hat{P}_{0}\notin[t,2t^{5}])\\
2t^{5}&(\hat{P}_{0}\in[t,2t^{5}]).\end{cases} $$

Note $P_{0}\geq\Omega(\log^{2}t\cdot\log(t\Delta))$ and $\log P_{0}\leq O(\log\log t+\log\log\Delta)$ . Every time in the beginning of RecoveryStep, we sample a uniformly random prime $p_{0}\in[P_{0},2P_{0}]$ by a Las Vegas algorithm in $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(P_{0})=O(\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log t+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log\Delta)$ expected time. (This is the only place in the algorithm with the $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log\Delta$ dependency.) We say index $i\in[2N-1]$ is bad, if $(A\star B-C)[i]\neq 0$ but $(A\star B-C)[i]\equiv_{p_{0}}0$ . Since $|(A\star B-C)[i]|\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t\Delta)$ , we have $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{p_{0}}[i\text{ is bad}]\leq O(\frac{\log(t\Delta)/\log P_{0}}{P_{0}/\log P_{0}})\leq O(\frac{1}{\log^{2}t})$ for every $i\in[2N-1]$ by the prime number theorem (similarly to Footnote 2). By linearity of expectation and Markov’s inequality, with at least $0.9$ probability, there are at most $O(\|A\star B-C\|_{0}/\log^{2}t)$ bad indices.

We choose the smallest integer $\kappa\geq 1$ so that $q:=p_{0}^{\kappa}\geq 2t^{5}$ , and we will work over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ (as we will see in the next paragraph, the choice of $2t^{5}$ here is made to simplify the finding of a large order element in $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ ). If $\kappa=1$ , then we can perform additions and multiplications over $\mathbb{F}_{q}=\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}$ in $O(1)$ time because elements in $\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}$ can fit into a constant number of machine words. Otherwise, $\kappa\geq 2$ , which implies $P_{0}\leq p_{0}<2t^{5}$ and hence $P_{0}<t$ by our definition of $P_{0}$ , and we can use the precomputation of Lemma 2.6 in $\widetilde{O}(q^{0.04}+\kappa^{4}p_{0}^{1/2})\leq\widetilde{O}((4P_{0}t^{5})^{0.04}+(2P_{0})^{1/2}\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t))\leq\widetilde{O}((t^{6})^{0.04}+t^{1/2})=o(t)$ time, so that additions and multiplications over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ also take $O(1)$ time.1212 12 Note that if we did not define $P_{0}$ as $2t^{5}$ when $\hat{P}_{0}\in[t,2t^{5}]$ , this case would cost $\widetilde{O}(t^{2.5})$ time, which we cannot afford.

We now find an $\omega\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}$ with multiplicative order at least $2N$ . For every $\sigma<2N$ , there are at most $\sigma$ elements $x\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}$ such that $x^{\sigma}=1$ , so the number of elements in $\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}$ with multiplicative order smaller than $2N$ is at most $1+2+\dots+(2N-1)<2N^{2}<2t^{2(2-\varepsilon)}<q/t$ , so a randomly chosen $\omega\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}$ has multiplicative order at least $2N$ with $\geq 1-1/t$ success probability. We can verify whether the multiplicative order of an element is at least $2N$ by baby-step giant-step (see e.g., [74]) in $O(\sqrt{N}\log(N))=o(t)$ time. Therefore, the expected time to find $\omega\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}$ is $o(t)$ . We also choose an $\omega_{b}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ with multiplicative order at least $2N$ . Similarly, we can do this in $o(t)$ expected time.

We will use the results in $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ to approximately recover the support, and use results in $\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ to recover the actual coefficients on the support.

7 Define vector $A^{(i)}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}^{N}$ by $A^{(i)}[k]:=A[k]\cdot\omega_{b}^{ki}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ (and similarly define vectors $B^{(i)}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}^{N},C^{(i)}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}^{2N-1}$ ) // Recall that we assume a large prime $p_{b}$ is given as stated in Assumption 1.
8 Compute vector $\widetilde{Z}^{(i)}\leftarrow h(\widetilde{A}^{(i)})\star_{p}h(\widetilde{B}^{(i)})-h(\widetilde{C}^{(i)})$ via FFT
9 Compute vector $Z^{(i)}\leftarrow h(A^{(i)})\star_{p}h(B^{(i)})-h(C^{(i)})$ via FFT
10 Initialize $R\leftarrow(0,\dots,0)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2N-1}$
11 for $k\in[p]$ do
12 $f(x)\leftarrow\textsc{RecoverBucket}\big(\{\widetilde{Z}^{(i)}[k]\}_{i=0}^{2s},\{Z^{(i)}[k]\}_{i=0}^{2s},k\big)$ , where $f(x)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{2N-2}f_{\ell}x^{\ell}\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a polynomial in sparse representation
13 $R\leftarrow R+(f_{0},\dots,f_{2N-2})$
14 for $i\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(R)$ do
15 if $|R[i]+C[i]|>\|A\|_{\infty}\|B\|_{\infty}t$ then $R[i]\leftarrow-C[i]$
16 return $R$

```

```
Input: Values $\widetilde{v}_{0},\dots,\widetilde{v}_{2s}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , $v_{0},\dots,v_{2s}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ and $k\in[p]$
1 Output: a polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ represented as a list of non-zero coefficients. For details see Lemma 3.1
2 Use Prony’s method over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ (Lemma 2.11) with degree bound $2N/p$ , sparsity bound $s$ and $\omega_{pm}=\omega^{p}$ to obtain $g(y)=\sum_{j=1}^{s^{\prime}}b_{j}y^{e_{j}}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[y]$ such that $g((\omega^{p})^{i})=\widetilde{v}_{i}/\omega^{ki}$ for all $0\leq i\leq 2s$ .
3 if Lemma 2.11 failed to find such a $g(y)\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[y]$ then return $0$
4 Determine $a_{1},\dots,a_{s^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ such that polynomial $f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{s^{\prime}}a_{j}x^{p\cdot e_{j}+k}$ satisfies $v_{i}=f(\omega_{b}^{i})$ for all $0\leq i<s^{\prime}$ , by solving a linear system over $\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ .

6 if $a_{j}\in[\lfloor p_{b}/2\rfloor]$ then $a^{\prime}_{j}\leftarrow a_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}$

8 return $f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{s^{\prime}}a_{j}^{\prime}x^{p\cdot e_{j}+k}$
