## Appendix A Removing the $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ dependency

The only place with the $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ dependency in our sparse convolution algorithms is to pick a prime $p_{b}=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(N\Delta)$ and work with the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ and an element $\omega_{b}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ with multiplicative order at least $2N$ .

In the following, we describe how to remove the $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\Delta)$ dependency by modifying our algorithms to work over $\mathbb{C}$ instead of $\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ . We choose an element $\omega_{b}=e(1/N^{\prime})$ for some $N^{\prime}$ , where $e(x)$ denotes $\exp(2\pi\sqrt{-1}x)$ (we assume this can be done in constant time in word RAM; see the discussion at the end of Section 2.2). We pick $N^{\prime}$ to be a prime in $[4N,8N]$ . This can be done in $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ Las Vegas time with high probability (recall that at this stage of the algorithm, we have $N\leq t^{2-\varepsilon}$ for our Monte Carlo algorithm in Lemma 3.1 and $N\leq t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ for our Las Vegas algorithm in Lemma 4.1).

Most parts of our algorithms involving field $\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ are numerically stable when ported to $\mathbb{C}$ , including FFT (see e.g., [50]). An issue is linear system solving involving the transposed Vandermonde matrix $A$ , where the nodes are $\omega_{b}^{i_{1}},\ldots,\omega_{b}^{i_{s}}$ for indices $i_{1},\ldots,i_{s}$ in a bucket. If $i_{1},\ldots,i_{s}$ are close to each other, the Vandermonde matrix can be ill-conditioned. By [46, Equation (4.5)] (which is implied by an inequality from [44]), if an $s\times s$ Vandermonde matrix $A$ has nodes $c_{1},\ldots,c_{s}$ which are all $m$ -th roots of unity for some $m\geq s$ , then the matrix $2$ -norm $\|A^{-1}\|_{2}$ can be upper bounded by

$$ \max_{1\leq k\leq s}\frac{2^{s-1}\sqrt{s}}{\prod_{j\neq k}|c_{j}-c_{k}|}. $$

In our case, the nodes are $\omega_{b}^{i_{1}},\ldots,\omega_{b}^{i_{s}}$ , so the above upper bound becomes

$$ \max_{1\leq k\leq s}\frac{2^{s-1}\sqrt{s}}{\prod_{j\neq k}|\omega_{b}^{i_{j}}-\omega_{b}^{i_{k}}|}. $$

If the smallest difference between two indices $i_{j}$ and $i_{k}$ is $\delta$ (differences measured in $\mathbb{F}_{N^{\prime}}$ ), then $|\omega_{b}^{i_{j}}-\omega_{b}^{i_{k}}|$ can be lower bounded by $|e(\delta/N^{\prime})-1|$ for every $j\neq k$ . Hence, $\|A^{-1}\|_{2}$ can be upper bounded by

$$ \frac{2^{s-1}\sqrt{s}}{|e(\delta/N^{\prime})-1|^{s-1}}=\frac{2^{s-1}\sqrt{s}}{(2\sin(\delta\pi/N^{\prime}))^{s-1}}\leq\frac{2^{s-1}\sqrt{s}}{(\delta\pi/N^{\prime})^{s-1}}\leq O(N^{\prime}/\delta)^{s}. $$

Note that $\|A^{-1}\|_{\max}$ , which is the maximum absolute value of all entries of $A^{-1}$ , is upper bounded by $\|A^{-1}\|_{2}$ . We adopt the definition of condition number used in [50]: $\text{cond}(A)=\big\||A||A^{-1}|\big\|_{\infty}$ , where $|\cdot|$ means we take absolute value entrywise, and $\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ denotes the matrix $\infty$ -norm. Thus,

$$ \text{cond}(A)=\big\||A||A^{-1}|\big\|_{\infty}\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)\|A\|_{\max}\|A^{-1}\|_{\max}\leq O(N^{\prime}/\delta)^{s}. $$

We use different ways to bound $\delta$ for our Monte Carlo and Las Vegas algorithms.

- • Monte Carlo (Lemma 3.1): Instead of $\omega_{b}=e(1/N^{\prime})$ , we can pick $\omega_{b}=e(r/N^{\prime})$ for a random integer $r\in[1,N^{\prime}-1]$ , as in [46, Theorem 4.3]. As shown in [46, Theorem 4.3], with constant probability, $\delta\geq\Omega(N^{\prime}/s^{2})$ . This would imply $\text{cond}(A)\leq O(s^{2})^{s}$ . Thus, we can verify that all values of $ri_{1}\bmod{N^{\prime}},\ldots,ri_{s}\bmod{N^{\prime}}$ are well-spaced (i.e., the minimum difference is $\Omega(N^{\prime}/s^{2})$ ) before solving the linear system, and only continue if so. This decreases the probability that an index can be recovered by a constant, but it does not affect the asymptotic behavior of the algorithm.

- • Las Vegas (Lemma 4.1): In our Las Vegas algorithms, we have $N=t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ at this stage of the algorithm, and all indices in each bucket are congruent modulo some $p\geq t/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ . Therefore, we already have $\delta\geq p$ , and thus $\text{cond}(A)\leq O(N^{\prime}/p)^{s}\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)^{s}$ .

In both cases, we have $\text{cond}(A)\leq 2^{\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log t}$ .

In [50, Equation (9.23)], it was shown that the solution $\hat{x}$ to $Ax=b$ for $s\times s$ matrix $A$ given by Gaussian elimination has (setting $u=2^{-O(f)}$ in their Equation (9.23), which is defined on [50, Page 38]) $\|\hat{x}-x\|_{\infty}/\|x\|_{\infty}\leq(1+\text{cond}(A))\cdot 2^{O(s-f)}$ , where $f$ is the precision of floating points. We need $\|\hat{x}-x\|_{\infty}/\|x\|_{\infty}=1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(N\Delta)$ , as we need to recover integer vector $x$ with $\|x\|_{\infty}\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(N\Delta)$ . Using $\text{cond}(A)\leq 2^{\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log t}$ , it suffices to set $f=O(\log(N\Delta)+s+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log t)=O(\log(N\Delta)+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log t)=O(\log(N\Delta))$ , so arithmetic operations for floating point with precision $f$ can still be implemented in the word RAM model with constant cost.

One final detail to check is that, due to numerical precision errors before solving the linear system, the vector $b$ might be slightly different from its actual value. Let $b_{0}$ be the accurate vector and let $Ax_{0}=b_{0}$ , and we will have $x-x_{0}=A^{-1}(b-b_{0})$ . We want $\|x-x_{0}\|_{\infty}\ll 1$ , which holds when $\|b-b_{0}\|_{\infty}\ll 1/(s\|A^{-1}\|_{\max})$ . Note that $\|b_{0}\|_{\infty}\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t\Delta)$ , so this requires multiplicative error $\leq\frac{1}{\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t\Delta)(s\|A^{-1}\|_{\max})}$ . As the previous steps are numerically stable, this can be achieved as long as $f\geq\log(s\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(N\Delta)\|A^{-1}\|_{\max})$ , so $f=\Theta(\log(N\Delta))$ is again sufficient.

## Appendix B Missing proofs

### B.1 Proof of Lemma 2.12

We work over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ where $\log p$ is much smaller than the machine word length $w=\Omega(\log t)$ . We usually assume the input/output arrays of $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ -elements are given in compact memory representation where each machine word holds $\Theta(\frac{\log t}{\log p})$ $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ -elements.

Recall $\widetilde{O}(f)$ denotes $f\cdot(\log f)^{O(1)}$ . We need the following algebraic primitives achieved via bit packing:

#### Lemma B.1.

Let $t$ be a parameter. Assume $d,p\leq t^{o(1)}$ and $p$ is prime. On a machine with word length $w=\Omega(\log t)$ bits, all the following tasks can be done in deterministic $\widetilde{O}(\lceil d\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ time (assuming compact input/output representation), after $t^{0.2+o(1)}$ preprocessing:

- 1. Adding or subtracting two degree- $d$ polynomials $f,g\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$ .

- 2. Multiplying two degree- $d$ polynomials $f,g\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$ .

- 3. Polynomial division with remainder for polynomials $f,g\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$ of degree at most $d$ .

- 4. Expanding the product $(x-a_{1})(x-a_{2})\cdots(x-a_{d})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$ given $a_{1},\dots,a_{d}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ .

- 5. Evaluating a degree- $d$ polynomial $f\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$ on $d$ given points $a_{1},\dots,a_{d}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ .

- 6. Given distinct points $a_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ and their evaluations $b_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ for $1\leq i\leq d$ , finding the unique interpolating polynomial $f\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$ of degree $\leq d-1$ satisfying $f(a_{i})=b_{i}$ for all $1\leq i\leq d$ .

#### Proof sketch.

We choose $\kappa=\lceil\frac{0.1\log t}{\log p}\rceil$ , and note that $\kappa$ elements from $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ fit into one machine word.

For Item 1, we need to perform additions (or subtractions) on $\kappa$ consecutive $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ -elements (packed into a single machine word) in a batch in $O(1)$ time. This can be achieved by precomputing a table that contains all possible $O((p^{\kappa})^{2})\leq O(t^{0.2}p^{2})\leq t^{0.2+o(1)}$ answers in $t^{0.2+o(1)}$ time, and each time performing a table look-up in $O(1)$ time. In this way we can add/subtract two degree- $d$ polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ in $O(\lceil d/\kappa\rceil)=O(\lceil d\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ time.

For polynomial multiplication (Item 2), we work over $\mathbb{F}_{p^{\kappa}}$ , and we can preprocess the multiplication table and inverses in $\widetilde{O}((p^{\kappa})^{2})\leq t^{0.2+o(1)}$ time, so that arithmetic operations in $\mathbb{F}_{p^{\kappa}}$ can be performed by table look-ups in constant time. Then, by a simple Kronecker substitution, we can reduce the multiplication of two degree- $d$ polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ to the multiplication of two degree- $O(\lceil d/\kappa\rceil)$ polynomials over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_{p^{\kappa}}$ , which can be done using the Schönhage–Strassen FFT algorithm [79] (see e.g., [83, Section 8.3]) in $O(\lceil d/\kappa\rceil\log\lceil d/\kappa\rceil\log\log\lceil d/\kappa\rceil)=\widetilde{O}(\lceil d\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ time as desired.

For Item 3, note that polynomial division with remainder reduces via Newton iteration (see e.g., [83, Section 9.1]) to logarithmically many polynomial multiplications with exponentially increasing lengths (for length smaller than $\kappa$ we again use precomputation and table look-ups), and hence also runs in time $\widetilde{O}(\lceil d\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ via bit packing.

For Item 4, we use a simple divide-and-conquer and polynomial multiplication via Item 2. The running time satisfies the recurrence $T(d)=2T(\lceil d/2\rceil)+\widetilde{O}(\lceil d\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ . When $d\leq\kappa=\lceil\frac{0.1\log t}{\log p}\rceil$ , we can again preprocess all the possible answers in $\widetilde{O}(p^{\kappa})\leq t^{0.1+o(1)}$ time and every time look up the answer in $T(d)=O(1)$ time. Hence, the recurrence still solves to $T(d)=\widetilde{O}(\lceil d\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ .

For Item 5, note that the classic divide-and-conquer algorithm of [39] also has time complexity $T(d)=2T(\lceil d/2\rceil)+\widetilde{O}(\lceil d\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ via bit packing, and when $d\leq\kappa$ we can look up answers in $T(d)=O(1)$ time after preprocessing in $\widetilde{O}((p^{\kappa})^{2})\leq t^{0.2+o(1)}$ time.

For Item 6, we observe that the divide-and-conquer algorithm (see e.g., [83, Section 10.2]) also admits speedup via bit packing, similarly to the previous algorithms. ∎

As a standard result in computer algebra, the minimal polynomial of a sequence $a$ of recursion order $\leq n$ can be computed in $\widetilde{O}(n)$ time given its first $2n$ entries $a_{0},\dots,a_{2n-1}$ , by solving a Hankel system [71, 14, 57].

#### Lemma B.2 (Solving linear recurrences, bit packed version).

Let $t$ be a parameter. Assume $k,p\leq t^{o(1)}$ and $p$ is prime. On a machine with word length $w=\Omega(\log t)$ bits, the following holds after $t^{0.2+o(1)}$ preprocessing: Given the first $2k$ entries $a_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{2k-1}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ of a linearly recurrent sequence $a$ of recursion order $\leq k$ , there is a deterministic algorithm that computes the minimal polynomial of $a$ in $O(k\log k+k\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(k))$ time.

#### Proof sketch.

As described in [83, Section 12.3], the task of computing the minimal polynomial of a linearly recurrent sequence can be solved by an application of the Extended Euclidean algorithm. So it suffices to analyze the running time of the Extended Euclidean algorithm under bit packing.

See [83, Section 11.1] for a description of the fast Extended Euclidean algorithm. The running time is

$$ T(k)=2T(\lfloor k/2\rfloor)+O(M(k))+O(k), $$

where $M(k)$ denotes the complexity of multiplying two length- $k$ polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . Without bit packing, Eq. 23 solves to $T(k)=O(M(k)\log k)=O(k\log^{2}k)$ . Here we improve the $M(k)$ term using bit packing from Lemma B.1. In this way, the total running time Eq. 23 becomes $T(k)=2T(\lfloor k/2\rfloor)+O(\lceil k/\kappa\rceil\log\lceil k/\kappa\rceil\log\log\lceil k/\kappa\rceil)+O(k)\leq O(\frac{k\log^{2}k\log\log k}{\kappa})+O(k\log k)\leq O(\frac{k\log^{2}k\log\log k}{\log t/\log p}+k\log k)$ . ∎

Another standard result in computer algebra is that transposed Vandermonde systems can be solved in near-linear time [57, 64, 75, 17]. Here we again need to use bit packing to slightly improve the running time.

#### Lemma B.3 (Solving transposed Vandermonde systems, bit packed version).

Let $t$ be a parameter. Assume $k,p\leq t^{o(1)}$ and $p$ is prime. On a machine with word length $w=\Omega(\log t)$ bits, the following holds after $t^{0.2+o(1)}$ preprocessing: Given distinct elements $a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{k}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ and a vector $(b_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{k})$ , there is a deterministic algorithm in $O(k\log k+k\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(k))$ time that solves the transposed Vandermonde system

$$ \left[\begin{array}[]{cccc}1&1&\cdots&1\\
a_{1}&a_{2}&\cdots&a_{k}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
a_{1}^{k-1}&a_{2}^{k-1}&\cdots&a_{k}^{k-1}\\
\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}x_{1}\\
x_{2}\\
\vdots\\
x_{k}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}b_{1}\\
b_{2}\\
\vdots\\
b_{k}\end{array}\right] $$

#### Proof sketch.

Here we adapt the algorithm described by Li [64]. In [64], the first step is to expand the polynomial product $(x-a_{1})(x-a_{2})\cdots(x-a_{k})$ , which can be done using Lemma B.1. The second step is to use this result to compute $s_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_{j}^{i}$ for all $0\leq i\leq 2k-2$ , which can be done by solving a Hankel system of order $O(k)$ . The third step also involves solving a Hankel system of order $O(k)$ . It is known that solving Hankel systems can be reduced to the Extended Euclidean algorithm (see [75, Section 2]), and thus also admits the speedup via bit packing described in the proof of Lemma B.2. The last step is to evaluate a univariate degree- $k$ polynomial on $k$ points, which can be done using Lemma B.1.

In summary, the total running time is $O(\frac{k\log^{2}k\log\log k}{\log t/\log p}+k\log k)$ . ∎

We adapt the modular composition algorithm of Kedlaya and Umans [61]. Given three univariate polynomials $f,g,h\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$ of degree smaller than $d$ , Kedlaya and Umans’ algorithm computes $f(g(x))\bmod h(x)$ in $d^{1+o(1)}\cdot(\log p)^{1+o(1)}$ bit complexity (their algorithm works for more general rings as well, but here we focus on prime fields). We will shave off roughly a $\log t$ factor in word RAM with $\Omega(\log t)$ -bit words.

#### Lemma B.4 (Modular composition with bit packing).

Let $t$ be a parameter. Assume $d,p\leq t^{o(1)}$ and $p$ is prime and $p\geq d^{2}$ . On a machine with word length $w=\Omega(\log t)$ bits, the following holds after $t^{0.2+o(1)}$ preprocessing:

Given three polynomials $f,g,h\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$ of degree smaller than $d$ , one can compute $f(g(x))\bmod h(x)$ by a deterministic algorithm in $O((\frac{d}{\log t}+1)\cdot(\log p)^{O(\sqrt{\log d})})$ time.

We defer the proof of Lemma B.4 to the Section B.2.

#### Lemma B.5 (Equal-degree factorization with bit packing).

Let $t$ be a parameter. Assume $k,p\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ and $p$ is prime, and $p\geq k^{2}$ . On a machine with word length $w=\Omega(\log t)$ bits, the following holds after $t^{0.2+o(1)}$ preprocessing:

Given a degree- $k$ polynomial $f\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[z]$ with $k$ distinct roots in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , we can factorize $f$ into linear factors by a Las Vegas algorithm in expected $O((\frac{k}{\log t}+1)\cdot(\log p)^{O(\sqrt{\log k})})$ time.

#### Proof sketch.

We use the equal-degree factorization algorithm in [51, Section 4.3] with expected running time (simplified in our prime field case here) $O\big((\mathsf{C}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(k)+\mathsf{M}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(k)\log(kp)+k\mathsf{D}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}})\log(k)\big)$ 1414 14 The algorithm involves recursion on $k$ , but this does not affect the stated time bound even with bit packing, since for lower levels of the recursion we can use the same precomputation idea as in the proof of Lemma B.1., where $\mathsf{C}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(k)$ is the cost for modular composition, and $\mathsf{M}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(k)$ is the cost for polynomial multiplication, and $\mathsf{D}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ is the cost for computing inverses in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . By preprocessing in $\widetilde{O}(p)$ time, we assume $\mathsf{D}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}=O(1)$ via table look-up. By Lemma B.1, the multiplication cost is $\mathsf{M}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(k)\leq\widetilde{O}(\lceil k\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ . By Lemma B.4, the modular composition cost is $\mathsf{C}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(k)=O((\frac{k}{\log t}+1)\cdot(\log p)^{O(\sqrt{\log k})})$ . Hence, the total time is $O((\frac{k}{\log t}+1)\cdot(\log p)^{O(\sqrt{\log k})})$ . ∎

Finally we prove Lemma 2.12. See 2.12

#### Proof.

Similar to the proof of Lemma 2.11, the algorithm involves solving a linear recurrence (a Hankel system) using Lemma B.2, performing an equal-degree factorization using Lemma B.5, computing discrete logarithms by table look-ups (after precomputing the answers in $\widetilde{O}(p)\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ time), and finally solving a transposed Vandermonde system using Lemma B.3. The randomization is only used in the factorization step, and similarly to the last paragraph in the proof of Lemma 2.11, we can make the failure probability $2^{-(\log t)^{0.1}}$ by blowing up the (worst case) running time by a $(\log t)^{0.1}$ factor. The total time is thus worst case $O\big(s\log s+(\frac{s}{\log t}+1)\cdot(\log t)^{0.1}\cdot(\log p)^{O(\sqrt{\log s})}\big)$ . ∎

### B.2 Proof of Lemma B.4

We assume the following setup throughout this section: Let $t$ be a parameter. Assume $d,p\leq t^{o(1)}$ and $p$ is prime. We assume a machine with word length $w=\Omega(\log t)$ bits and allow $o(t)$ preprocessing to compute look-up tables (we actually only need $t^{0.2+o(1)}$ precomputation time).

We need a few more word RAM primitives.

#### Lemma B.6 (Transposing a matrix).

Suppose an $n\times m$ matrix with $b$ -bit elements is stored in row-major order in compact representation. Then we can transpose the matrix (i.e., store it in column-major order) in $O((\frac{nmb}{\log t}+1)\cdot\log n)$ time. Alternatively it can also be done in $O((\frac{nmb}{\log t}+1)\cdot\log m)$ time.

#### Proof sketch.

This is done by a simple divide-and-conquer algorithm with recursion depth $\log n$ , similar to [81, Lemma 9]. The input matrix is represented as $n$ length- $m$ lists, and each of these lists corresponds to a leaf of the recursion tree. Then, at each internal node of the recursion tree, we interleave the lists returned by its two child nodes. Note that interleaving two lists can be done with time complexity linear in the number of words in their compact representations, using word operations (which can be replaced by table look-ups after preprocessing).

To get dependency $\log m$ instead of $\log n$ , simply change the roles of $n$ and $m$ and do the procedure described above in the reverse order. ∎

#### Lemma B.7 (Batch small table look-up).

Given a compact array $(a_{0},\dots,a_{n-1})$ where each $a_{i}$ has $b$ bits, and a compact list of indices $(i_{0},\dots,i_{N-1})\in[n]^{N}$ , one can produce the look-up results $(a_{i_{0}},a_{i_{1}},\dots,a_{i_{N-1}})$ in time

$$ O\Big(\Big\lceil\frac{(n+N)(\log n+\log N+b)}{\log t}\Big\rceil\cdot\log N\Big). $$

#### Proof.

We assume $b+\log n+\log N\leq 0.1\log t$ ; otherwise the brute force algorithm runs in $O((n+N)\lceil\frac{b}{\log t}\rceil)$ time, which already satisfies the claimed bound.

We perform the following steps:

- • We augment each query index $i_{j}$ into a query pair $(i_{j},j)$ (with description length $\log n+\log N+O(1)$ bits), and obtain the compact list of the pairs $(i_{0},0),\dots,(i_{N-1},N-1)$ . Then, we sort these query pairs in increasing order of $i_{j}$ (the first coordinate). The initial augmentation step can be done in linear time in the number of resulting words, $O(\lceil\frac{N(\log n+\log N)}{\log t}\rceil)$ , as follows: given $j\in[N]$ and a sequence of $k=\lfloor\frac{0.1\log t}{\log n}\rfloor$ indices $(i^{\prime}_{0},\dots,i^{\prime}_{k-1})$ (whose total description length is at most $\lceil\log N\rceil+0.1\log t\leq 0.2\log t+O(1)$ bits), we can use table look-ups (after pre-computation in $t^{0.2+o(1)}$ time) to obtain the compact list $((i^{\prime}_{0},j),(i^{\prime}_{1},j+1),(i^{\prime}_{2},j+2),\dots,(i^{\prime}_{k-1},j+k-1))$ . The entire compact list $(i_{0},0),\dots,(i_{N-1},N-1)$ can be obtained by repeating this look-up operation and concatenation. The sorting step can be done using packed merge sort (e.g., [6]): in the merging step of merge sort, we use $O(1)$ word operations (using pre-computed look-up tables) to implement $\Theta(\frac{\log t}{\log n+\log N})$ pointer advancements (involving $\Theta(\log t)$ bits of data). The time complexity is the number of words times a logarithmic factor (the number of recursive levels in merge sort), which is at most $O(\lceil\frac{N(\log n+\log N)}{\log t}\rceil\cdot\log N)$ .

- • Then, we augment each query pair $(i_{j},j)$ into a triple $(i_{j},j,0^{b})$ , where $0^{b}$ is a $b$ -bit placeholder which is supposed to be replaced by the look-up result $a_{i_{j}}$ later. Similarly, the time complexity is linear in the number of resulting words in the augmented query array, $O(\lceil\frac{N(\log n+\log N+b)}{\log t}\rceil)$ .

- • Then, we run a two-pointer scan on the data array $(a_{0},\dots,a_{n-1})$ and the query array, which can fill in all look-up results in linear time in the total number of words. In more detail: suppose the pointer on the data array currently points to a word $(a_{s},a_{s+1},\dots,a_{s+\ell-1})$ (where $\ell\cdot b=\Theta(\log t)$ ), and the pointer on the query array points to a word $((i^{\prime}_{t},\cdot,\cdot),\dots,(i^{\prime}_{t+r-1},\cdot,\cdot))$ (where $r\cdot(\log n+\log N+b)=\Theta(\log t)$ ). If the interval $[i^{\prime}_{t},i^{\prime}_{t+r-1}]$ has non-empty intersection with $[s,s+\ell-1]$ , then we replace all placeholders associated with query indices in $[i^{\prime}_{t},i^{\prime}_{t+r-1}]\cap[s,s+\ell-1]$ by the corresponding $b$ -bit answers, which can be implemented in $O(1)$ time given these two words by table look-up. Then, we advance the pointer on the data array if $s+\ell-1\leq i^{\prime}_{t+r-1}$ , or advance the pointer on the query array otherwise. The time complexity is linear in the number of words in the data array and the query array, $O(\lceil\frac{N(\log n+\log N+b)+nb}{\log t}\rceil)$ .

- • Finally, we sort the query array back to its original order in the input (i.e., sorted by the second coordinate in the triple), remove the augmented indices (namely the first and the second coordinates in the triple) while keeping the $b$ -bit answer, and repack the answers into a compact list. Similarly, this step has time complexity $O(\lceil\frac{N(\log n+\log N+b)}{\log t}\rceil\log N)$ .

Thus, the overall time complexity can be loosely upper-bounded by the claimed bound. ∎

In [61, Theorem 3.1], the modular composition problem is reduced to the Multivariate Multipoint Evaluation (MME) problem. Then, [61, Corollary 4.3] gave an efficient algorithm for MME. Here, we need to speed up both the reduction and the MME algorithm via bit packing.

#### Reduction to MME.

The MME problem with parameters $d,m,N$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ is defined as follows: Given $f(x_{0},\dots,x_{m-1})$ in $\mathbb{F}_{p}[x_{0},\dots,x_{m-1}]$ with individual degrees at most $d-1$ , and evaluation points $\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{N-1}$ in $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ , output $f(\alpha_{i})$ for $i=0,1,\dots,N-1$ .

In our word RAM setting with word length $w=\Omega(\log t)$ bits, we assume inputs and outputs are arrays of $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ elements stored in compact representation. More precisely, in the MME problem, the input polynomial $f\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x_{0},\dots,x_{m-1}]$ is described by $d^{m}$ coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , which are flattened into a one-dimensional sequence where the $x_{0}^{a_{0}}x_{1}^{a_{1}}\dots x_{m-1}^{a_{m-1}}$ -term’s coefficient ( $0\leq a_{j}\leq d-1$ ) is the $\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a_{j}d^{j}$ -th element, and this one-dimensional sequence is packed into $\Omega(\log t)$ -bit words in the usual way. Each evaluation point in the MME instance is stored as a chunk of $m$ $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ -elements, and the list of evaluation points is represented as the concatenation of these chunks, packed into $\Omega(\log t)$ -bit words.

#### Lemma B.8 (Direct adaptation of [61, Theorem 3.1]).

Given $f(X),g(X),h(X)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[X]$ with degrees at most $N-1$ (where $h(X)$ is monic), there is, for every $2\leq d_{0}<N$ , an algorithm that outputs $f(g(X))\bmod h(X)$ in

$$ O\Big(\big(1+N\cdot\tfrac{\log p}{\log t}\big)\cdot d_{0}\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)\Big) $$

time plus one invocation of MME (with compact input/output representation) with parameters $d_{0},m=\lceil\log_{d_{0}}N\rceil,N^{\prime}=Nmd_{0}$ , provided $N^{\prime}\leq p$ .

#### Proof.

This lemma follows from essentially the same proof as the original [61, Theorem 3.1], with every step implemented using bit packing:

- • Step 1: Define $f^{\prime}=\psi_{d_{0},m}(f)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[Y_{0},Y_{1},\dots,Y_{m-1}]$ , where $\psi_{d_{0},m}$ maps each monomial $X^{a}$ to the monomial $Y_{0}^{a_{0}}Y_{1}^{a_{1}}\cdots Y_{m-1}^{a_{m-1}}$ where $a$ is written in base- $d_{0}$ as $a=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a_{j}d_{0}^{j}$ . By our convention of how multivariate polynomials are stored, the memory representation of the result $f^{\prime}$ is actually the same as the memory representation of the input univariate polynomial $f$ , so this step does not require actual computation.

- • Step 2: Compute $g_{j}:=g(X)^{d_{0}^{j}}\bmod h(X)$ for all $j=0,1,\dots,{m}-1$ . For each $j$ this takes $O(\log d_{0}^{j})\cdot\widetilde{O}(\lceil N\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ time using Lemma B.1 and repeated squaring. Over all $0\leq j<{m}$ it takes $\widetilde{O}(\lceil N\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil{m}^{2}\log d_{0})$ time in total. Note that $a(X):=f^{\prime}(g_{0}(X),g_{1}(X),\dots,g_{m-1}(X))$ is a polynomial of degree smaller than $N^{\prime}$ which satisfies $a(X)\bmod h(X)=f(g(X))\bmod h(X)$ . The following steps aim to compute $a(X)$ .

- • Step 3: Let $\beta_{0},\dots,\beta_{N^{\prime}-1}$ be distinct points in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ (which exist by the assumption $N^{\prime}\leq p$ ). Compute $\alpha_{j,k}:=g_{j}(\beta_{k})$ for all $j\in[{m}],k\in[N^{\prime}]$ using fast univariate multipoint evaluation. By Lemma B.1, this takes $\widetilde{O}({m}\cdot\lceil N^{\prime}\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ time in total (recalling $\deg(g_{j})<N\leq N^{\prime}$ ). The results $\alpha_{j,k}$ are stored as ${m}$ compact arrays each of $N^{\prime}\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}+O(1)$ words.

- • Step 4: Compute $f^{\prime}(\alpha_{0,k},\alpha_{1,k},\dots,\alpha_{{m}-1,k})$ for all $k\in[N^{\prime}]$ . This involves solving MME for $f^{\prime}$ on $N^{\prime}$ evaluation points. In order to invoke the MME algorithm, we need to first use Lemma B.6 to transpose the representation of $\{\alpha_{j,k}\}_{j\in[{m}],k\in[N^{\prime}]}$ so that the coordinates $\alpha_{0,k},\alpha_{1,k},\dots,\alpha_{{m}-1,k}$ of each evaluation point are stored consecutively in the same word. By Lemma B.6, the time to do the transposition is $O((\frac{mN^{\prime}\log p}{\log t}+1)\cdot\log m)=\widetilde{O}({m}\cdot\lceil N^{\prime}\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ . By definition of $\alpha_{j,k}$ and $a(X)$ , the answers computed in this step are precisely the values $a(\beta_{0}),\dots,a(\beta_{N^{\prime}-1})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ .

- • Step 5: Interpolate to recover $a(X)$ (which has degree smaller than $N^{\prime}$ ) from the evaluations $a(\beta_{0}),\dots,a(\beta_{N^{\prime}-1})$ computed in the previous step. We use Lemma B.1 to do this in $\widetilde{O}(\lceil N^{\prime}\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ time.

- • Step 6: Output the $a(X)\bmod h(X)$ as the desired answer. We use Lemma B.1 to do this in $\widetilde{O}(\lceil N^{\prime}\cdot\frac{\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ time.

Using $m=\lceil\log_{d_{0}}N\rceil$ and $N^{\prime}=Nmd_{0}$ , the total time complexity can be bounded by $O\Big(\big(1+N\cdot\tfrac{\log p}{\log t}\big)\cdot d_{0}\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)\Big)$ as claimed. ∎

#### The MME algorithm.

We first describe [61]’s MME algorithm for small prime fields:

#### Lemma B.9 (Direct adaptation of [61, Theorem 4.1]).

Given a polynomial $f(X_{0},\dots,X_{m-1})\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}[X_{0},\dots,X_{m-1}]$ ( $p_{0}\leq t^{o(1)}$ prime) with degree at most $d_{0}-1$ in each variable, and $\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{N-1}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}^{m}$ , there is a deterministic algorithm that outputs $f(\alpha_{i})$ for $i=0,\dots,N-1$ in

$$ O\Big(\Big\lceil\frac{N+p_{0}^{m}+d_{0}^{m}}{\log t}\Big\rceil\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(m,d_{0},p_{0},\log N)\Big). $$

time.

#### Proof.

We follow the original proof of [61, Theorem 4.1] with minor modifications. The idea is to first evaluate $f(\alpha)$ on all points $\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}^{m}$ via a recursive approach, and then use table look-ups to obtain the desired answers. Now we describe our bit-packed implementation in more detail.

Let $k\geq 0$ be the largest integer such that $k\leq m$ and $\max\{p_{0}^{k},d_{0}^{k}\}\lceil\log p_{0}\rceil\leq 0.1\log t$ . Recall that we allow $o(t)$ time pre-computation at the very beginning. We pre-compute a look-up table (one for every possible pair of $p_{0},d_{0}\leq 0.1\log t$ ) that, given a polynomial $g\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}[X_{0},\dots,X_{k-1}]$ with individual degree at most $d_{0}-1$ , returns all evaluations $\{g(\alpha)\}_{\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}^{k}}$ . The polynomial $g$ and the list of evaluations $\{g(\alpha)\}_{\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}^{k}}$ have description lengths $d_{0}^{k}\lceil\log p_{0}\rceil,p_{0}^{k}\lceil\log p_{0}\rceil\leq 0.1\log t$ bits respectively, and can be packed into a machine word. The total number of possibilities for the polynomial $g$ is $p_{0}^{d_{0}^{k}}\leq t^{0.1}$ , so the look-up table has at most $t^{0.1}$ entries and can be pre-computed in $\widetilde{O}(t^{0.1})$ time.

Consider the following recursive algorithm which takes as input an $m^{\prime}$ -variate $(m^{\prime}\geq k)$ polynomial $g\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}[X_{0},\dots,X_{m^{\prime}-1}]$ with individual degree at most $d_{0}-1$ (in the outermost level, $g=f$ and $m^{\prime}=m$ ), and outputs a compact list of evaluations $g(\alpha)$ for all $\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}^{m^{\prime}}$ . For convenience, the output is organized as $p_{0}^{m^{\prime}-k}$ machine words, each of which is associated with $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}^{m^{\prime}-k}$ and holds the list of evaluations $\{g(\gamma,\beta)\}_{\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}^{k}}$ .

- • If $m^{\prime}=k$ , then directly look up the answers from the look-up table in constant time.

- • If $m^{\prime}\geq k+1$ , then write $g=\sum_{j=0}^{d_{0}-1}g_{j}(X_{0},\dots,X_{m^{\prime}-2})\cdot X_{m^{\prime}-1}^{j}$ . Recursively solve $d_{0}$ subproblems on the $(m^{\prime}-1)$ -variate polynomials $g_{j}$ . Then, use the answers to the subproblems to compute the evaluation results, $g(\alpha)=\sum_{j=0}^{d_{0}-1}g_{j}(\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{m^{\prime}-2})\cdot\alpha_{m^{\prime}-1}^{j}$ . More precisely, denoting the result of the $j$ -th subproblem ( $j\in[d_{0}]$ ) as a vector $R_{j}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}^{(p_{0}^{m^{\prime}-1})}$ , represented as $p_{0}^{m^{\prime}-1-k}$ words, we need to output the vector (which is the concatenation of $p_{0}$ vectors)

$$ \big(g(\alpha)\big)_{\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}^{m^{\prime}}}=\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{d_{0}-1}0^{j}R_{j},\sum_{j=0}^{d_{0}-1}1^{j}R_{j},\dots,\sum_{j=0}^{d_{0}-1}(p_{0}-1)^{j}R_{j}\Big). $$

This involves $p_{0}d_{0}$ many additions and scalar multiplications of vectors in $\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}^{(p_{0}^{m^{\prime}-1})}$ , each of which can be implemented in $O(p_{0}^{m^{\prime}-1-k})$ time using word operations (after pre-computing the needed look-up tables in $\widetilde{O}((p_{0}^{p_{0}^{k}})^{2})=\widetilde{O}(t^{0.2})$ time). In total there are $d_{0}^{m-m^{\prime}}$ subproblems at level $m^{\prime}$ in the recursion tree, so the total time complexity is

$$ \sum_{m^{\prime}=k}^{m}O(d_{0}^{m-m^{\prime}}\cdot p_{0}d_{0}\cdot p_{0}^{m^{\prime}-1-k})=O\big(m\cdot(\max\{p_{0},d_{0}\})^{m+1-k}\big). $$

Since $k\leq m^{\prime}-1\leq m-1$ , the definition of $k$ implies $\max\{p_{0},d_{0}\}^{k+1}\lceil\log p_{0}\rceil\geq 0.1\log t$ , so the time complexity can be bounded by

$$ O\Big(m\cdot\frac{(\max\{p_{0},d_{0}\})^{m+2}}{\log t}\Big). $$

Having computed $f(\alpha)$ for all $\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}^{m}$ , we use the batch table look-up algorithm from Lemma B.7 to output the list of $f(\alpha_{i}),i=0,1,\dots,N-1$ . The parameters for Lemma B.7 are $b=\lceil\log p_{0}\rceil,N=N$ , and $n=p_{0}^{m}$ (we convert $\mathbb{F}_{p_{0}}^{m}$ into an integer in $[p_{0}^{m}]$ in the natural way), and its time complexity is

$$ O\Big(\Big\lceil\frac{(N+n)(\log n+\log N+b)}{\log t}\Big\rceil\cdot\log N\Big)=O\Big(\frac{(N+p_{0}^{m})\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(Np_{0}^{m})}{\log t}+\log N\Big). $$

Therefore, the total time complexity of the two parts can be bounded by

$$ O\Big(\Big\lceil\frac{N+p_{0}^{m}+d_{0}^{m}}{\log t}\Big\rceil\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(m,d_{0},p_{0},\log N)\Big). $$

∎

#### Lemma B.10 (Direct adaptation of [61, Theorem 4.2, Corollary 4.3]).

MME over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ with parameters $d_{0},m,N$ can be solved in

$$ O\Big(\Big(\frac{N+d_{0}^{m}}{\log t}+1\Big)\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\big((32m\log p)^{m}d_{0}\log N\big)\Big) $$

time.

#### Proof.

We closely follow the proof of [61, Theorem 4.2] and adapt it to our bit-packed setting. The algorithm consists of the following steps:

- 1. Lift the polynomial $f\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[X_{0},\dots,X_{m-1}]$ to $\widetilde{f}\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{0},\dots,X_{m-1}]$ , and lift the evaluation points $\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ to $\widetilde{\alpha}_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}$ , by identifying $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ with $\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}\subset\mathbb{Z}$ . This type conversion does not incur any actual steps in the algorithm. Note that $\widetilde{f}(\widetilde{\alpha}_{i})\in\mathbb{Z}$ is at most $d_{0}^{m}(p-1)^{md_{0}}$ .

- 2. Compute the primes $p_{1},\dots,p_{k}$ less than or equal to

$$ \ell:=16\log(d_{0}^{m}(p-1)^{md_{0}}), $$

and note that $k\leq\ell$ . (It is shown in [61, Lemma 2.4] that the product $p_{1}\cdots p_{k}$ is greater than $d_{0}^{m}(p-1)^{md_{0}}$ .)

- 3. For $h=1,\dots,k$ , compute the reduction $f_{h}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{h}}[X_{0},\dots,X_{m-1}]$ of $\widetilde{f}$ modulo $p_{h}$ . For $h=1,\dots,k$ and $i=0,\dots,N-1$ , compute the reduction $\alpha_{h,i}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{h}}^{m}$ of $\widetilde{\alpha}_{i}$ modulo $p_{h}$ . Recall that $\widetilde{f}$ and $\{\widetilde{\alpha}_{i}\}_{i}$ are stored as compact lists of $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ elements, and we need to reduce them modulo $p_{h}$ , resulting in lists of $\mathbb{F}_{p_{h}}$ elements (which are more compactly represented since $p_{h}$ is much smaller than $p$ ). We implement this step by pre-computing look-up tables (one for each possible $p_{h}$ ), so that given $(x_{1},\dots,x_{s})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{s}$ (where $s\cdot\log p=\Theta(\log t)$ ), we can obtain $(x_{1}\bmod p_{h},\dots,x_{s}\bmod p_{h})$ in constant time. The total time complexity to perform the reductions is linear in the total number of words processed, $O(k\cdot\lceil\frac{(d_{0}^{m}+Nm)\cdot\log p}{\log t}\rceil)$ .

- 4. For $h=1,2,\dots,k$ , invoke Lemma B.9 to compute $f_{h}(\alpha_{h,i})$ for all $i\in[N]$ . The total time complexity of invoking Lemma B.9 is

$$ \sum_{h=1}^{k}O\Big(\Big\lceil\frac{N+p_{h}^{m}+d_{0}^{m}}{\log t}\Big\rceil\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(m,d_{0},p_{h},\log N)\Big). $$

Using $p_{h},k,d_{0},m\leq\ell$ , we can further bound the time complexity by

$$ O\Big(\Big(\frac{N+\ell^{m}}{\log t}+1\Big)\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(\ell\log N)\Big). $$

- 5. For $i\in[N]$ , recover $\widetilde{f}(\alpha_{i})\in\mathbb{Z}$ as the unique integer in $[p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{k}]$ congruent to $f_{h}(\alpha_{h,i})$ modulo $p_{h}$ for $h=1,\dots,k$ , and return $\widetilde{f}(\alpha_{i})\bmod p$ as the answer $f(\alpha_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . Before doing this, we first need to transpose the results obtained from the previous step, so that $f_{1}(\alpha_{1,i}),f_{2}(\alpha_{2,i}),\dots,f_{k}(\alpha_{k,i})$ are compactly and consecutively stored in memory, using Lemma B.6 in time $O((\frac{Nk\log\ell}{\log t}+1)\log k)$ . Then, we perform Chinese remaindering for all $i\in[N]$ in a bit-packed fashion using pre-computed look-up tables, so that given a list of $s$ tuples $((x_{1}^{(1)},\dots,x_{k}^{(1)}),\dots,(x_{1}^{(s)},\dots,x_{k}^{(s)}))\in(\mathbb{F}_{p_{1}}\times\dots\times\mathbb{F}_{p_{k}})^{s}$ (where $s\cdot k\cdot\log\ell=\Theta(\log t)$ ), we can look up the Chinese remaindering results for all $s$ tuples in constant time. The total time for performing the Chinese remaindering is thus $O(\frac{Nk\log\ell}{\log t}+1)$ .

Using $k,d_{0},m\leq\ell$ , the total time complexity of all steps can be loosely bounded by

$$ O\Big(\Big(\frac{N+\ell^{m}}{\log t}+1\Big)\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(\ell\log N)\Big). $$

Since $\ell=16\log(d_{0}^{m}(p-1)^{md_{0}})=16m(\log d_{0}+d_{0}\log(p-1))\leq 32md_{0}\log p$ , we can further bound the time complexity by

$$ O\Big(\Big(\frac{N+d_{0}^{m}}{\log t}+1\Big)\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\big((32m\log p)^{m}d_{0}\log N\big)\Big). $$

∎

#### Proof of Lemma B.4.

We first invoke Lemma B.8 with $N=d$ by choosing $d_{0}=2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log d})}$ . Then we reduce to an MME problem over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ with parameters $d_{0}$ and $m=\lceil\log_{d_{0}}d\rceil=\Theta(\sqrt{\log d})$ and $N^{\prime}=Nmd_{0}\leq O(d\,2^{O(\sqrt{\log d})})$ (we have $N^{\prime}\leq p$ since $p\geq d^{2}$ by assumption). By Lemma B.8, the time complexity of this reduction is

$$ O\Big(\Big(1+\frac{d\log p}{\log t}\Big)\cdot d_{0}\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(d)\Big). $$

We solve this MME problem using Lemma B.10 in time

$$ \displaystyle O\Big(\Big(\frac{d+d_{0}^{m}}{\log t}+1\Big)\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\big((32m\log p)^{m}d_{0}\log d\big)\Big) \displaystyle=\  \displaystyle O\Big(\Big(\frac{d}{\log t}+1\Big)\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\big((32m\log p)^{m}d_{0}\log d\big)\Big) d_{0}^{m}\leq dd_{0} \displaystyle=\  \displaystyle O\Big(\Big(\frac{d}{\log t}+1\Big)\cdot(\log p)^{O(\sqrt{\log d})}\Big), m=\Theta(\sqrt{\log d}) d_{0}=2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log d})} p\geq d^{2} $$

which dominates the total time complexity. ∎

### B.3 Proof of Lemma 2.16

We restate Lemma 2.16 below for convenience.

See 2.16

The rest of this section proves Lemma 2.16.

We first consider the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ case. Precompute $z^{-1}$ for $z\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{*}$ in $O(p)\leq O(t)$ time using [20, Lemma 4.3]. Let $\kappa$ be the smallest integer such that $p^{\kappa}>2t^{2-\varepsilon}$ . Let $q=p^{\kappa}$ , and let $\omega\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ be an element with multiplicative order at least $2t^{2-\varepsilon}$ . Recalling the discussion in Section 3.1, such an element $\omega$ can be found in $o(t)$ time. Compute $\omega^{-1}$ in $O(\log q)\leq O(\log t)$ time and then precompute $\omega^{-i}$ for all $i\in[t]$ in $O(t)$ time.

#### Claim B.11.

If $\|A\star B-C\|_{0}\leq 2^{-1.5^{\ell}}\cdot t/\log^{2}t$ for some integer $\ell\geq 0$ , then there is a Monte Carlo algorithm that computes $R$ such that $\|A\star B-C-R\|_{0}\leq 2^{-1.5^{\ell+1}}\cdot t/\log^{2}t$ with error probability $\delta^{\prime}$ in time

$$ O\left((\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0}+t)\cdot(1+\log(1/\delta^{\prime})/1.5^{\ell})\right). $$

#### Proof.

We repeat the following round $\lceil\log(1/\delta^{\prime})/(0.5\cdot 1.5^{\ell})\rceil$ times.

In each round, we pick a random prime $r\in[c_{r}t/\log t,2c_{r}t/\log t]$ for some sufficiently large constant $c_{r}$ (this can be done in worst-case $O(t)$ time by precomputing all primes in the range and sampling from them), and define $h(x):=x\bmod{r}$ . Define $\widetilde{A}$ as $\widetilde{A}[i]=\omega^{i}\cdot A[i]$ , and similarly define $\widetilde{B}$ and $\widetilde{C}$ . We use FFT to compute $Z:=h(A)\star_{r}h(B)-h(C)$ and $\widetilde{Z}:=h(\widetilde{A})\star_{r}h(\widetilde{B})-h(\widetilde{C})$ in $O(r\log r)=O(t)$ time.

Among all rounds, we keep $r,Z,\widetilde{Z}$ for which $\|Z\|_{0}$ is maximized. Then we do the following for this triple $(r,Z,\widetilde{Z})$ .

Compute $\omega^{r}$ in $O(\log r)\leq O(\log t)$ time, and then precompute a discrete log hash table, $\text{Log}[\omega^{ri}]=ri$ for all integers $0\leq i<2t^{2-\varepsilon}/r$ , in $O(t^{2-\varepsilon}/r)=o(t)$ time. For every $i\in[r]$ where $Z[i]\neq 0$ , we compute $(\widetilde{Z}[i]/Z[i])\cdot\omega^{-i}$ in $O(1)$ time using the precomputed $\omega^{-i}$ and $z^{-1}$ for all $z\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{*}$ , and then check in $O(1)$ time whether $(\widetilde{Z}[i]/Z[i])\cdot\omega^{-i}$ can be found in the discrete log table; if so, we add $Z[i]$ to $R[i+\text{Log}[(\widetilde{Z}[i]/Z[i])\cdot\omega^{-i}]]$ . At the end, we update $C\leftarrow C+R$ .

The idea is that, if some $0\leq j<2t^{2-\varepsilon}$ with nonzero $(A\star B-C)[j]$ is in a bucket by itself, then $Z[h(j)]=(A\star B-C)[j]$ and $\widetilde{Z}[h(j)]=\omega^{j}\cdot(A\star B-C)[j]$ . Therefore, we can find $(\widetilde{Z}[h(j)]/Z[h(j)])\cdot\omega^{-h(j)}=\omega^{j-(j\bmod{r})}$ from the discrete log table, and successfully add $Z[h(j)]=(A\star B-C)[j]$ to $R[(j\bmod{r})+\text{Log}[\omega^{j-(j\bmod{r})}]]=R[j]$ .

We consider the expected size of $\|A\star B-C-R\|_{0}$ for any particular round.

For every $j\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B-C)$ , the probability that it collides with any other element with respect to the hash function $h$ is bounded by $O(\|A\star B-C\|_{0}\cdot\frac{\log t}{c_{r}t/\log t})\leq\|A\star B-C\|_{0}\cdot\frac{\log^{2}t}{4t}$ by picking sufficiently large $c_{r}$ . Therefore, in expectation, the number of non-isolated elements is $\leq\|A\star B-C\|_{0}^{2}\cdot\frac{\log^{2}t}{4t}\leq 2^{-2\cdot 1.5^{\ell}}\cdot\frac{t}{4\log^{2}t}$ . Therefore, for any particular round, the probability that the number of non-isolated elements exceeds $2^{-1.5\cdot 1.5^{\ell}}\cdot\frac{t}{4\log^{2}t}$ is $\leq 2^{-0.5\cdot 1.5^{\ell}}$ , by Markov’s inequality. As we repeated $\lceil\log(1/\delta^{\prime})/(0.5\cdot 1.5^{\ell})\rceil$ rounds, with $\delta^{\prime}$ error probability, there exists a round where the number of non-isolated elements is upper bounded by $2^{-1.5\cdot 1.5^{\ell}}\cdot\frac{t}{4\log^{2}t}$ . When this happens, $\|Z\|_{0}\geq\|A\star B-C\|_{0}-2^{-1.5\cdot 1.5^{\ell}}\cdot\frac{t}{4\log^{2}t}$ . Since we pick the round with the biggest $\|Z\|_{0}$ , the final $\|Z\|_{0}$ we pick has $\|Z\|_{0}\geq\|A\star B-C\|_{0}-2^{-1.5^{\ell+1}}\cdot\frac{t}{4\log^{2}t}$ . This in turn implies that the number of non-isolated elements is at most $2\cdot(\|A\star B-C\|_{0}-\|Z\|_{0})\leq 2^{-1.5^{\ell+1}}\cdot\frac{t}{2\log^{2}t}$ (this can be seen as follows. We first identify one element for each bucket appearing in $\|Z\|_{0}$ , then we add all $\|A\star B-C\|_{0}-\|Z\|_{0}$ non-identified elements one by one. Each new element can make at most one identified element become non-isolated). We will correctly recover all isolated elements; for the remaining elements, we might erroneously put some entry into $R$ . Therefore, $\|A\star B-C-R\|_{0}\leq 2^{-1.5^{\ell+1}}\cdot\frac{t}{\log^{2}t}$ . ∎

Now, it suffices to apply Claim B.11 with $\ell=0,1,\ldots,O(\log\log t)$ and with $\delta^{\prime}=\Theta(\delta/\log\log t)$ in order to apply a union bound. The overall running time is

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell=0}^{O(\log\log t)}O\left((\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0}+t)\cdot(1+\log(1/\delta^{\prime})/1.5^{\ell})\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle O\left((\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0}+t)\cdot(\log\log t+\log(1/\delta^{\prime}))\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle O\left((\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0}+t)\cdot(\log\log t+\log(1/\delta))\right). $$

Finally, $\log\log t=O(\log(1/\delta))$ by the assumption $\log t\leq 1/\delta$ , so we obtain the claimed running time.

Next, we state the main differences for applying the result to $\mathbb{Z}$ . We compute $\widetilde{Z}^{\prime}:=h(\partial(A\star B-C))$ instead of $\widetilde{Z}$ , which can be computed via $h(\partial A)\star_{r}h(B)+h(A)\star_{r}h(\partial B)-h(\partial C)$ . Then, we add $Z[i]$ to $R[\widetilde{Z}^{\prime}[i]/Z[i]]$ if $\widetilde{Z}^{\prime}[i]/Z[i]$ is an integer within range. The analysis follows similarly.

### B.4 Proof of Eq. 15

We need the following lemma from [20].

#### Lemma B.12 ([20, Corollary 11.3]).

Let $X\subseteq[N]$ be a set of $k$ keys. Randomly pick a hash function $h$ from Definition 5.11 with parameters $p>4N^{2}$ and $m\leq N$ . Fix a key $x\notin X$ and buckets $a,b\in[m]$ . Moreover, let $F=\sum_{y\in X}\mathbf{1}[h(y)=b]$ . Then:

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}[F\mid h(x)=a] \displaystyle=\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}[F]=\frac{k}{m}\pm\Theta(1), $$

and, for any $\lambda>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[|F-\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}(F)|\geq\lambda\sqrt{\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}(F)}\mid h(x)=a\right]\leq O\left(\frac{N\log N}{\lambda^{2}k}\right). $$

We restate Eq. 15 below. See 5.12

#### Proof.

We closely follow the proof in [20, Lemma 5.5]. Since by definition $\widetilde{X}=\pi(X)+\{0,p\}$ , we may fix offsets $o,o^{\prime}\in\{0,p\}$ so that $y=\pi(x)+o,y^{\prime}=\pi(x^{\prime})+o^{\prime}$ , and instead bound the probability of

$$ \left\lvert\left\{x\in X:\sum_{x^{\prime}\in X}\mathbf{1}\left[h(x)+o\equiv h(x^{\prime})+o^{\prime}\pmod{m}\right]>\frac{2t}{m}\right\}\right\rvert\leq\frac{mN\log^{3}N}{4t}. $$

Indeed, if the event in Eq. 25 happens for all $o,o^{\prime}\in\{0,p\}$ , then the event in Eq. 15 also happens.

Fix $o,o^{\prime}\in\{0,p\}$ and fix any $x\in X$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[\sum_{x^{\prime}\in X}\mathbf{1}\left[h(x)+o\equiv h(x^{\prime})+o^{\prime}\pmod{m}\right]>\tfrac{2t}{m}\right] \displaystyle=\  \displaystyle\sum_{a\in[m]}\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[h(x)=a]\cdot\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[\sum_{x^{\prime}\in X}\mathbf{1}\left[h(x^{\prime})\equiv(a+o-o^{\prime})\pmod{m}\right]>\tfrac{2t}{m}\middle|\,h(x)=a\right]. $$

To bound the conditional probability in Eq. 26, apply Lemma B.12 to the set $X\setminus\{x\}$ and the buckets $a$ and $b=(a+o-o^{\prime})\mod m$ : Let $F^{\prime}=\sum_{x^{\prime}\in X\setminus\{x\}}\mathbf{1}[h(x^{\prime})=b]$ , and then Lemma B.12 states that $\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}[F^{\prime}]=|X|/m+O(1)$ , and that (here we are using $|X|\leq t$ )

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[F^{\prime}>\tfrac{2t}{m}\,\middle|\,h(x)=a\right] \displaystyle\leq\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[|F^{\prime}-\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}[F^{\prime}]|>\tfrac{t}{m}-O(1)\,\middle|\,h(x)=a\right] \displaystyle\leq O(\tfrac{mN\log N}{t^{2}}), $$

where we set $\lambda=\sqrt{t^{2}/(m|X|)}-O(1)$ in Lemma B.12. Plugging back into Eq. 26 (and noting that the contribution of $x$ to the sum is at most $1$ ), we get

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[\sum_{x^{\prime}\in X}\mathbf{1}\left[h(x)+o\equiv h(x^{\prime})+o^{\prime}\pmod{m}\right]>\tfrac{2t}{m}\right]\leq O(\tfrac{mN\log N}{t^{2}}) $$

for fixed $x,o,o^{\prime}$ . Now, by summing over $x\in X$ , we know the expected value of the left hand side of Eq. 25 is $|X|\cdot O(\frac{mN\log N}{t^{2}})=O(\frac{mN\log N}{t})$ . Then, by Markov’s inequality, we know the event in Eq. 25 happens with at least $1-O(1/\log^{2}N)$ probability (for fixed $o,o^{\prime}$ ). Then, by a union bound, we know the event in Eq. 25 happens for all $o,o^{\prime}\in\{0,p\}$ with at least $1-O(1/\log^{2}N)$ probability. Since the event in Eq. 25 for all $o,o^{\prime}\in\{0,p\}$ implies the event in Eq. 15, this finishes the proof. ∎

## Abstract

The 3SUM problem is one of the cornerstones of fine-grained complexity. Its study has led to countless lower bounds, but as has been sporadically observed before—and as we will demonstrate again—insights on 3SUM can also lead to algorithmic applications.

The starting point of our work is that we spend a lot of technical effort to develop new algorithms for 3SUM-type problems such as approximate 3SUM-counting, small-doubling 3SUM-counting, and a deterministic subquadratic-time algorithm for the celebrated Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers theorem from additive combinatorics. All of these are relevant in their own right and may prove useful for future research on 3SUM.

But perhaps even more excitingly, as consequences of these tools, we derive diverse new results in fine-grained complexity and pattern matching algorithms, answering open questions from many unrelated research areas. Specifically:

A recent line of research on the “short cycle removal” technique culminated in tight 3SUM-based lower bounds for various graph problems via randomized fine-grained reductions [Abboud, Bringmann, Fischer; STOC ’23] [Jin, Xu; STOC ’23]. In this paper we derandomize the reduction to the important 4-Cycle Listing problem, answering a main open question of [Fischer, Kaliciak, Polak; ITCS ’24].

We establish that #3SUM and 3SUM are fine-grained equivalent under deterministic reductions, derandomizing a main result of [Chan, Vassilevska Williams, Xu; STOC ’23].

We give a deterministic algorithm for the $(1+\epsilon)$ -approximate Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances problem in time $n^{1+o(1)}\cdot\epsilon^{-1}$ . While there is a large body of work addressing the randomized complexity, this is the first deterministic improvement over Karloff’s $\widetilde{O}(n\epsilon^{-2})$ -time algorithm in over 30 years.

In the $k$ -Mismatch Constellation problem the input consists of two integer sets $A,B\subseteq[N]$ , and the goal is to test whether there is a shift $c$ such that $|(c+B)\setminus A|\leq k$ (i.e., whether $B$ shifted by $c$ matches $A$ up to $k$ mismatches). For moderately small $k$ the previously best running time was $\widetilde{O}(|A|\cdot k)$ [Cardoze, Schulman; FOCS ’98] [Fischer; SODA ’24]. We give a faster $|A|\cdot k^{2/3}\cdot N^{o(1)}$ -time algorithm in the regime where $|B|=\Theta(|A|)$ . This result also has implications for the $k$ -Mismatch String Matching with Wildcards problem.

## 1 Introduction

The famous 3SUM problem is to test whether a given set $A$ of $n$ integers contains a solution to the equation $a+b=c$ . It was hypothesized long ago that the naive $O(n^{2})$ -time algorithm for 3SUM is essentially best-possible [GO95], and this hypothesis has since evolved into a corner stone of fine-grained complexity theory, forming the basis of countless conditional lower bounds. In a recent result, Chan, Jin, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu [CJVX23] showcased that, quite surprisingly, some of the carefully crafted lower bound techniques can be turned into algorithms for seemingly unrelated problems, such as pattern matching on strings.

In this work we explore this paradigm further. We develop a colorful palette of new tools tailored towards 3SUM-type questions, often with a particular focus on deterministic algorithms, and often aided by tools from additive combinatorics such as the celebrated Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers (BSG) theorem. Then we apply these tools to derive various new fine-grained lower bounds—but also to design new and faster algorithms for pattern matching problems. We start with an exposition of our applications.

### 1.1 Application 1: Deterministic 3SUM-hardness

Recently, there has been an emerging interest in derandomizing fine-grained reductions from the 3SUM problem [CH20, CX24, FKP24]. This line of research follows two conceptual goals: (1) understanding the power of randomization in fine-grained complexity, and (2) establishing lower bounds that endure even if there turns out to be a truly subquadratic randomized algorithm for 3SUM. Formally, the goal is to establish conditional lower bound under the following deterministic hypothesis:

#### Hypothesis 1 (Deterministic 3SUM Hypothesis).

For any $\epsilon>0$ , there is no deterministic algorithm that solves 3SUM on $n$ numbers in $O(n^{2-\epsilon})$ time.

This is a weaker hypothesis than the usual 3SUM hypothesis, which commonly also allows randomized algorithms. See [FKP24] for a detailed discussion on the motivations of studying deterministic reductions from 3SUM.

Historically, the first result for derandomizing reductions from 3SUM is due to Chan and He [CH20], who derandomized the reduction from 3SUM to 3SUM Convolution. Said reduction, originally due to Pătraşcu [Păt10], plays a key role in complexity as it first related 3SUM to a non-geometric problem. Recently, Chan and Xu [CX24] showed a deterministic reduction from 3SUM to the All-Edges Sparse Triangle problem11 1 Given an $m$ -edge graph, determine whether each edge in the graph is in a triangle., whose randomized version was again shown in [Păt10].22 2 Technically, the reduction in [CX24] is from Exact Triangle to All-Edges Sparse Triangle (derandomizing an earlier reduction from [VX20]). Combined with prior work [CH20, VW13] this entails the claimed deterministic reduction from 3SUM to All-Edges Sparse Triangle. Independent to [CX24], Fischer, Kaliciak, and Polak [FKP24] studied deterministic reductions from 3SUM in a more systematic way. They derandomized the majority of formerly randomized reductions from 3SUM, including the reduction from 3SUM to All-Edges Sparse Triangle, $3$ -Linear Degeneracy Testing, Local Alignment and many more. This leads to an almost-complete derandomization, with the notable exception of the hardness results from three recent papers [ABKZ22, ABF23, JX23].

These three works [ABKZ22, ABF23, JX23] establish strong lower bounds for important graphs problems such as 4-Cycle Listing and Distance Oracles. They commonly rely on the “short cycle removal” technique, a technique that was first proposed by Abboud, Bringmann, Khoury and Zamir [ABKZ22] and independently optimized in [ABF23, JX23]. It is based on a structure-versus-randomness paradigm, on graphs or on numbers, which seems inherently randomized. Specifically, the key step in the refined proof [ABF23, JX23] is to reduce 3SUM to 3SUM instances with small additive energy33 3 The additive energy $\mathsf{E}(A)$ of an integer set $A$ is the number of tuples $(a,b,c,d)\in A^{4}$ with $a+b=c+d$ . . This key step utilizes the popular BSG theorem from additive combinatorics, and obtaining a deterministic algorithm for the BSG theorem is the main technical challenge for desired derandomization [FKP24]. Jin and Xu [JX23] additionally showed 3SUM-hardness for 4-Linear Degeneracy Testing, which also remained underandomized.

In this paper we derandomize the key step in [ABF23, JX23] and successfully design a deterministic reduction from general 3SUM instances to 3SUM instances with small additive energy:

#### Theorem 1.1.

For any constant $\delta>0$ , there is a deterministic fine-grained reduction from 3SUM to 3SUM with additive energy at most $n^{2+\delta}$ .

Naturally one of the main ingredients of the above theorem is a deterministic subquadratic-time algorithm for the constructive BSG theorem, which may be of independent interest (see Section 1.3).

With some more work, Theorem 1.1 implies the following lower bound for the 4-Cycle Listing problem (where the goal is to list all $4$ -cycles in a given undirected graph), resolving a main open question left by [FKP24].

#### Theorem 1.2.

Under the deterministic 3SUM hypothesis, there is no deterministic algorithm for 4-Cycle Listing on $n$ -node $m$ -edge graphs in $O(n^{2-\delta}+t)$ time or $O(m^{4/3-\delta}+t)$ time for any $\delta>0$ , where $t$ is the number of $4$ -cycles in the graph.

These lower bounds tightly match the upper bounds for 4-Cycle Listing [JX23, AKLS23].

We remark that the additional work needed to derive Theorem 1.2 from Theorem 1.1 does not easily follow from previous work, and is in fact somewhat technically involved. In [ABF23, JX23], the way to derive a randomized version of Theorem 1.2 from a randomized version of Theorem 1.1 is to first reduce low-energy 3SUM to All-Edges Sparse Triangle with few $4$ -cycles (morally, this is a “low-energy” variant of triangle detection in graphs). These reductions in [ABF23, JX23] are both randomized. Even though deterministic reductions from 3SUM to All-Edges Sparse Triangle are known [CX24, FKP24], they do not seem to preserve low energies. Our alternative reduction looks more like a direct derandomization of [ABF23], which makes the reduction more technically heavy. For instance, as a key technical tool it relies on derandomized version of the almost-additive hash functions used in [ABF23, JX23].

Utilizing our deterministic subquadratic-time algorithm for the constructive BSG theorem (which was a main ingredient in Theorem 1.1) we also show a deterministic fine-grained equivalence between 3SUM and #3SUM—the problem of counting the number of 3SUM solutions. This equivalence was first shown by Chan, Vassilevska Williams and Xu [CVX23] (by means of randomized reductions). As a technical bonus, and in contrast to [CVX23], our new reduction avoids the use of fast matrix multiplication (it relies on FFT instead).

#### Theorem 1.3.

#3SUM and 3SUM are subquadratically equivalent, under deterministic reductions.

### 1.2 Application 2: Pattern matching algorithms

Inspired by the previously observed connection [CJVX23] between tools in the fine-grained complexity of 3SUM on the one hand, and the design of pattern matching algorithms on the other hand, we have investigated how our toolset can further be algorithmically exploited. We offer two algorithms for natural pattern matching tasks.

#### Problem 1: Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances.

In the Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances problem (also known as Sliding Window Hamming Distances), we are given a pattern string $P$ of length $m$ and a text $T$ of length $n$ over some common alphabet $\Sigma$ , and the goal is to compute the Hamming distance (i.e., the number of mismatches) between $P$ and $T[i\mathinner{.\,.}i+m-1]$ for every shift $i\in[n-m]$ . This fundamental text-processing problem has been extensively studied in various settings [FP74, Abr87, Kar93, FG13, AGW13, KP15, KP18, CGK+20].

Of particular interest is approximate setting, where the typical goal is to compute $(1+\epsilon)$ -approximations of the Hamming distances. The history of this problem is rich, starting with a classical algorithm due to Karloff [Kar93] running in time $\widetilde{O}(n\epsilon^{-2})$ . At the time this was believed to be best-possible (in light of certain $\Omega(\epsilon^{-2})$ communication lower bounds [Woo04, JKS08]), and it was surprising when Kopelowitz and Porat [KP15] came up with an algorithm in time $\widetilde{O}(n\epsilon^{-1})$ ; see also [KP18] for a more streamlined algorithm. Then, in a very recent breakthrough, Chan, Jin, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu [CJVX23] gave an algorithm in $\widetilde{O}(n/\epsilon^{0.93})$ time, improving the dependence on $\epsilon^{-1}$ to sublinear. However, all of these algorithms are randomized.

Karloff [Kar93] also designed a deterministic algorithm running in time $O(n\epsilon^{-2}\log^{3}m)$ . In stark contrast to the progress by randomized algorithms, however, Karloff’s deterministic algorithm from more than 30 years ago has remained the state of the art. In our work we finally improve this $\epsilon^{-2}$ factor to $\epsilon^{-1}$ (albeit at the cost of incurring an extra $m^{o(1)}$ factor):

#### Theorem 1.4.

There is a deterministic algorithm solving $(1+\epsilon)$ -approximate Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances in $nm^{o(1)}/\epsilon$ time.

This answers an open question explicitly asked by Kociumaka in a video talk on [CGK+20]44 4 https://youtu.be/WEiQjjTBX-4?t=2820 and by [CJVX23].

#### Problem 2: $k$ -Mismatch Constellation.

The Constellation problem is a natural geometric pattern matching task: Given two sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ of at most $n$ points, the goal is to find all shifts $c\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ satisfying that $B+c\subseteq A$ . Intuitively, this models the task of identifying a certain constellation of stars $B$ in the night sky $A$ . But what if the constellation contains some mistakes? In the generalized $k$ -Mismatch Constellation problem the goal is to report all shifts $c$ with $|(c+B)\setminus A|\leq k$ (i.e., all occurrences that match the constellation in the night sky up to $k$ mismatches). It is known that we can assume all input points are in $\mathbb{Z}$ instead of $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ without loss of generality [CS98, Fis24].

The study of this problem was initiated by Cardoze and Schulman [CS98]. Assuming the natural technical condition $k\leq(1-\eta)|B|$ for any fixed constant $\eta>0$ (which implies the output size is at most $n/\eta$ ), they designed a randomized algorithm in time $\widetilde{O}(nk)$ . Recently, Fischer [Fis24] revisited this problem and gave a deterministic $\widetilde{O}(nk)\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)$ time algorithm. Both of these results left open whether it is possible to achieve better algorithms, in time $O(nk^{1-\epsilon})$ , say, or perhaps even in near-linear time $\widetilde{O}(n)$ .

In fact, a side result by Chan, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu [CVX23, Lemma 8.4] implies an $n^{2-\Omega(1)}$ -time algorithm for this problem, which beats time $\widetilde{O}(nk)$ whenever $k$ is very large in terms of $n$ . As our second algorithmic contribution we significantly widen the range of $k$ for which we can improve upon the time $\widetilde{O}(nk)$ :

#### Theorem 1.5.

Let $A,B\subseteq[N]$ and let $1\leq k\leq 0.3|B|$ . There is a deterministic algorithm that solves $k$ -Mismatch Constellation in $|A|\cdot k^{2/3}\cdot(|A|/|B|)^{2/3}\cdot N^{o(1)}$ time. If randomization is allowed, then the $N^{o(1)}$ factor can be replaced by $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)$ .

Notably, this algorithm runs in time $nk^{2/3}N^{o(1)}$ in the regime where $|B|=\Theta(|A|)$ (and $k$ is arbitrary). We improve upon the $\widetilde{O}(nk)$ baseline in the broader range $|B|\gg|A|/\sqrt{k}$ . (Counterintuitively, this problem indeed becomes harder the smaller $B$ is as then there could be completely separate structured regions in $A$ in which $B$ could be approximately matched.)

But can we do even better? In particular, there is no evidence that the problem cannot even be solved in near-linear time $\widetilde{O}(n)$ , irrespective of $k$ . Relatedly, in the $k$ -Bounded Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances problem (where all distances exceeding $k$ can be reported as $\infty$ in Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances), an algorithm in time $\widetilde{O}(n+k\sqrt{n})$ is known [GU18], in the setting where the text and pattern both have length $\Theta(n)$ . This running time becomes near-linear when $k$ is small ( $k\leq n^{\epsilon}$ , say). These two problems appear similar in nature in that for both problems the task is about shifts that result in at most $k$ mismatches. So can we achieve a similar result for $k$ -Mismatch Constellation?

Perhaps surprisingly, we prove that this is not possible—at least not by combinatorial55 5 In the context of fine-grained complexity and algorithm design, we informally say that an algorithm is combinatorial if it does not rely on algebraic fast matrix multiplication. It has emerged as a powerful paradigm to prove lower bounds for combinatorial based on the BMM hypothesis stating that there is no combinatorial algorithm for Boolean matrix multiplication in time $O(n^{3-\epsilon})$ (for all $\epsilon>0$ ). See e.g. [AV14, Wil18, GU18] and the references therein. algorithms:

#### Theorem 1.6.

Under the BMM hypothesis, combinatorial algorithms solving $k$ -Mismatch Constellation requires $\sqrt{k}n^{1-o(1)}$ time for sets of size $\Theta(n)$ .

This lower bound leaves a gap of $k^{1/6}$ to our algorithm. We leave it as an open question to close this gap, and to make further progress on the setting where $|B|\ll|A|$ .

#### Problem 3: $k$ -Mismatch String Matching with Wildcards.

Interestingly, our algorithm for $k$ -Mismatch Constellation also implies a new algorithm for the following well-studied problem [CEPR09, CEPR10, CP10, NR17, BCS24]: given a text string $T\in\Sigma^{n}$ , a pattern string $P\in(\Sigma\cup\{\diamondsuit\})^{m}$ , and integer $1\leq k\leq m$ , find all occurrences of $P$ inside $T$ allowing up to $k$ Hamming mismatches, where the wildcard $\diamondsuit\notin\Sigma$ can match any single character. Note that the wildcards appear only in the pattern and not in the text.

By a simple reduction from this problem to the $k$ -Mismatch Constellation problem, we obtain the following result as an immediate corollary of Theorem 1.5:

#### Corollary 1.7.

There is a deterministic algorithm that solves $k$ -Mismatch String Matching with Wildcards (in the pattern only) in time $k^{2/3}n^{1+o(1)}$ . If randomization is allowed, then the $n^{o(1)}$ factor can be replaced by $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(n)$ .

The proof of this corollary from Theorem 1.5 is short and straightforward (see Section 11.4). Moreover, we can get a faster algorithm by adjusting parameters and simplifying a few steps in the proof of Theorem 1.5:

#### Theorem 1.8.

There is a deterministic algorithm that solves $k$ -Mismatch String Matching with Wildcards (in the pattern only) in time $k^{1/2}n^{1+o(1)}$ . If randomization is allowed, then the $n^{o(1)}$ factor can be replaced by $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(n)$ .

We now briefly compare Theorem 1.8 with previous algorithms for $k$ -Mismatch String Matching with Wildcards (see [BCS24] for a more comprehensive overview). When wildcards are allowed in both the text and the pattern, [CEPR09, CEPR10] gave an algorithm in $\widetilde{O}(\min\{nk,n\sqrt{m}\})$ time. When wildcards are allowed either in the text only or in the pattern only, [CP10] gave an algorithm in $\widetilde{O}(n(mk)^{1/3})$ time. Our Theorem 1.8 is faster than these algorithms but only applies when all wildcards are in the pattern. More recent works [NR17, BCS24] gave fast algorithms parameterized by the number of wildcards and/or the number of contiguous segments of wildcards in the input.

### 1.3 Technical tools and overview

In this section, we list some of our new technical tools for proving the aforementioned results and also discuss some intuition for proving some of the results.

#### Tool I: Approximate 3SUM counting.

The first tool is an efficient deterministic algorithm for approximate 3SUM counting: Given integer (multi-)sets $A$ and $B$ , it approximately counts the number of times each number $c$ can be represented as a sum $a+b$ for $a\in A$ and $b\in B$ .

Formally, we write $1_{A}$ to denote the indicator vector of a (multi-)set $A$ , and use $\star$ between two vectors to denote their convolution (see formal definitions in Section 2). In particular, $1_{A}\star 1_{B}$ denotes a vector whose $c$ -th coordinate is the number of choices for picking $(a,b)\in A\times B$ so that $a+b=c$ .

#### Theorem 1.9 (Deterministic Popular Sums Approximation).

Let $A,B\subseteq[N]$ be multisets of size at most $N$ and let $\epsilon>0$ . There is a deterministic algorithm that runs in time $(\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|)\cdot N^{o(1)}$ and computes a vector $f$ of sparsity $\lVert f\rVert_{0}\leq O(\epsilon^{-1}|A|\log^{2}N)$ , such that $\lVert f-(1_{A}\star 1_{B})\rVert_{\infty}\leq\epsilon|B|$ .

To the best of our knowledge, this lemma has not explicitly appeared in the literature (even with randomization allowed). A randomized version of Theorem 1.9 is simple,66 6 We can randomly pick a prime $p=\Theta(\epsilon^{-1}|A|\log N)$ , and then compute $\sum_{i\equiv s\pmod{p}}(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i]$ for every $s\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ using FFT in $O(p\log p)=\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1}|A|)$ time. For every index $i$ , the expected value of $\sum_{i^{\prime}\equiv i\pmod{p},i\neq i^{\prime}}(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i^{\prime}]$ can be bounded by $O(\frac{|A||B|}{p/\log N})=O(\epsilon|B|)$ . Thus, by repeating $O(\log N)$ times, there must be one iteration where the mod $p$ bucket of $i$ is an additive $O(\epsilon|B|)$ approximation of $i$ , with high probability (we also have to recover the index of $i$ given its bucket, which can be achieved, say, by random sampling) but the deterministic version needs more care.

Theorem 1.9 is used as a subroutine in almost every result in this paper. For example, one useful application is to estimate the number of 4SUM solutions (which can be used for estimating the additive energy of a set) on inputs $A,B,C,D$ . To do this, we simply approximate $1_{A}\star 1_{B}$ by $f$ and approximate $1_{C}\star 1_{D}$ by $g$ using Theorem 1.9, and sum up $\sum_{x}f[x]g[-x]$ . Theorem 1.9 is also used in the proof of our deterministic BSG theorem (to be described later).

As another important application, combining Theorem 1.9 with the previous techniques due to Gawrychowski and Uznański [GU18] also implies our deterministic Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances algorithm (Theorem 1.4). For the details, we refer to Section 8. But to illustrate the intuition behind the connection to Theorem 1.9, we will describe a very simple $\epsilon^{-1}n^{1+o(1)}$ time algorithm computing an additive $\epsilon m$ -approximation here.

For each symbol $s\in\Sigma$ , let $A_{s}:=\{j:T[j]=s\}$ and $B_{s}:=\{k:P[k]=s\}$ . Then the Hamming distance between $T[i+1\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}i+m]$ and $P[1\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}m]$ can be expressed as

$$ |P|-\sum_{s\in\Sigma}(1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}})[i]. $$

For each $s\in\Sigma$ , we can use Theorem 1.9 to compute in $(\epsilon^{-1}|A_{s}|+|B_{s}|)\cdot n^{o(1)}$ time a sparse vector $f_{s}$ satisfying that $\|f_{s}-1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}}\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon|B_{s}|$ . Thus, for each index $i$ we can approximate the Hamming distance by $|P|-\sum_{s\in\Sigma}f_{s}[i]$ with an additive error of at most

$$ \sum_{s\in\Sigma}\big\lvert\big(f_{s}-1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}}\big)[i]\big\rvert\leq\sum_{s\in\Sigma}\epsilon|B_{s}|=\epsilon m. $$

The total time complexity is $\sum_{s\in\Sigma}(\epsilon^{-1}|A_{s}|+|B_{s}|)\cdot n^{o(1)}=\epsilon^{-1}n^{1+o(1)}$ .

#### Tool II: Small-doubling 3SUM counting.

The next technical tool is also for 3SUM counting, but in a different setting. This time we insist on exact counts, but we assume that the input is additively structured. Specifically, recall the definition of the sumset $A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\}$ . The doubling constant of a set is defined as the ratio $K=\frac{|A+A|}{|A|}$ . Intuitively, highly additively-structured sets (such as intervals or arithmetic progressions) have small doubling constant, whereas unstructured sets (such as random sets) have large doubling constant. The following theorem states that we can solve 3SUM counting exactly, provided that at least one input set has sufficiently small doubling constant:

#### Theorem 1.10 (Deterministic small-doubling 3SUM-counting; simplified from Theorem 4.1).

Given sets $A,B,C\subseteq[N]$ , where $|A+A|=K|A|$ , we can deterministically compute $(1_{C}\star 1_{-B})[a]$ for all $a\in A$ in time complexity $O\big(K\sqrt{|A||B||C|}\cdot N^{o(1)}\big)$ .

In particular, when $|A|,|B|,|C|\leq n$ , the time complexity becomes $O(Kn^{1.5}N^{o(1)})$ , which for small $K$ improves upon the standard quadratic-time algorithm for 3SUM. Previously, Jin and Xu [JX23] showed a randomized 3SUM algorithm in this regime in $O(Kn^{1.5}\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log N)$ time (and Abboud, Bringmann, and Fischer [ABF23] also independently showed a randomized algorithm in $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(K)n^{2-\Omega(1)}$ time). Our Theorem 4.1 simultaneously (i) derandomizes these results, (ii) extends them to the counting version of 3SUM, and (iii) also allow $A,B,C$ to differ in size. The latter two new features turn out to be crucial for our $k$ -Mismatch Constellation algorithm.

The randomized version of this small-doubling 3SUM algorithm is a key step in the randomized fine-grained reductions in [ABF23, JX23] from 3SUM to small-energy 3SUM (and thus a stepping stone in the chain of reductions to 4-Cycle Listing and Approximate Distance Oracles). Small doubling instances for $k$ -SUM and integer programming have also been studied by Randolph in his thesis [Ran24].

#### Tool III: Almost-additive hashing with small seed length.

A family of hash functions $h$ is called additive if it satisfies $h(x+y)=h(x)+h(y)$ , and almost-additive if $h(x+y)-h(x)-h(y)$ takes only constantly many different values. (Almost-)additive hashing has been playing an important role for 3SUM for a long time [BDP08, Păt10], and also the modern fine-grained reductions oftentimes rely on such hash functions. The most common use cases is to reduce the universe size in the 3SUM problem (typically at the cost of introducing some few false solutions). In [FKP24] it was shown that this application can be derandomized building on the family of hash functions $h(x)=x\;\,({\bmod}\>p)$ (where $p$ is a random prime).

Unfortunately, for our purposes this derandomization result is often not sufficient. The reason is technical: For some applications, specifically the reductions based on arithmetic short cycle removal [ABF23, JX23], we additionally need the hash function to be 3-wise independent. While it is provably impossible for a hash family to be (almost-)linear and 3-wise independent at the same time, this can at least approximately be achieved (see Section 5). To derandomize this more constrained hash family, we come up with a creative construction that besides the hash function $h(x)=x\;\,({\bmod}\>p)$ from before, also throws derandomization by $\epsilon$ -biased sets [AGHP92] into the mix.

#### Tool IV: Deterministic BSG theorem.

Putting together the previous three tools, we manage show a deterministic subquadratic-time algorithm to compute the Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers (BSG) theorem:

#### Theorem 1.11 (Deterministic subquadratic-time BSG theorem; simplified from Theorem 6.1).

Given set $A\subseteq[N]$ and $K\geq 1$ such that the additive energy is $\mathsf{E}(A)\geq|A|^{3}/K$ , we can deterministically find a subset $A^{\prime}\subseteq A$ in $(|A|^{2}/K^{2}+K^{13}|A|)N^{o(1)}$ time, such that $|A^{\prime}|\geq|A|/(64K)$ and $|A^{\prime}+A^{\prime}|\leq K^{16}|A|\cdot N^{o(1)}$ .

In words, the BSG theorem [BS94, Gow01] states that a set with high additive energy must contain a large subset of small doubling. The constructive BSG theorem was first used by Chan and Lewenstein [CL15], and later played a crucial role in the randomized fine-grained reductions of [ABF23, JX23], and different versions of BSG theorem were proved in [CVX23]. All previous proofs for (versions of) the constructive BSG theorem were randomized, except the one in [CL15]: they showed a deterministic algorithm that runs in $O(n^{\omega})$ time for constant values of $K$ , where $\omega<2.372$ [DWZ23, VXXZ24] is the matrix multiplication exponent. But this running time is not efficient enough for our purposes; we really need subquadratic time. All other previous proofs for constructive BSG theorem use randomness crucially. One (less crucial) use of randomness was for approximating the degree of nodes in certain bipartite graphs defined by the additive relation of the input sets; for this part, the degrees actually correspond to 3SUM solution counts, and hence can be derandomized using our Theorem 1.9. However, a more crucial use of randomness in the previous proof is due to the probabilistic method, specifically the method of dependent random choice. For this part, a naive derandomization would require enumerating all possibilities, taking (at least) quadratic time.

Although our deterministic constructive BSG is slower than known randomized versions (which run in $\widetilde{O}(|A|\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(K))$ time [CL15, ABF23, JX23]), and provide worse quantitative bounds, it still runs in subquadratic time when $K$ is not too small.

Roughly speaking, the proof of our deterministic BSG theorem uses the following strategy: We do not know how to overcome the aforementioned quadratic barrier for derandomizing the probabilistic method, but we can afford to run this slow derandomization on some much smaller subset $A_{0}\subseteq A$ . Then, we will use the results computed on this small subset $A_{0}$ to extract the desired small-doubling large subset $A^{\prime}\subseteq A$ . Naturally, if $A_{0}$ is chosen smaller, then this derandomization is faster, at the cost of worsening the doubling constant of the extracted subset $A^{\prime}$ . In order to make such extraction possible, we need to make subset $A_{0}\subseteq A$ inherit the high additive energy of $A$ (roughly speaking, if $\mathsf{E}(A)\geq|A|^{3}/K$ , then we would like $\mathsf{E}(A_{0})\geq|A_{0}|^{3-o(1)}/K$ ). Simply uniformly subsampling $A_{0}\subseteq A$ would cause too much loss, and we need to do something more technical: we (deterministically) pick a certain almost-additive hash function (see Section 5), mapping $A$ to roughly $|A|/|A_{0}|$ buckets, and then pick one of the buckets as our $A_{0}$ . This is exactly where our tool III, the deterministic almost-additive hash functions, come into play. We find it interesting that these hash families find an application here that is completely different from their original intent [ABF23, JX23].

#### Tool V: 3SUM counting for popular sums.

The fifth and final tool we introduce is yet another variant of 3SUM counting: This time the goal is to exactly count 3SUM solutions, but only those involving the most popular elements (i.e., those elements $s$ that are contained in many 3-sums):

#### Theorem 1.12 (Deterministic 3SUM-counting for popular sums).

Given sets $A,B\subseteq[N]$ , $|A|,|B|\leq n$ , and a parameter $k\geq 1$ , there is a deterministic algorithm that returns $S=\{s:(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]\geq|A|/k\}$ and exactly computes $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]$ for all $s\in S$ in $O(k^{2}|A|^{2-3/128}\cdot N^{o(1)})$ time.

Chan, Vassilevska Williams and Xu [CVX23, Lemma 8.4] gave a randomized subquadratic-time algorithm for this task using fast matrix multiplication. Our Theorem 1.12 derandomizes [CVX23, Lemma 8.4], and does not require fast matrix multiplication, but the running time has a worse exponent (but is still subquadratic).

In fact, establishing Theorem 1.12 immediately completes the proof of Theorem 1.3. Recall that this theorem was originally proven in [CVX23] (by means of randomized reductions), and tracing through their proofs it is easy to check that replacing their Lemma 8.4 by our Theorem 1.3 replaces the only randomized step by a deterministic alternative.

#### Techniques for the $k$ -Mismatch Constellation algorithm.

Throughout the overview we have encountered hints for the proofs of all our algorithmic applications, except for the algorithm for $k$ -Mismatch Constellation; let us finally provide some overview for this result.
