$$ \{s:(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]\geq|A|/k\}\subseteq\widetilde{S}\subseteq\{s:(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]\geq|A|/(2k)\} $$

in $O((|A|+k|B|)N^{o(1)})$ time, where $|\widetilde{S}|\leq\frac{|A||B|}{|A|/2k}=2k|B|$ . Our goal is to exactly compute $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]$ for all $s\in\widetilde{S}$ .

For every $1\leq i\leq g$ , use Theorem 1.9 to deterministically approximate $(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{B})[s]$ for all $s\in\widetilde{S}$ up to additive error $\frac{|A_{i}|}{12k}$ , in time $\widetilde{O}((k|B|+|A_{i}|)N^{o(1)})$ , and total time $O((Kk|B|+|A|)N^{o(1)})$ for all $1\leq i\leq g$ . Then we define a partition $\widetilde{S}=S_{1}\cup S_{2}\cdots\cup S_{g}\cup\hat{S}$ as follows: for each $s\in\widetilde{S}$ , pick an arbitrary $1\leq i\leq g$ such that the approximate value of $(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{B})[s]$ is at least $\frac{|A_{i}|}{6k}$ (so that the real value satisfies $(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{B})[s]\geq\frac{|A_{i}|}{12k}$ ), and put $s$ in $S_{i}$ . If no such $i$ exists, then put $s$ in $\hat{S}$ . Note that every $s\in\hat{S}$ satisfies

$$ (1_{\hat{A}}\star 1_{B})[s]=(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]-\sum_{i=1}^{g}(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{B})[s]\geq\frac{|A|}{2k}-\sum_{i=1}^{g}(\frac{|A_{i}|}{6k}+\frac{|A_{i}|}{12k})\geq\frac{|A|}{4k}. $$

We have the following claims:

#### Claim 7.1.

For all $1\leq i\leq g$ , $|S_{i}+B_{i}|\leq O(kK^{6}|B|N^{o(1)})$ .

#### Proof.

For any $s\in S_{i},b\in B_{i}$ , there are at least $(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{B})[s]\geq\frac{|A_{i}|}{12k}$ many distinct representations of $s+b=(s-a)+(a+b)$ such that $a\in A_{i},s-a\in B$ , $a+b\in A_{i}+B_{i}$ . Hence, $(1_{B}\star 1_{A_{i}+B_{i}})[s+b]\geq\frac{|A_{i}|}{12k}$ . Therefore, $|S_{i}+B_{i}|\leq\frac{|B|\cdot|A_{i}+B_{i}|}{|A_{i}|/(12k)}\leq 12k|B|\cdot 64K^{6}N^{o(1)}$ , where the last step uses Eq. 17. ∎

We use Theorem 4.1 (applied to $(A,B,C,S):=(S_{i},-B,A,B_{i})$ ) to compute $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]$ for all $s\in S_{i}$ , in time complexity

$$ \displaystyle O\Big(\frac{|S_{i}+B_{i}|\sqrt{|-B||A|}}{\sqrt{|B_{i}|}}\cdot N^{o(1)}\Big) \displaystyle\leq O\Big(\frac{kK^{6}|B|\sqrt{|B||A|}}{\sqrt{\frac{|A|}{K^{1/3}}/K^{6}}}\cdot N^{o(1)}\Big) \displaystyle\leq O(|B|^{1.5}kK^{55/6}N^{o(1)}). $$

Summing over all $1\leq i\leq g$ , the total time is $O(|B|^{1.5}kK^{61/6}N^{o(1)})$ .

#### Claim 7.2.

$|\hat{S}|\leq O\left(k^{2}\sqrt{\frac{|B|^{3}}{K|A|}}\right)$ .

#### Proof.

By Eq. 18,

$$ |\hat{S}|\cdot\left(\frac{|A|}{4k}\right)^{2}\leq\sum_{s\in\hat{S}}((1_{\hat{A}}\star 1_{B})[s])^{2}\leq\mathsf{E}(\hat{A},B)\leq\sqrt{\mathsf{E}(\hat{A})\mathsf{E}(B)}\leq\sqrt{\frac{2|A|^{3}}{K}\cdot|B|^{3}}, $$

so $|\hat{S}|\leq O\left(k^{2}\sqrt{\frac{|B|^{3}}{K|A|}}\right)$ . ∎

We use brute force to compute $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]$ for all $s\in\hat{S}$ , in $\widetilde{O}(|B|+|\hat{S}||A|)=\widetilde{O}(k^{2}\sqrt{|A||B|^{3}/K})$ time.

Therefore, we have computed $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]$ for all $s\in\widetilde{S}=S_{1}\cup S_{2}\cdots\cup S_{g}\cup\hat{S}$ , in total time

$$ O\Big(\Big((|A|^{2}/K+K^{14}|A|)+(|B|^{1.5}kK^{61/6})+k^{2}\sqrt{|A||B|^{3}/K}\Big)\cdot N^{o(1)}\Big) $$

By setting $K=|A|^{3/64}$ , the total time becomes

$$ O\Big((|A|^{2-3/64}+k^{2}|B|^{1.5}|A|^{61/128})\cdot N^{o(1)}\Big)\leq O(k^{2}\cdot|A|^{2-3/128}N^{o(1)}). $$

∎

## 8 Deterministic Approximate Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances

We use our deterministic approximate 3SUM-counting algorithm (Theorem 1.9) to show an $O(nm^{o(1)}/\epsilon)$ -time deterministic algorithm for $(1+\epsilon)$ -approximate Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances, proving Theorem 1.4.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.4.

Let $T[1\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}n]$ and $P[1\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}m]$ denote the input text and pattern strings over an alphabet $\Sigma$ . By dividing $T$ into $O(n/m)$ chunks, we can assume $n=O(m)$ without loss of generality.

We start by describing a very simple $\epsilon m$ -additive approximation algorithm. For each symbol $s\in\Sigma$ , let $A_{s}:=\{j:T[j]=s\}$ and $B_{s}:=\{k:P[k]=s\}$ . Then the Hamming distance between $T[i+1\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}i+m]$ and $P[1\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}m]$ can be expressed as

$$ |P|-\sum_{s\in\Sigma}(1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}})[i]. $$

For each $s\in\Sigma$ , use Theorem 1.9 to compute in $\widetilde{O}((\epsilon^{-1}|A_{s}|+|B_{s}|)\cdot m^{o(1)})$ time a sparse vector $f_{s}$ such that $\|f_{s}-1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}}\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon|B_{s}|$ . The total time complexity is $\widetilde{O}((\epsilon^{-1}\sum_{s\in\Sigma}|A_{s}|+\sum_{s\in\Sigma}|B_{s}|)\cdot m^{o(1)})=\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1}m^{1+o(1)})$ . Then, sum up the vectors $f_{s}$ over $s\in\Sigma$ , and output $|P|-\sum_{s\in\Sigma}f_{s}[i]$ as our approximation for the Hamming distance at shift $i$ , which clearly has additive error at most $\sum_{s\in\Sigma}\big\lvert\big(f_{s}-1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}}\big)[i]\big\rvert\leq\sum_{s\in\Sigma}\epsilon|B_{s}|=\epsilon m$ .

This algorithm already achieves $(1+\epsilon)$ -approximation for distances that are $\Theta(m)$ , but in general we still need to handle smaller distances $\Theta(k)$ and achieve better additive error $O(\epsilon k)$ for them. Similarly to [CJVX23, Lemma 3.5], we handle this using the technique of Gawrychowski and Uznański [GU18], which reduced $k$ -bounded Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances to the special case where both text and pattern strings have run-length encodings bounded by $O(k)$ (i.e., they are concatenations of $O(k)$ blocks of identical characters). This reduction runs in near-linear time, and preserves additive approximation. In the following we show how to approximate $\sum_{s\in\Sigma}(1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}})$ with $O(\epsilon k)$ coordinate-wise additive error in this special case in $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1}m^{1+o(1)})$ time, from which the theorem follows.

Now each $A_{s},B_{s}$ is a union of blocks (intervals), and there are $O(k)$ blocks in total over all symbols $s\in\Sigma$ . Since these $O(k)$ blocks have total length $O(m)$ , we can assume each block has length $O(m/k)$ (by possibly breaking up longer blocks). Then, we use the same strategy as [CJVX23, Lemma 3.5] and assume each block is dyadic (i.e., it takes the form $\{z\cdot 2^{u},z\cdot 2^{u}+1,\dots,(z+1)\cdot 2^{u}-1\}$ for some integers $z,u\geq 0$ ), by breaking up each original block into at most $2\log(m/k)+O(1)$ blocks; the total number of blocks becomes $O(k\log m)$ . For $s\in\Sigma$ and $1\leq 2^{u}\leq O(m/k)$ , define set $A^{u}_{s}$ as the left endpoints of $2^{u}$ -length blocks in $A_{s}$ , and define $B^{u}_{s}$ similarly. In particular, $1_{A_{s}}=\sum_{u}(1_{A^{u}_{s}}\star 1_{\{0,1,\dots,2^{u}-1\}})$ . We can decompose $(1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}})$ into the sum of contribution from pairs of blocks, and obtain

$$ \sum_{s\in\Sigma}(1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}})=\sum_{s\in\Sigma}\sum_{u,v}1_{A_{s}^{u}}\star 1_{-B_{s}^{v}}\star\underbrace{1_{\{0,\dots,2^{u}-1\}}\star 1_{-\{0,\dots,2^{v}-1\}}}_{=:L_{u,v}}. $$

For each $s,u,v$ , we use Theorem 1.9 to compute $f_{s,u,v}$ such that $\|f_{s,u,v}-1_{A_{s}^{u}}\star 1_{-B_{s}^{v}}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\epsilon k}{m}|B_{s}^{v}|$ , in $O\big(\big((\epsilon^{-1}m/k)|A_{s}^{u}|+|B_{s}^{v}|\big)\cdot m^{o(1)}\big)$ time. The total time complexity over all $s,u,v$ is $O(\epsilon^{-1}m^{1+o(1)})$ since $\sum_{u,s}|A_{s}^{u}|,\sum_{v,s}|B_{s}^{v}|\leq O(k\log m)$ and $u,v\leq O(\log m)$ . When $u\geq v$ (the $u<v$ case is symmetric), $L_{u,v}$ is a multiset with multiplicity at most $2^{v}$ and supported on an interval of length $<2\cdot 2^{u}$ , and $A_{s}^{u}$ and $B_{s}^{v}$ only contain multiples of $2^{v}$ , so for any $i$ the absolute difference between $(1_{A_{s}^{u}}\star 1_{-B_{s}^{v}}\star L_{u,v})[i]$ and $(f_{s,u,v}\star L_{u,v})[i]$ (WLOG assuming $f_{s,u,v}$ is only supported on multiples of $2^{v}$ ) is at most

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j}\big\lvert(f_{s,u,v}-1_{A_{s}^{u}}\star 1_{-B_{s}^{v}})[j]\big\rvert\cdot L_{u,v}[i-j] \displaystyle\leq\frac{2\cdot 2^{u}}{2^{v}}\|f_{s,u,v}-1_{A_{s}^{u}}\star 1_{-B_{s}^{v}}\|_{\infty}\|L_{u,v}\|_{\infty} \displaystyle\leq\frac{2\cdot 2^{u}}{2^{v}}\cdot\frac{\epsilon k}{m}|B_{s}^{v}|\cdot 2^{v} \displaystyle=O(\epsilon|B_{s}^{v}|). $$

Hence, if we use $f_{s,u,v}$ to replace $1_{A_{s}^{u}}\star 1_{-B_{s}^{v}}$ in Eq. 19 and compute the summation using FFT in $\widetilde{O}(m)$ time, we can obtain an approximation of $\sum_{s\in\Sigma}(1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}})$ with coordinate-wise additive error $\sum_{s,u,v}O(\epsilon|B_{s}^{v}|)\leq O(\epsilon k\log^{2}m)$ . This error can be made $O(\epsilon k)$ by suitably decreasing $\epsilon$ . The total time complexity is $O(\epsilon^{-1}m^{1+o(1)})$ . ∎

## 9 Deterministic 3SUM Reductions

In this section, we prove the deterministic fine-grained reduction from 3SUM to 3SUM with small additive energy Theorem 1.1. The overall framework is the same as previous randomized reductions in [ABF23, JX23], but here we need to make everything deterministic, by combining the derandomized versions of the BSG theorem, the small-doubling 3SUM algorithm, and the derandomized almost additive hashing from previous sections.

### 9.1 From high-energy to moderate-energy

Throughout this section, we consider the following version of 3SUM: given $A\subset\{-n^{3},\dots,n^{3}\}$ of size $|A|=n$ , determine if there exists $(a,b,c)\in A\times A\times A$ such that $a+b+c=0$ .99 9 The case where $A$ comes from a larger universe can be deterministically reduced to this version by [FKP24, Theorem 1.2]. The additive energy of the 3SUM instance is $n^{2}<\mathsf{E}(A)<n^{3}$ .

#### Lemma 9.1.

There is a deterministic fine-grained reduction from 3SUM to 3SUM with additive energy at most $n^{2.95}$ .

#### Proof.

The randomized version of this reduction was already given by [ABF23] and [JX23] using a randomized algorithmic version of the BSG theorem. Our derandomized version follows the same idea, except that we need to use the deterministic BSG theorem and deterministic energy approximation algorithm.

Let $A_{0}$ denote the 3SUM instance, $|A_{0}|=n$ . Let $K=n^{0.05}$ . Maintain a subset $A\subseteq A_{0}$ , which initially equals $A_{0}$ . We iteratively proceed as follows. In each iteration:

- 1. If $|A|\leq n^{0.9}$ , then solve 3SUM on $A$ in $O(|A|^{2})=O(n^{1.8})$ time, and return the 3SUM answer.

- 2. Use Corollary 3.4 to deterministically approximate $\mathsf{E}(A)$ up to additive error $\frac{|A|^{3}}{3K}$ , in $O(K|A|n^{o(1)})$ time. If the approximate value is at most $\frac{2|A|^{3}}{3K}$ , then we know $\mathsf{E}(A)\leq|A|^{3}/K\leq|A|^{2.95}$ , and we can use the moderate-energy 3SUM solver to solve $A$ , and return the 3SUM answer.

- 3. Otherwise, we have $\mathsf{E}(A)\geq\frac{|A|^{3}}{3K}$ . We apply the deterministic BSG algorithm (Theorem 6.1 with $r=3$ ) to $A$ with parameter $3K$ , and in $O(|A|^{2}/K^{2}+K^{13}|A|)\cdot n^{o(1)}$ time we can obtain $A^{\prime}\subseteq A$ of size $|A^{\prime}|\geq|A|/(192K)$ and another set $B^{\prime}$ such that $|B^{\prime}|\geq|A|/(K^{6}n^{o(1)}),|A^{\prime}+B^{\prime}|\leq K^{5}|A|n^{o(1)}$ . We then use Theorem 4.1 (applied to $(A,B,C,S):=(A^{\prime},A,-A,B^{\prime})$ ) to decide whether $(1_{-A}\star 1_{-A})[a]>0$ for some $a\in A^{\prime}$ (i.e., there exists $(a,b,c)\in A^{\prime}\times A\times A$ such that $-b-c=a$ ), in time complexity $\displaystyle O\Big(\frac{|A^{\prime}+B^{\prime}|\sqrt{|A||A|}}{\sqrt{|B^{\prime}|}}\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(n)+\big(|A^{\prime}+B^{\prime}|+|A|\big)\cdot n^{o(1)}\Big)$ $\displaystyle=O((\frac{K^{5}|A|^{2}}{\sqrt{|A|/K^{6}}}+K^{5}|A|)n^{o(1)})$ $\displaystyle=O(K^{8}|A|^{1.5}n^{o(1)}).$ If a 3SUM solution is found, then we return and terminate. Otherwise, we know $A$ has no 3SUM solutions that involve numbers in $A^{\prime}$ , so we can remove $A^{\prime}$ and let $A\leftarrow A\setminus A^{\prime}$ , and proceed to the next iteration.

Since $|A^{\prime}|\geq|A|/(192K)$ , each iteration decreases $|A|$ to at most $(1-1/(192K))|A|$ , so the number of iteration before $|A|$ drops below $n^{0.9}$ is at most $O(K\log n)$ . The time complexity in each iteration is

$$ O(K|A|n^{o(1)})+O((|A|^{2}/K^{2}+K^{13}|A|)n^{o(1)})+O(K^{8}|A|^{1.5}n^{o(1)}), $$

so over all $O(K\log n)$ iterations, the total time is at most

$$ n^{o(1)}\cdot O(K^{14}n+K^{9}n^{1.5}+n^{2}/K)\leq O(n^{1.95+o(1)}). $$

So the time complexity of this reduction is truly subquadratic. ∎

### 9.2 From moderate-energy to low-energy

In this section, we use our almost additive hash family $\mathcal{H}$ from Definition 5.5 and the deterministic energy approximation algorithm (Corollary 3.4) to show the following fine-grained reduction:

#### Lemma 9.2.

Let $\alpha\in(0,1)$ be a fixed constant. There is a deterministic fine-grained reduction from 3SUM with additive energy at most $n^{2+\alpha}$ to 3SUM with additive energy at most $n^{2+\beta}$ , where $\beta=\alpha-\alpha(1-\alpha)/30\in(0,\alpha)$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose all 3SUM instances of additive energy at most $n^{2+\beta}$ can be solved in $n^{2-\delta}$ time for some $\delta>0$ .

Let $A\subset[N]$ be the input 3SUM instance with $\mathsf{E}(A)\leq|A|^{2+\alpha}$ , with $|A|=n$ , $N=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(n)$ . We will perform the standard 3SUM self-reduction using the hash family $\mathcal{H}\subset\{h\colon\{-N,\dots,N\}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}\}$ from Lemma 5.1, with parameter $k=3$ , and prime $2\leq p<|A|$ to be determined later.

By almost linearity of $\mathcal{H}$ (Lemma 5.6), any 3SUM solution $a+b+c=0$ satisfies $h(0)-h(a)-h(b+c)\in\Delta_{h}$ and $h(b+c)-h(b)-h(c)\in\Delta_{h}$ , so $h(a)+h(b)+h(c)\in h(a)+h(b+c)-\Delta_{h}\in h(0)-2\Delta_{h}$ . For $h\in\mathcal{H}$ and $i\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , let $h^{-1}(i)=\{x\in\{-N,\dots,N\}:h(x)=i\}$ . Define $\Delta^{\prime}_{h}=h(0)-2\Delta_{h}$ which has size $|\Delta^{\prime}_{h}|\leq|\Delta_{h}|^{2}=n^{o(1)}$ . So in order to solve the original 3SUM instance, we only need to solve the smaller 3-partite 3SUM instances $\big(h^{-1}(i)\cap A,h^{-1}(j)\cap A,h^{-1}(k)\cap A\big)$ , where $i+j+k\in\Delta^{\prime}_{h}$ . (There are $p\cdot p\cdot|\Delta^{\prime}_{h}|=p^{2}n^{o(1)}$ such instances.)

We need to reduce these 3-partite 3SUM instances back to the one-partite version that we are working with, as follows: suppose $X,Y,Z\subseteq\{-N,\dots,N\}$ are the three input sets of the 3-partite 3SUM. we define set $W=(X+30N)\cup(Y+100N)\cup(Z-130N)$ as the one-partite 3SUM instance. Note that any original 3SUM solution $(x,y,z)\in X\times Y\times Z$ , $x+y+z=0$ implies a solution $(x+30N)+(y+100N)+(z-130N)=0$ in the new instance. One can verify that, conversely, any 3SUM solution in $W$ correspond to an original solution, due to the way we shifted the sets. Furthermore, we can similarly verify that any Sidon 4-tuple in $W$ can be divided into two pairs, $(a,b),(c,d)$ , where $a-b=c-d$ , and the two numbers in each pair come from the same part ( $X+30N$ , $Y+100N$ , or $Z-130N$ ). So it actually corresponds to a (shifted) Sidon 4-tuple from the original instance in $X,Y,Z,$ or between $X,Y$ , between $Y,Z$ , or between $Z,X$ . This means the new one-partite 3SUM instance $W$ has additive energy

$$ \mathsf{E}(W)=\mathsf{E}(X)+\mathsf{E}(Y)+\mathsf{E}(Z)+\mathsf{E}(X,Y)+\mathsf{E}(Y,Z)+\mathsf{E}(Z,X). $$

Our goal is to deterministically pick a $h\in\mathcal{H}$ to perform the 3SUM self-reduction mentioned above, so that the produced instances have low total additive energy. To do this, we try every $h\in\mathcal{H}$ , and check whether $h$ is good. Recall from Definition 5.5 that $|\mathcal{H}|\leq 4m^{2}p^{12}$ .

We first need to analyze the expected total energy of the produced instances under a random $h\in\mathcal{H}$ . To do this, we consider each individual Sidon 4-tuple in $A$ , $a+b=c+d$ , and analyze its expected contribution to the total energy of all produced instances. Given the discussion above, the contribution of this 4-tuple to the total energy (under a specific $h\in\mathcal{H}$ ) is determined as follows:

- • If $h(a)=h(b)=h(c)=h(d)=i^{*}$ for some $i^{*}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , then they are hashed to the same bucket $i^{*}$ , and it corresponds to a Sidon 4-tuple in every instance $\big(h^{-1}(i^{*})\cap A,h^{-1}(j)\cap A,h^{-1}(k)\cap A\big)$ , where $i^{*}+j+k\in\Delta^{\prime}_{h}$ . There are $O(p\cdot|\Delta^{\prime}|)$ such choices of $j,k$ , so this Sidon 4-tuple contributes $O(p\cdot|\Delta^{\prime}|)$ to the total energy.

- • If $h(a),h(b),h(c),h(d)$ are not distinct but not all equal, then by a similar reasoning, this Sidon 4-tuple can contribute at most $O(|\Delta^{\prime}|)$ to the total energy.

- • If $h(a),h(b),h(c),h(d)$ are distinct, then they are hashed to four different buckets, and hence do not contribute to the total energy.

Now we can analyze the expected contribution of the Sidon 4-tuple $a+b=c+d$ to the total energy, by distinguishing several cases:

- • if $a=b=c=d$ , then clearly $h(a)=h(b)=h(c)=h(d)$ . There are only $|A|$ such 4-tuples.

- • Otherwise, there are at least two distinct values among $a,b,c,d$ . Say they are $a,b$ . Note that $a\neq b$ cannot have any $2$ -term $\ell$ -relation as defined in Definition 5.8, so by Lemma 5.9 we know $h(a)=h(b)$ happens with at most $n^{o(1)}/p$ probability. Now we look at more subcases. – If $a,b,c$ has no $O(Q^{2})$ -relation, then by Lemma 5.9, $h(a)=h(b)=h(c)$ happens with probability at most $n^{o(1)}/p^{2}$ . The number of such 4-tuples are trivially upper-bounded by $\mathsf{E}(A)$ . – Otherwise, $a,b,c$ has a $O(Q^{2})$ -relation. Then there are at most $(O(Q^{2}))^{2}-1=n^{o(1)}$ ways to pick the coefficients $\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\beta_{3}=0$ of this relation, and there are $|A|^{2}$ possibilities for $(a,b)\in A^{2}$ , which then uniquely determine $c$ by the relation $\beta_{1}a+\beta_{2}b+\beta_{3}c=0$ , and then uniquely determine $d$ by $a+b=c+d$ . Hence, in total there are at most $n^{o(1)}|A|^{2}$ such 4-tuples.

Hence, the expected number of tuples $(a,b,c,d)\in A^{4}$ such that $h(a)=h(b)=h(c)=h(d)$ can be bounded by $|A|+\mathsf{E}(A)\cdot n^{o(1)}/p^{2}+n^{o(1)}|A|^{2}\cdot n^{o(1)}/p$ . The expected number of $(a,b,c,d)\in A^{4}$ such that $h(a),h(b),h(c),h(d)$ are not distinct can be bounded by $|A|+\mathsf{E}(A)\cdot n^{o(1)}/p$ . Together, their contribution to the total energy of all instances is in expectation

$$ \displaystyle\big(|A|+\mathsf{E}(A)\cdot n^{o(1)}/p^{2}+n^{o(1)}|A|^{2}\cdot n^{o(1)}/p\big)\cdot O(p\cdot|\Delta^{\prime}|)+\big(|A|+\mathsf{E}(A)\cdot n^{o(1)}/p\big)\cdot O(|\Delta^{\prime}|) \displaystyle=O((|A|p+\mathsf{E}(A)/p+|A|^{2})\cdot n^{o(1)}). $$

We can also use a similar (and simpler) argument to bound the expected total squared size of the buckets, by

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\Big[\sum_{i}|h^{-1}(i)\cap A|^{2}\Big]\leq O(|A|^{2}\cdot n^{o(1)}/p). $$

By Markov’s inequality and a union bound, we know there is an $h\in\mathcal{H}$ such that both upper bounds Eqs. 20 and 21 hold (up to a constant factor) without taking expectation. The goal is to find such $h$ (or any other good enough $h$ ), by enumerating $h\in\mathcal{H}$ and checking whether $h$ is good deterministically.

Let $\epsilon>0$ be some constant to be determined later. For each $h\in\mathcal{H}$ , do the following steps:

- • If the bound in Eq. 21 is violated for $h$ then we terminate this procedure and start to check the next hash function. Otherwise, use $h$ to perform the 3SUM self-reduction described above and obtain $p^{2}|\Delta^{\prime}|=p^{2}n^{o(1)}$ smaller 3SUM instances.

- • All instances of size $<|A|^{1-\epsilon}/p$ are marked as light. All buckets of size $|h^{-1}(i)\cap A|\geq\frac{1}{3}|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p$ are marked as heavy. All instances that include at least one heavy buckets are marked as heavy.

- • Let $\mu:=|A|^{\alpha-1-4\epsilon}$ . For each non-heavy instance (which can have size $\leq|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p$ ), use Corollary 3.4 to approximate its additive energy up to additive error $\mu\cdot\big(|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p\big)^{3}=|A|^{2+\alpha-\epsilon}/p^{3}$ . If the approximate energy is greater than $0.5|A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}$ , then mark this instance as high-energy. The total time of this step over all $p^{2}n^{o(1)}$ instances is $p^{2}n^{o(1)}\cdot O(\mu^{-1}\cdot|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p\cdot n^{o(1)})=p|A|^{2-\alpha+5\epsilon+o(1)}$ .

- • If the sum of the approximate energy (from the previous step) over all non-heavy instances is greater than $|A|^{2+\alpha+\epsilon}/p$ , then $h$ is bad, and we terminate this procedure and start to check the next hash function. Otherwise, we declare $h$ as good, and we will not try other hash functions any more. The following steps are only run for the good $h$ .

- • We solve all light, and high-energy instances by brute force in quadratic time. For each item $a\in A$ landing in a heavy bucket, use $\widetilde{O}(|A|)$ time to find 3SUM solutions involving it.

- • For each remaining instance that is non-heavy, it has size $s\in[|A|^{1-\epsilon}/p,|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p]$ , and has additive energy at most $0.5|A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}+\mu\big(|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p\big)^{3}\leq|A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}$ . We will set parameters later so that

$$ |A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}\leq(|A|^{1-\epsilon}/p)^{2+\beta} $$

holds, which is equivalent to

$$ |A|^{\alpha+(6+\beta)\epsilon-\beta}\leq p^{1-\beta}. $$

(22) Then this instance has additive energy at most $s^{2+\beta}$ , and hence can be solved in $s^{2-\delta}$ time by assumption.

To show the correctness of this reduction, we need to show at least one $h$ is good. Note that when estimating the total additive energy of all $p^{2}n^{o(1)}$ instances, the total additive error incurred is

$$ \mu\cdot\big(|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p\big)^{3}\cdot p^{2}n^{o(1)}=|A|^{2+\alpha-\epsilon+o(1)}/p. $$

By Eq. 20 we know there is some $h$ such that the total energy is at most

$$ O((|A|^{2}+|A|^{2+\alpha}/p))\cdot n^{o(1)}\leq O(|A|^{2+\alpha+o(1)}/p). $$

For such $h$ , the approximate total energy is at most $O(|A|^{2+\alpha+o(1)}/p)+|A|^{2+\alpha-\epsilon+o(1)}/p\leq|A|^{2+\alpha+\epsilon}/p$ , so our algorithm will declare this $h$ as good. On the other hand, if we declare some $h$ as good, then we know the total additive energy of all non-heavy instances is at most $|A|^{2+\alpha+\epsilon}/p+|A|^{2+\alpha-\epsilon+o(1)}/p\leq 2|A|^{2+\alpha+\epsilon}/p$ .

Now it remains to analyze the time complexity of the whole algorithm.

- • The energy estimation step takes $p|A|^{2-\alpha+5\epsilon+o(1)}$ time for each $h\in\mathcal{H}$ . We need to enumerate all $h\in\mathcal{H}$ (where $|\mathcal{H}|\leq n^{o(1)}p^{12})$ , so the total time is

$$ p^{13}|A|^{2+5\epsilon-\alpha+o(1)}. $$

(23)

- • By Eq. 21, the total size of heavy buckets $i$ (that is, with size $|h^{-1}(i)\cap A|\geq\frac{1}{3}|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p$ ) is at most $O(|A|^{2}\cdot n^{o(1)}/p)/\big(\frac{1}{3}|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p\big)\leq O(|A|^{1-\epsilon+o(1)})$ . For each of them we spend $\widetilde{O}(|A|)$ time to find 3SUM solutions involving it, which is $O(|A|^{2-\epsilon+o(1)})$ total time.

- • The total time for solving (at most $p^{2}n^{o(1)}$ many) light instances is $p^{2}n^{o(1)}\cdot\big(|A|^{1-\epsilon}/p\big)^{2}=|A|^{2-2\epsilon+o(1)}$ .

- • Since the total additive energy of all non-heavy instances is $\leq 2|A|^{2+\alpha+\epsilon}/p$ , the number of instances with that are marked as high-energy (which should have energy at least $0.5|A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}-\mu\cdot\big(|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p\big)^{3}\geq 0.4|A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}$ ) is at most $\frac{2|A|^{2+\alpha+\epsilon}/p}{0.4|A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}}=5p^{2}/|A|^{3\epsilon}$ . The total time for solving these high-energy non-heavy instances is at most $\big(5p^{2}/|A|^{3\epsilon}\big)\cdot O((|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p)^{2})\leq O(|A|^{2-\epsilon+o(1)})$ .

- • The remaining instances are solved by the assumed subquadratic-time algorithm on lower energy instances. The total time is

$$ p^{2}n^{o(1)}\cdot(|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p)^{2-\delta} $$

(24)

The remaining goal is to set parameters $\beta\in(0,\alpha),p$ , and $\epsilon>0$ , so that Eq. 22 holds, and Eqs. 23 and 24 are truly-subquadratic in $|A|$ . This is achieved by setting

$$ \displaystyle\beta \displaystyle=\alpha-\alpha(1-\alpha)/30, \displaystyle p \displaystyle=\Theta(|A|^{\alpha/15}), $$

and $\epsilon>0$ small enough (in particular, $\epsilon:=\min\{\alpha(1-\alpha)/420,\delta/100\}$ ). To verify, note that Eq. 22 holds because

$$ |A|^{\alpha+(6+\beta)\epsilon-\beta}=|A|^{\alpha(1-\alpha)/30+(6+\beta)\epsilon}\leq|A|^{\alpha(1-\alpha)/20}=\Theta(p^{0.75(1-\alpha)}), $$

whereas $p^{1-\beta}=p^{(1-\alpha)(1+\alpha/30)}\geq p^{0.75(1-\alpha)}$ . Eq. 23 can be upper-bounded by

$$ |A|^{13\alpha/15}\cdot|A|^{2+5\epsilon-\alpha+o(1)}\leq|A|^{2+5\epsilon-2\alpha/15+o(1)}\leq|A|^{2-\alpha/15+o(1)}. $$

And Eq. 24 can be upper-bounded by $|A|^{(1+\epsilon)(2-\delta)+o(1)}p^{\delta}\leq|A|^{2+2\epsilon-\delta+\delta\alpha/15+o(1)}\leq|A|^{2-0.9\delta+o(1)}$ . ∎

Now we can prove Theorem 1.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1.

For any given constant $\delta>0$ , we deterministically reduce from 3SUM to 3SUM with additive energy at most $n^{2+\delta}$ as follows: first apply Lemma 9.1 to reduce from 3SUM to 3SUM with additive energy at most $n^{2.95}$ . Then, starting with $\alpha_{0}:=0.95$ , repeatedly apply Lemma 9.2 to reduce from 3SUM with additive energy at most $\alpha_{i}$ to 3SUM with additive energy at most $\alpha_{i+1}=\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{i}(1-\alpha_{i})/30$ . One can check that the sequences $\{\alpha_{i}\}$ converges to $0$ . Hence, there is some step where we arrive at 3SUM instances of additive energy at most $n^{2+\delta}$ as desired.

Recall that we initially start from 3SUM with universe $O(n^{3})$ (which is allowed by [FKP24, Theorem 1.2]). There are only finitely many steps of reductions. In each step, one can verify that Lemma 9.2 only blows up the universe size by a fixed polynomial (strictly speaking, the universe size does not change, but the instance size shrinks by a fixed polynomial factor). Hence, in the end we arrive at 3SUM instances whose universe size is still $n^{O(1)}$ (where the $O(1)$ depends on $\delta$ ). ∎

## 10 Reduction to Triangle Listing

In this section, we prove the following theorem.

#### Theorem 10.1.

Given a 3SUM instance on a size $n$ set $A\subset[n^{O(1)}]$ with additive energy $\mathsf{E}(A)\leq n^{2+\delta}$ , a small parameter $\epsilon>0$ , and a parameter $P=n^{k\cdot\epsilon}\leq n$ for some integer $k$ , there is a deterministic reduction that reduces the 3SUM instance to $n^{o(1)}$ Triangle Listing instances on graphs with

- • $P^{2}\cdot n^{O(\epsilon)}$ nodes;

- • $O(n^{1+\epsilon}/P)$ maximum degree;

- • $n^{2+\delta+o(1)}/P+n^{4+o(1)}/P^{4}$ $4$ -cycles,

and we are required to report $n^{3+o(1)}/P^{2}$ triangles for each graph. Furthermore, the running time of the reduction is $O(n^{2-\epsilon}+n^{1+O(\epsilon)}\cdot P)$ .

### 10.1 Warm-up: randomized reduction

Before we prove Theorem 10.1, we first show a randomized version of the reduction and we later derandomize it. The reduction is similar to [ABF23]’s reduction from low-energy 3SUM to Triangle Listing with few $4$ -cycles (the difference is that they work over the group $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{d}$ for some prime $p$ and integer $d$ , while we work over integers), and also shares similar high-level structure with [JX23]’s reduction from strong 3SUM to Triangle Detection.

Let $p=\Theta(P)$ be a prime. Let $\mathcal{H}\colon\{-N,\ldots,N\}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , for $N=n^{O(1)}$ be the hash family constructed in Definition 5.5, which is almost linear “almost” almost $k$ -wise independent by Lemma 5.9. Note that in this case, two integers $x_{1}\neq x_{2}$ cannot have an $n^{o(1)}$ -relation, so the hash family is actually almost $2$ -wise independent.

Let $f,g,h$ be three hash functions sampled from $\mathcal{H}$ .

For any $a\neq b\in A$ , the probability $f(a)=f(b)$ is $O(1/p)$ . Therefore,

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}\left[\sum_{a,b\in A}[f(a)=f(b)]\right]=O(n^{2}/p). $$

Therefore, the number of $a\in A$ that is in the same hash bucket (under hash function $f$ ) with $\geq n^{1+\epsilon}/p$ numbers in $A$ is $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ . For these numbers, we can detect whether they are in any 3SUM solution in $O(n^{2-\epsilon})$ total time, using the naive algorithm for 3SUM. Afterwards, we can remove these numbers from $A$ , so that all hash bucket (under hash function $f$ ) contains at most $n^{1+\epsilon}/p$ numbers.

Similarly, after $\widetilde{O}(n^{2-\epsilon})$ time pre-processing we can ensure that any number in $A$ is mapped to the same bucket with $\leq n^{1+\epsilon}/p$ other numbers under either $g$ or $h$ .

We will construct $n^{o(1)}$ graphs, one for every $(\delta_{f,1},\delta_{f,2},\delta_{f,3},\delta_{g,1},\delta_{g,2},\delta_{g,3},\delta_{h,1},\delta_{h,2},\delta_{h,3})\in\Delta_{f}^{3}\times\Delta_{g}^{3}\times\Delta_{h}^{3}$ . The constructed graph will be a tripartite graph, where the nodes of the three parts are labeled by

$$ \{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p},\quad\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p},\quad\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\} $$

respectively. Next we describe the edges of the graph. We add an edge from a vertex $(x_{1},y_{1},z_{1})\in\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ to $(x_{2},y_{2},z_{2})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ if there is some $a\in A$ such that $x_{2}-x_{1}=f(a)+\delta_{f,1}$ , $y_{2}-y_{1}=g(a)+\delta_{g,1}$ and $z_{2}-z_{1}=h(a)+\delta_{h,1}$ . Edges between other parts are similarly added, except that we replace $(\delta_{f,1},\delta_{g,1},\delta_{h,1})$ with $(\delta_{f,2},\delta_{g,2},\delta_{h,2})$ or $(\delta_{f,3},\delta_{g,3},\delta_{h,3})$ depending on which part it is. More precisely:

- • For any $a\in A$ , we add an edge with label $a$ (the label is purely for convenience in the analysis, and does not technically appear in the Triangle Listing instances) between $(0,y_{1},z_{1})\in\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ and $(x_{2},0,z_{2})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ if $x_{2}=f(a)+\delta_{f,1}$ , $-y_{1}=g(a)+\delta_{g,1}$ and $z_{2}-z_{1}=h(a)+\delta_{h,1}$ .

- • For any $a\in A$ , we add an edge with label $a$ between $(x_{2},0,z_{2})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ and $(x_{3},y_{3},0)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{q}\times\{0\}$ if $x_{3}-x_{2}=f(a)+\delta_{f,2}$ , $y_{3}=g(a)+\delta_{g,2}$ and $-z_{2}=h(a)+\delta_{h,2}$ .

- • For any $a\in A$ , we add an edge with label $a$ between $(x_{3},y_{3},0)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\}$ and $(0,y_{1},z_{1})\in\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ if $-x_{3}=f(a)+\delta_{f,3}$ , $y_{1}-y_{3}=g(a)+\delta_{g,3}$ and $z_{1}=h(a)+\delta_{h,3}$ .

We only keep one copy of all duplicated edges.

The construction of the graph is efficient. For instance, to find all edges between the first two parts, we enumerate $a\in A$ and $z\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , and then add edges between $(0,-g(a)-\delta_{g,1},z)\in\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ and $(f(a)+\delta_{f,1},0,z+h(a)+\delta_{h,1})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . The running time is essentially linear in the number of edges.

#### Number of Vertices.

Clearly, the number of vertices in the constructed graph is $O(p^{2})$ .

#### Maximum Degree.

Consider a vertex $(0,y,z)\in\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ in the first node part. In order for it to connect to some node in the second node part, there must exist some $a\in A$ where $-y=g(a)+\delta_{g,1}$ . By the pre-processing, the number of such $a$ is at most $n^{1+\epsilon}/p$ . Similarly, in order for $(0,y,z)$ to connect to some node in the third node part, we need to have some $a\in A$ where $z=h(a)+\delta_{h,3}$ , so the number of such $a$ again is at most $n^{1+\epsilon}/p$ . Thus, the degree of $(0,y,z)$ is $O(n^{1+\epsilon}/p)$ . By symmetry, the maximum degree of the graph is $O(n^{1+\epsilon}/p)$ .

#### Number of Triangles.

First of all, if $a,b,c\in A$ have $a+b+c=0$ , then $f(a)+f(b)+f(c)\in f(a+b+c)-2\Delta_{f}\subseteq-3\Delta_{f}$ (note that as $f(0+0)-f(0)-f(0)\in\Delta_{f}$ , we must have $f(0)\in-\Delta_{f}$ ). Thus, there must exist $\delta_{f,1},\delta_{f,2},\delta_{f,3}\in\Delta_{f}$ , so that $(f(a)+\delta_{f,1})+(f(b)+\delta_{f,2})+(f(c)+\delta_{f,3})=0$ . Similarly, must exist $\delta_{g,1},\delta_{g,2},\delta_{g,3}\in\Delta_{g}$ , so that $(g(a)+\delta_{g,1})+(g(b)+\delta_{g,2})+(g(c)+\delta_{g,3})=0$ , and $\delta_{h,1},\delta_{h,2},\delta_{h,3}\in\Delta_{h}$ , so that $(h(a)+\delta_{h,1})+(h(b)+\delta_{h,2})+(h(c)+\delta_{h,3})=0$ . Then the following three vertices must form a triangle in the graph constructed with parameters $(\delta_{f,1},\delta_{f,2},\delta_{f,3},\delta_{g,1},\delta_{g,2},\delta_{g,3},\delta_{h,1},\delta_{h,2},\delta_{h,3})$ :

$$ (0,-(g(a)+\delta_{g,1}),h(c)+\delta_{h,3}),\quad(f(a)+\delta_{f,1},0,-(h(b)+\delta_{h,2})),\quad(-(f(c)+\delta_{f,3}),g(b)+\delta_{g,2},0). $$

For any triangle in the constructed graph, it is not difficult to verify that the edge labels $a,b,c$ of the three edges of the triangle satisfy

$$ \begin{gathered}(f(a)+\delta_{f,1})+(f(b)+\delta_{f,2})+(f(c)+\delta_{f,3})=0,\\
(g(a)+\delta_{g,1})+(g(b)+\delta_{g,2})+(g(c)+\delta_{g,3})=0,\\
(h(a)+\delta_{h,1})+(h(b)+\delta_{h,2})+(h(c)+\delta_{h,3})=0.\end{gathered} $$

Thus, triples $(a,b,c)$ satisfying Eq. 25 are in one-to-one correspondence with triangles in the graph.

Eq. 25 implies that

$$ f(a+b+c)\in 2\Delta_{f}-3\Delta_{f},\quad g(a+b+c)\in 2\Delta_{g}-3\Delta_{g},\quad h(a+b+c)\in 2\Delta_{h}-3\Delta_{h}. $$

If $a+b+c\neq 0$ , then by Lemma 5.10, each of these equations holds with probability $n^{o(1)}/p$ , so the probability that they all hold is $n^{o(1)}/p^{3}$ . Furthermore, each triple $(a,b,c)$ can contribute at most $1$ triangle in each constructed graph. Thus, the expected number of triangles in each graph with edge labels $a,b,c$ for $a+b+c\neq 0$ is $n^{3+o(1)}/p^{3}$ , and it suffices to list more triangles than this number before we find an actual 3SUM solution if an actual 3SUM solution exists.

#### Number of Four-Cycles.

By symmetry, it suffices to consider the following two types of four-cycles:

- • The $4$ -cycle (with edge labels) is $(0,y_{1},z_{1})\overset{a_{1}}{-}(x_{2},0,z_{2})\overset{a_{2}}{-}(x_{3},y_{3},0)\overset{a_{3}}{-}(x_{4},0,z_{4})\overset{a_{4}}{-}(0,y_{1},z_{1})$ . Such a $4$ -cycle exists only if the following set of equations hold: $\displaystyle x_{2}\in f(a_{1})+\Delta_{f},\quad$ $\displaystyle x_{3}-x_{2}\in f(a_{2})+\Delta_{f},\quad$ $\displaystyle x_{3}-x_{4}\in f(a_{3})+\Delta_{f},\quad$ $\displaystyle x_{4}\in f(a_{4})+\Delta_{f},$ $\displaystyle-y_{1}\in g(a_{1})+\Delta_{g},\quad$ $\displaystyle y_{3}\in g(a_{2})+\Delta_{g},\quad$ $\displaystyle y_{3}\in g(a_{3})+\Delta_{g},\quad$ $\displaystyle-y_{1}\in g(a_{4})+\Delta_{g},$ $\displaystyle z_{2}-z_{1}\in h(a_{1})+\Delta_{h},\quad$ $\displaystyle-z_{2}\in h(a_{2})+\Delta_{h},\quad$ $\displaystyle-z_{4}\in h(a_{3})+\Delta_{h},\quad$ $\displaystyle z_{4}-z_{1}\in h(a_{4})+\Delta_{h}.$ These equations imply

$$ \displaystyle f(a_{1})+f(a_{2})-f(a_{3})-f(a_{4})\in 2\Delta_{f}-2\Delta_{f}, $$



$$ \displaystyle g(a_{1})-g(a_{4})\in\Delta_{g}-\Delta_{g},\quad g(a_{2})-g(a_{3})\in\Delta_{g}-\Delta_{g} $$



$$ \displaystyle h(a_{1})+h(a_{2})-h(a_{3})-h(a_{4})\in 2\Delta_{h}-2\Delta_{h}, $$

which further imply

$$ \begin{gathered}f(a_{1}+a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4})\in 3\Delta_{f}-4\Delta_{f},\\ g(a_{1}-a_{4})\in\Delta_{g}-2\Delta_{g},\quad g(a_{2}-a_{3})\in\Delta_{g}-2\Delta_{g}\\ h(a_{1}+a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4})\in 3\Delta_{h}-4\Delta_{h}.\end{gathered} $$

(26) Furthermore, each tuple $(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})$ satisfying Eq. 26 can contribute at most $n^{o(1)}$ such $4$ -cycles. Notice that if $a_{2}=a_{3}$ or $a_{1}=a_{4}$ , then the above walk from $(0,y_{1},z_{1})$ back to $(0,y_{1},z_{1})$ actually uses duplicated edges, so it is not a $4$ -cycle. Thus, we can assume $a_{2}\neq a_{3}$ and $a_{1}\neq a_{4}$ . We consider the following types of tuples $(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})$ satisfying Eq. 26: – $a_{1}+a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4}=0$ . In this case, the probability that $g(a_{1}-a_{4})\in\Delta_{g}-2\Delta_{g}$ is $n^{o(1)}/p$ , so the expected number of such tuples satisfying Eq. 26 is bounded by $\mathsf{E}(A)\cdot n^{o(1)}/p=n^{2+\delta+o(1)}/p$ . – $a_{1}+a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4}=0$ . Fix any tuple $(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})$ with $a_{1}+a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4}\neq 0$ . By Lemma 5.10, the probability that $f(a_{1}+a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4})\in 3\Delta_{f}-4\Delta_{f}$ is $n^{o(1)}/p$ , and the probability that $h(a_{1}+a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4})\in 3\Delta_{h}-4\Delta_{h}$ is $n^{o(1)}/p$ . So the probability that the tuple satisfies these two conditions is $n^{o(1)}/p^{2}$ . We then consider two subcases: * $a_{1}-a_{4},a_{2}-a_{3},0$ have a $3$ -term $n^{o(1)}$ -relation. In this case, given $a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}$ , there can only be $n^{o(1)}$ choices for $a_{4}$ , so the number of such tuples is $n^{3+o(1)}$ . For each such tuple, the probability that $g(a_{1}-a_{4})\in\Delta_{g}-2\Delta_{g}$ is $n^{o(1)}/p$ . Combined with the probability that $f(a_{1}+a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4})\in 3\Delta_{f}-4\Delta_{f}$ and $h(a_{1}+a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4})\in 3\Delta_{h}-4\Delta_{h}$ both hold, each such tuple satisfies Eq. 26 with probability $n^{o(1)}/p^{3}$ , so the expected number of such tuples satisfying Eq. 26 is $n^{3+o(1)}/p^{3}$ . * $a_{1}-a_{4},a_{2}-a_{3},0$ have no $3$ -term $n^{o(1)}$ -relation. In this case, the probability that $g(a_{1}-a_{4})\in\Delta_{g}-2\Delta_{g},g(a_{2}-a_{3})\in\Delta_{g}-2\Delta_{g}$ both hold is $n^{o(1)}/p^{2}$ by Lemma 5.10. Thus, the expected number of such tuples satisfying Eq. 26 is $n^{4+o(1)}/p^{4}$ .

- • The $4$ -cycle (with edge labels) is $(0,y_{1},z_{1})\overset{a_{1}}{-}(x_{2},0,z_{2})\overset{a_{2}}{-}(0,y_{3},z_{3})\overset{a_{3}}{-}(x_{4},0,z_{4})\overset{a_{4}}{-}(0,y_{1},z_{1})$ . Such a $4$ -cycle exists only if the following set of equations hold: $\displaystyle x_{2}\in f(a_{1})+\Delta_{f},\quad$ $\displaystyle x_{2}\in f(a_{2})+\Delta_{f},\quad$ $\displaystyle x_{4}\in f(a_{3})+\Delta_{f},\quad$ $\displaystyle x_{4}\in f(a_{4})+\Delta_{f},$ $\displaystyle-y_{1}\in g(a_{1})+\Delta_{g},\quad$ $\displaystyle-y_{3}\in g(a_{2})+\Delta_{g},\quad$ $\displaystyle-y_{3}\in g(a_{3})+\Delta_{g},\quad$ $\displaystyle-y_{1}\in g(a_{4})+\Delta_{g},$ $\displaystyle z_{2}-z_{1}\in h(a_{1})+\Delta_{h},\quad$ $\displaystyle z_{2}-z_{3}\in h(a_{2})+\Delta_{h},\quad$ $\displaystyle z_{4}-z_{3}\in h(a_{3})+\Delta_{h},\quad$ $\displaystyle z_{4}-z_{1}\in h(a_{4})+\Delta_{h}.$ These equations imply

$$ \displaystyle f(a_{1})-f(a_{2})\in\Delta_{f}-\Delta_{f},\quad f(a_{4})-f(a_{3})\in\Delta_{f}-\Delta_{f}, $$



$$ \displaystyle g(a_{1})-g(a_{4})\in\Delta_{g}-\Delta_{g},\quad g(a_{2})-g(a_{3})\in\Delta_{g}-\Delta_{g} $$



$$ \displaystyle h(a_{1})+h(a_{3})-h(a_{2})-h(a_{4})\in 2\Delta_{h}-2\Delta_{h}, $$

which further imply

$$ \begin{gathered}f(a_{1}-a_{2})\in\Delta_{f}-2\Delta_{f},\quad f(a_{4}-a_{3})\in\Delta_{f}-2\Delta_{f},\\ g(a_{1}-a_{4})\in\Delta_{g}-2\Delta_{g},\quad g(a_{2}-a_{3})\in\Delta_{g}-2\Delta_{g}\\ h(a_{1}+a_{3}-a_{2}-a_{4})\in 3\Delta_{h}-4\Delta_{h}.\end{gathered} $$

(27) Additionally, for every tuple $(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})\in A^{4}$ satisfying Eq. 27, there can be at most $n^{o(1)}p$ $4$ -cycles of this type in the graph with labels $a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}$ (the $p$ factor comes from the $p$ choices of $z_{1}$ ). Similar as before, we can assume $a_{1}\neq a_{2},a_{2}\neq a_{3},a_{3}\neq a_{4},a_{4}\neq a_{1}$ , as otherwise the $4$ -cycle degenerates to a $4$ -walk. We consider the following types of tuples satisfying Eq. 27 (and the number of corresponding $4$ -cycles is a factor of $n^{o(1)}\cdot p$ larger): – $a_{1}-a_{4}=a_{2}-a_{3}$ . The number of such tuples is $\mathsf{E}(A)$ . For each such tuple, the probability that $f(a_{1}-a_{2})\in\Delta_{f}-2\Delta_{f}$ is $n^{o(1)}/p$ , and the probability that $g(a_{1}-a_{4})\in\Delta_{g}-2\Delta_{g}$ is $n^{o(1)}/p$ . These two events are independent, so the probability that each tuple satisfies Eq. 27 is $n^{o(1)}/p^{2}$ , and thus the expected number of $(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})$ with $a_{1}-a_{4}=a_{2}-a_{3}$ satisfying Eq. 27 is $\mathsf{E}(A)\cdot n^{o(1)}/p^{2}=n^{2+\delta+o(1)}/p^{2}$ . – $a_{1}-a_{4}\neq a_{2}-a_{3}$ . In this case, we consider four subcases: * $a_{1}-a_{2},a_{4}-a_{3},0$ have a $3$ -term $n^{o(1)}$ -relation and $a_{1}-a_{4},a_{2}-a_{3},0$ have a $3$ -term $n^{o(1)}$ -relation. In this case, there are rational numbers $C$ and $D$ whose denominator and numerator are both $n^{o(1)}$ such that $a_{1}-a_{2}=C(a_{4}-a_{3})$ and $a_{1}-a_{4}=D(a_{2}-a_{3})$ . Rearranging the equations, we get that $a_{1}-a_{2}=C(a_{4}-a_{3})$ and $a_{1}-Da_{2}=a_{4}-Da_{3}$ . We know $D\neq 1$ as $a_{1}-a_{4}\neq a_{2}-a_{3}$ , so we can uniquely solve $a_{1},a_{2}$ given $a_{3},a_{4},C,D$ . Therefore, the number of $(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})\in A^{4}$ falling into this case is $n^{2+o(1)}$ . For each such $(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})$ , the probability they satisfy Eq. 27 is $n^{o(1)}/p^{3}$ , so the expected number of tuples satisfying Eq. 27 this case is $n^{2+o(1)}/p^{3}$ . * $a_{1}-a_{2},a_{4}-a_{3},0$ have a $3$ -term $n^{o(1)}$ -relation and $a_{1}-a_{4},a_{2}-a_{3},0$ have no $3$ -term $n^{o(1)}$ -relation. Here, the number of such tuples is $n^{3+o(1)}$ , as given $a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}$ and the coefficients for the $3$ -term $n^{o(1)}$ -relation, we can uniquely determine $a_{4}$ . For each such tuple, the probability that $g(a_{1}-a_{4})\in\Delta_{g}-2\Delta_{g}$ and $g(a_{2}-a_{3})\in\Delta_{g}-2\Delta_{g}$ is $n^{o(1)}/p^{2}$ , as $a_{1}-a_{4},a_{2}-a_{3},0$ have no $3$ -term $n^{o(1)}$ -relation. The probability that $f(a_{1}-a_{2})\in\Delta_{f}-2\Delta_{f}$ and the probability that $h(a_{1}+a_{3}-a_{2}-a_{4})\in 3\Delta_{h}-4\Delta_{h}$ are both $n^{o(1)}/p$ . The previous three events are independent, so the expected number of tuples satisfying Eq. 27 this case is $n^{3+o(1)}/p^{4}$ . * $a_{1}-a_{2},a_{4}-a_{3},0$ have no $3$ -term $n^{o(1)}$ -relation and $a_{1}-a_{4},a_{2}-a_{3},0$ have a $3$ -term $n^{o(1)}$ -relation. This case is symmetric to the previous case, and the expected number is $n^{3+o(1)}/p^{4}$ . * Both $a_{1}-a_{2},a_{4}-a_{3},0$ and $a_{1}-a_{4},a_{2}-a_{3},0$ have no $3$ -term $n^{o(1)}$ -relations. The number of such tuples is $O(n^{4})$ , and each tuple satisfies Eq. 27 with probability $n^{o(1)}/p^{5}$ by Lemma 5.10. Thus, the expected number of tuples satisfying Eq. 27 this case is $n^{4+o(1)}/p^{5}$ .

Overall, the expected number of $4$ -cycles is

$$ n^{2+\delta+o(1)}/p+n^{4+o(1)}/p^{4}+n^{2+o(1)}/p^{2}+n^{3+o(1)}/p^{4}+n^{4+o(1)}/p^{4}=n^{2+\delta+o(1)}/p+n^{4+o(1)}/p^{4}. $$

### 10.2 Derandomization

The randomness of the above construction comes from the random choices of the hash functions $f,g,h$ . By Definition 5.5, the size of the hash family is $p^{O(1)}$ , so it will be expensive to enumerate over all triples of hash functions when $p$ is big. Similar to [FKP24], the idea for derandomization is to pick hash functions from smaller families (say when $p=n^{\epsilon}$ , the hash family will have size $n^{O(\epsilon)}$ ), and taking their direct product to get the final hash function.

We need the following lemma.

#### Lemma 10.2.

Let $A\subset[n^{O(1)}]$ be a size- $n$ set without 3SUM solutions, and $p=\Theta(n^{\epsilon})$ be a prime. Let $F,G,H:\{-N,\ldots,N\}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k}$ for some constant $k$ be hash functions, where for any $x,y\in\{-N,\ldots,N\}$ , $F(x+y)-F(x)-F(y)\in\Delta_{F},G(x+y)-G(x)-G(y)\in\Delta_{G},H(x+y)-H(x)-H(y)\in\Delta_{H}$ for $|\Delta_{F}|,|\Delta_{G}|,|\Delta_{H}|=n^{o(1)}$ . Additionally, evaluating $F,G,H$ takes $n^{o(1)}$ time. For any $f,g,h\in\mathcal{H}$ from the family in Definition 5.5 with parameter $p$ , define $F\times f:\{-N,\ldots,N\}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k+1}$ by $(F\times f)(x)=(F(x),f(x))$ , and define $\Delta_{F\times f}=\Delta_{F}\times\Delta_{f}$ , and similarly define $G\times g,\Delta_{G\times g}$ and $H\times h,\Delta_{H\times h}$ . Then there exist $f,g,h\in\mathcal{H}$ , so that the following properties hold:

$$ \sum_{a\neq b\in A}[(F\times f)(a)=(F\times f)(b)]\leq O(1/p)\cdot\sum_{a\neq b\in A}[F(a)=F(b)]. $$

The same holds when replacing $(F,f)$ with $(G,g)$ or $(H,h)$ .

- 2. It holds that:

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a,b,c\in A\end{subarray}}[(F\times f)(a)+(F\times f)(b)+(F\times f)(c)\in-3\Delta_{F\times f}]\leq\frac{n^{o(1)}}{p}\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a,b,c\in A\end{subarray}}[F(a)+F(b)+F(c)\in-3\Delta_{F}]. $$

The same holds when replacing $(F,f)$ with $(G,g)$ or $(H,h)$ .

- 5. It holds that: $\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}\in A^{4}\\ a_{2}\neq a_{3},a_{1}\neq a_{4}\\ a_{1}-a_{4}\neq a_{3}-a_{2}\\ a_{1}-a_{4},a_{2}-a_{3},0\text{ do not have }n^{o(1)}\text{-relation}\end{subarray}}\mathcal{C}_{F\times f,G\times g,H\times h}(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})$ $\displaystyle\leq\frac{n^{o(1)}}{p^{4}}\cdot{}$ $\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}\in A^{4}\\ a_{2}\neq a_{3},a_{1}\neq a_{4}\\ a_{1}-a_{4}\neq a_{3}-a_{2}\\ a_{1}-a_{4},a_{2}-a_{3},0\text{ do not have }n^{o(1)}\text{-relation}\end{subarray}}\mathcal{C}_{F,G,H}(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}).$ The same holds for any permutation of $(F,f),(G,g),(H,h)$ .

It holds that: $\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}\in A^{4}\\ a_{1}\neq a_{2},a_{2}\neq a_{3},a_{3}\neq a_{4},a_{4}\neq a_{1}\\ a_{1}-a_{4}\neq a_{2}-a_{3}\\ \text{exactly one of }(a_{1}-a_{2},a_{4}-a_{3},0)\text{ and }(a_{1}-a_{4},a_{2}-a_{3},0)\\ \text{has 3-term }n^{o(1)}\text{-relation}\end{subarray}}\mathcal{D}_{F\times f,G\times g,H\times h}(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})$ $\displaystyle\leq\frac{n^{o(1)}}{p^{4}}\cdot{}$ $\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}\in A^{4}\\ a_{1}\neq a_{2},a_{2}\neq a_{3},a_{3}\neq a_{4},a_{4}\neq a_{1}\\ a_{1}-a_{4}\neq a_{2}-a_{3}\\ \text{exactly one of }(a_{1}-a_{2},a_{4}-a_{3},0)\text{ and }(a_{1}-a_{4},a_{2}-a_{3},0)\\ \text{has 3-term }n^{o(1)}\text{-relation}\end{subarray}}\mathcal{D}_{F,G,H}(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}).$ The same holds for any permutation of $(F,f),(G,g),(H,h)$ .

- 9. It holds that: $\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}\in A^{4}\\ a_{1}\neq a_{2},a_{2}\neq a_{3},a_{3}\neq a_{4},a_{4}\neq a_{1}\\ a_{1}-a_{4}\neq a_{2}-a_{3}\\ \text{neither }(a_{1}-a_{2},a_{4}-a_{3},0)\text{ nor }(a_{1}-a_{4},a_{2}-a_{3},0)\\ \text{has 3-term }n^{o(1)}\text{-relation}\end{subarray}}\mathcal{D}_{F\times f,G\times g,H\times h}(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})$ $\displaystyle\leq\frac{n^{o(1)}}{p^{5}}\cdot{}$ $\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}\in A^{4}\\ a_{1}\neq a_{2},a_{2}\neq a_{3},a_{3}\neq a_{4},a_{4}\neq a_{1}\\ a_{1}-a_{4}\neq a_{2}-a_{3}\\ \text{neither }(a_{1}-a_{2},a_{4}-a_{3},0)\text{ nor }(a_{1}-a_{4},a_{2}-a_{3},0)\\ \text{has 3-term }n^{o(1)}\text{-relation}\end{subarray}}\mathcal{D}_{F,G,H}(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}).$ The same holds for any permutation of $(F,f),(G,g),(H,h)$ .

Additionally, we can find such $f,g,h$ in time

$$ n^{O(\epsilon)}\cdot\left(n+p^{k}+\sum_{W\in\{F,G,H\}}\sum_{a\neq b\in A}[W(a)-W(b)\in\Delta_{W}-\Delta_{W}]\right). $$

#### Proof Sketch.

For random $f,g,h\in\mathcal{H}$ , one can show that the expectation of the left hand side is upper bounded by the right hand side, for each of the inequalities, by Lemma 5.10 (similar to Section 10.1). Therefore, by union bound, there exist $f,g,h$ where the left hand side is upper bounded by $100$ times its expectation, for all the inequalities.

The majority of the proof is dedicated to computing the right hand sides given $F,G,H$ (and also similarly the left hand sides given $F,G,H,f,g,h$ ) deterministically. Then it suffices to try all possible choices of $f,g,h$ and choose one that satisfy the inequalities.

- • Computing Item 1. Clearly, we can compute the right hand side in $n^{1+o(1)}$ time.

- • Computing Item 2. Here, we can embed $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k}$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ (i.e., view all elements in $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k}$ as a number in base $3p$ ), and then use FFT to compute the right hand side in $\widetilde{O}((3p)^{k})=\widetilde{O}(p^{k})$ time.

- • Computing Items 3, 4 and 5. For every pair of integers $C,D$ bounded by $n^{o(1)}$ in absolute values, we aim to compute

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}\in A^{4}\\ a_{2}\neq a_{3},a_{1}\neq a_{4}\\ C(a_{1}-a_{4})+D(a_{2}-a_{3})=0\end{subarray}}\mathcal{C}_{F,G,H}(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}). $$

Clearly, the above values are sufficient for computing Items 3, 4 and 5. Recall $\mathcal{C}_{F,G,H}(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})$ is the indicator variable for the following conditions:

$$ \begin{gathered}F(a_{1})+F(a_{2})-F(a_{3})-F(a_{4})\in 2\Delta_{F}-2\Delta_{F},\\ G(a_{1})-G(a_{4})\in\Delta_{G}-\Delta_{G},\quad G(a_{2})-G(a_{3})\in\Delta_{G}-\Delta_{G}\\ H(a_{1})+H(a_{2})-H(a_{3})-H(a_{4})\in 2\Delta_{H}-2\Delta_{H}.\end{gathered} $$

First, we enumerate $a_{1}\neq a_{4}\in A$ where $G(a_{1})-G(a_{4})\in\Delta_{G}-\Delta_{G}$ (after an $n^{1+o(1)}$ preprocessing, we can perform this enumeration in $O(n^{1+o(1)}+\sum_{a\neq b\in A}[G(a)-G(b)\in\Delta_{G}-\Delta_{G}])$ ) time, and then insert

$$ \left(F(a_{1})-F(a_{4}),H(a_{1})-H(a_{4}),C(a_{1}-a_{4})\right) $$

to a multiset. Then we enumerate $a_{2}\neq a_{3}\in A$ where $G(a_{2})-G(a_{3})\in\Delta_{G}-\Delta_{G}$ , and we add the number of points in the multiset inside

$$ \left(F(a_{3})-F(a_{2})+2\Delta_{F}-2\Delta_{F},H(a_{3})-H(a_{2})+2\Delta_{H}-2\Delta_{H},-D(a_{2}-a_{3})\right) $$

to the final answer. The running time of this algorithm is

$$ n^{1+o(1)}+n^{o(1)}\cdot\sum_{a\neq b\in A}[G(a)-G(b)\in\Delta_{G}-\Delta_{G}]. $$

- • Computing Items 6, 7, 8 and 9. For every integers $C_{1},D_{1},C_{2},D_{2}$ bounded by $n^{o(1)}$ in absolute values, we aim to compute

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}\in A^{4}\\ a_{1}\neq a_{2},a_{2}\neq a_{3},a_{3}\neq a_{4},a_{4}\neq a_{1}\\ C_{1}(a_{1}-a_{2})=D_{1}(a_{4}-a_{3})\\ C_{2}(a_{1}-a_{4})=D_{2}(a_{2}-a_{3})\end{subarray}}\mathcal{D}_{F,G,H}(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}). $$

Clearly, we can compute Items 6, 7, 8 and 9 once we compute the above values for all $C_{1},D_{1},C_{2},D_{2}$ . Recall $\mathcal{D}_{F,G,H}(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})$ is the indicator variable for the following conditions:

$$ \begin{gathered}F(a_{1})-F(a_{2})\in\Delta_{F}-\Delta_{F},\quad F(a_{4})-F(a_{3})\in\Delta_{F}-\Delta_{F},\\ G(a_{1})-G(a_{4})\in\Delta_{G}-\Delta_{G},\quad G(a_{2})-G(a_{3})\in\Delta_{G}-\Delta_{G}\\ H(a_{1})+H(a_{3})-H(a_{2})-H(a_{4})\in 2\Delta_{H}-2\Delta_{H}.\end{gathered} $$

First, we enumerate $a_{1}\neq a_{4}\in A$ where $G(a_{1})-G(a_{4})\in\Delta_{G}-\Delta_{G}$ . Similar to the previous case, this can be done in $O(n^{1+o(1)}+\sum_{a\neq b\in A}[G(a)-G(b)\in\Delta_{G}-\Delta_{G}])$ time. Then we add

$$ \left(F(a_{1}),F(a_{4}),H(a_{1})-H(a_{4}),a_{1},a_{4}\right) $$

to a multiset. Then we enumerate $a_{2}\neq a_{3}\in A$ where $G(a_{2})-G(a_{3})\in\Delta_{G}-\Delta_{G}$ , query how many points in the multiset are in

$$ \left(F(a_{2})+\Delta_{F}-\Delta_{F},F(a_{3})+\Delta_{F}-\Delta_{F},H(a_{2})-H(a_{3})+2\Delta_{H}-2\Delta_{H},\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{a_{2}\},\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{a_{3}\}\right), $$

and add this count to the final answer. Using data structure, each insertion and query can be performed in $n^{o(1)}$ time, so the overall running time is

$$ n^{1+o(1)}+n^{o(1)}\cdot\sum_{a\neq b\in A}[G(a)-G(b)\in\Delta_{G}-\Delta_{G}]. $$

∎

Now the idea is to apply Lemma 10.2 $O(1/\epsilon)$ times to find the final hash functions. However, the running time Lemma 10.2 has a dependency on $\sum_{W\in\{F,G,H\}}\sum_{a\neq b\in A}[W(a)-W(b)\in\Delta_{W}-\Delta_{W}])$ which can be as large as $O(n^{2})$ . Therefore, we need to perform the next lemma several times first.

#### Lemma 10.3.

Let $A\subset[n^{O(1)}]$ be a size- $n$ set, and $p=\Theta(n^{\epsilon})$ be a prime. Let $F:\{-N,\ldots,N\}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k}$ for some constant $k$ be a hash function, where for any $x,y\in\{-N,\ldots,N\}$ , $F(x+y)-F(x)-F(y)\in\Delta_{F}$ and $|\Delta_{F}|=n^{o(1)}$ . Additionally, evaluating $F$ takes $n^{o(1)}$ time. For any $f\in\mathcal{H}$ from the family in Definition 5.5 with parameter $p$ , define $F\times f:\{-N,\ldots,N\}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k+1}$ by $(F\times f)(x)=(F(x),f(x))$ , and define $\Delta_{F\times f}=\Delta_{F}\times\Delta_{f}$ . Then there exists $f\in\mathcal{H}$ , so that

$$ \sum_{a\neq b\in A}[(F\times f)(a)-(F\times f)(b)\in\Delta_{F\times f}-\Delta_{F\times f}]\leq\frac{n^{o(1)}}{p}\sum_{a\neq b\in A}[F(a)-F(b)\in\Delta_{F}-\Delta_{F}]. $$

Additionally, we can find $f$ in $n^{1+O(\epsilon)}$ time.

We omit the proof of 10.3 as it is similar to (and simpler than) the proof of Lemma 10.2.

Finally, we are ready to prove Theorem 10.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 10.1.

We first call Lemma 10.3 $\ell=O(1)$ times iteratively, and reset $F:=F\times f$ after every iteration, to obtain $F$ , so that

$$ \sum_{a\neq b\in A}[(F\times f)(a)-(F\times f)(b)\in\Delta_{F\times f}-\Delta_{F\times f}]\leq n^{2-C\epsilon} $$

for a sufficiently large constant $C$ . The running time is $n^{1+O(\epsilon)}$ .

Then we set $G,H=F$ , and then call Lemma 10.2 $k=\log_{n}P/\epsilon$ times iteratively (after each call, set $F:=F\times f,G:=G\times g,H:=H\times h$ ). The running time will be $n^{1+O(\epsilon)}+n^{O(\epsilon)+2-C\epsilon}$ . As $C$ is sufficiently large, the running time can be made $n^{1+O(\epsilon)}+n^{2-\epsilon}$ .

One caveat is that Lemma 10.2 requires that $A$ to not contain 3SUM solutions. However, we can run Lemma 10.2 on $A$ regardless, and if at any point, the lemma fails, we can immediately conclude that $A$ has a 3SUM solution. Thus, even if $A$ contains 3SUM solutions, we will end up getting desired hash functions $F,G,H$ .

The remainder of the proof is largely similar to the proof in Section 10.1. The key differences are that the nodes of the graph is

$$ \{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\ell+k}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\ell+k},\quad\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\ell+k}\times\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\ell+k},\quad\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\ell+k}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\ell+k}\times\{0\} $$

where $p^{\ell+k}=P\cdot n^{O(\epsilon)}$ , and the hash functions to use if $(F,G,H)$ instead of $(f,g,h)$ . The number of vertices becomes $O((P\cdot n^{O(\epsilon)})^{2})=P^{2}\cdot n^{O(\epsilon)}$ . By Lemma 10.2 Item 1, we have

$$ \sum_{a\neq b\in A}[F(a)=F(b)]=O(1/p^{k})\cdot n^{2}=O(n^{2}/P). $$

The number of elements that are in bucket (under $F$ ) with $\geq n^{1+\epsilon}/P$ elements is $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ , so we can test whether any of them is in a 3SUM solution and then remove them in $O(n^{2-\epsilon})$ time. We can similarly do so for buckets under $G$ and $H$ as well. Thus, then the maximum degree of the graph is bounded by $O(n^{1+\epsilon}/P)$ , similar to Section 10.1. The running time for constructing the graphs is essentially the total number of edges of all graphs, which is $P^{2}\cdot n^{O(\epsilon)}\cdot n^{1+\epsilon}/P=n^{1+O(\epsilon)}\cdot P$ .

The bound on the number of triangles and the number of $4$ -cycles similarly follow from a combination of the bounds in Lemma 10.2 and the analysis in Section 10.1. We omit the details for conciseness. ∎

Next we use Theorem 10.1 to prove Theorem 1.2, which we recall below: See 1.2

#### Proof.

For the sake of contradiction, suppose such an $O(n^{2-\delta}+t)$ time or $O(m^{4/3-\delta}+t)$ time algorithm for $4$ -Cycle Listing exists for some $\delta>0$ , and we will use it to design a deterministic truly subquadratic time algorithm for 3SUM, violating the deterministic 3SUM hypothesis.

First, by Theorem 1.1, it suffices to solve 3SUM instances with additive energy $\leq n^{2.01}$ . Then we run Theorem 10.1 with $\epsilon=\delta/C$ for a sufficiently large $C$ with $C/\delta$ being an integer and $k=1+C/\delta$ (so that $P=n^{1/2+\delta/C}$ ) in $O(n^{2-\delta/C}+n^{3/2+O(\delta/C)})$ time to further reduce to $n^{o(1)}$ Triangle Listing instances on graphs with

- • $n^{1+O(\delta/C)}$ nodes;

- • $n^{0.5}$ maximum degree (thus, $n^{1.5+O(\delta/C)}$ edges);

- • $n^{1.51-\delta/C+o(1)}+n^{2-4\delta/C+o(1)}$ $4$ -cycles,

and for each graph we need to list $n^{2-2\delta/C+o(1)}$ triangles. The running time becomes $O(n^{2-\delta/C})$ for sufficiently large $C$ , which is truly subquadratic.

For each produced Triangle Listing instance on some graph $G$ , we use the following standard reduction [ABKZ22, ABF23, JX23] to reduce it to a $4$ -Cycle Listing instance. We create four node sets $V_{1},V_{2},V_{3},V_{4}$ , each being a copy of $V(G)$ . Between $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ , we add a matching. Between $V_{2}$ and $V_{3}$ , $V_{3}$ and $V_{4}$ , and $V_{4}$ and $V_{1}$ , we add copies of $E(G)$ . Observe that $4$ -cycles in the new graph that use one node from each of $V_{1},V_{2},V_{3},V_{4}$ correspond to triangles in $G$ , while all other $4$ -cycles correspond to $4$ -cycles in $G$ . Furthermore, each $4$ -cycle in $G$ only adds $O(1)$ $4$ -cycles in the new graph. Therefore, it suffices to list $n^{1.51-\delta/C+o(1)}+n^{2-4\delta/C+o(1)}+n^{2-2\delta/C+o(1)}=n^{2-2\delta/C+o(1)}$ $4$ -cycles (for sufficiently large $C$ ) in the new graph.

The bounds on number of nodes and edges in the new graph are only a constant factor larger than those in $G$ . Thus, we can apply the assumed $4$ -Cycle Listing algorithm on the new graph to obtain a running time

$$ \left(n^{1+O(\delta/C)}\right)^{2-\delta}+n^{2-2\delta/C+o(1)} $$

or

$$ \left(n^{1.5+O(\delta/C)}\right)^{4/3-\delta}+n^{2-2\delta/C+o(1)}, $$

either of which achieves a truly subquadratic running time for sufficiently large $C$ . ∎

## 11 $k$ -Mismatch Constellation

Recall that in the Constellation with mismatches problem, we are given integer sets $A,B\subseteq[N]$ with $|A|,|B|\leq n$ and a parameter $1\leq k\leq|B|$ , and the task is to compute the set

$$ \{c\in\mathbb{Z}:|(c+B)\setminus A|<k\}. $$

As in previous works on this question, we impose the condition $k\leq(1-\eta)|B|$ for a fixed constant $\eta\in(0,1)$ , so that the output size is at most $\frac{|A||B|}{|B|-k}\leq\eta^{-1}|A|=O(n)$ . Here we let $\eta=0.7$ . The case where $\eta$ is a smaller (but fixed) constant in $(0,0.7)$ (in particular, $k=\Theta(|B|)$ ) can be solved via different methods: using [CVX23, Lemma 8.4] (randomized) or our Theorem 1.12 (deterministic), we can solve it in $n^{2-\Omega(1)}=k^{1-\Omega(1)}\cdot n$ time.

Our algorithm for Constellation with $k$ mismatches first reduces the original problem to the following partial convolution problem with promise (Problem 11.1). This reduction is simple but randomized, so the algorithm obtained this way will be randomized as well (we stress that our result is new even allowing randomization). Later in Section 11.2 we will describe how to derandomize this algorithm.

#### Problem 11.1.

Given sets $A,B,C\subseteq[N]$ , and parameter $k\leq(1-\eta)|B|$ for some fixed constant $\eta\in(0,1)$ , with the promise that

$$ |(c+B)\setminus A|\leq k $$

for all $c\in C$ , the task is to compute $(1_{A}\star 1_{-B})[c]$ for all $c\in C$ .

#### Proposition 11.2 (Simple reduction via subsampling).

There is a randomized reduction from Constellation with $k_{0}$ mismatches (where $k_{0}\leq(1-\eta_{0})|B|$ ) to Problem 11.1 with the same input sets $A,B$ , and parameter $k=(1+\eta_{0}/20)k_{0}\leq(1-0.95\eta_{0})|B|$ , and $|C|\leq 2\eta_{0}^{-1}|A|$ . The reduction takes time $\widetilde{O}(|A|+|B|)$ .

#### Proof.

Denote $n:=|A|+|B|$ . First, assume $k_{0}\geq 100\eta_{0}^{-2}\log n$ , since otherwise the algorithm of [CS98, Fis24] already solves Constellation with $k_{0}$ mismatches in $\widetilde{O}(nk_{0})\leq\widetilde{O}(n)$ time.

Subsample $B^{\prime}\subseteq B$ by keeping each $b\in B$ independently with probability $p=\frac{100\log n}{\eta_{0}^{2}k_{0}}$ . By Chernoff bound and $|B|>k_{0}\geq 100\eta_{0}^{-2}\log n$ , we have $|B^{\prime}|\in(1\pm\eta_{0}/20)p|B|$ with $1-\exp(-\Omega(\eta_{0}^{2}p|B|))=1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(n)$ probability. Let $k^{\prime}=(1+\eta_{0}/40)pk_{0}$ . Then, for every $c\in\mathbb{Z}$ , the following holds with $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(n)$ probability by Chernoff bound:

- 1. If $|(c+B)\setminus A|\leq k_{0}$ , then $|(c+B^{\prime})\setminus A|\leq k^{\prime}$ .

- 2. If $|(c+B)\setminus A|>(1+\eta_{0}/20)k_{0}$ , then $|(c+B^{\prime})\setminus A|>k^{\prime}$ .

By a union bound, the properties above hold for all $c\in A-B$ , with $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(n)$ probability. Hence we can run the algorithm of [CS98, Fis24] to solve the Constellation with $k^{\prime}$ mismatches instance $(A,B^{\prime})$ in $\widetilde{O}(nk^{\prime})=\widetilde{O}(n)$ time (note $k^{\prime}<(1-0.1\eta_{0})|B^{\prime}|$ still holds), and obtain $C=\{c\in\mathbb{Z}:|(c+B^{\prime})\setminus A|\leq k^{\prime}\}$ . By Item 1 above, $C$ is a set of candidates which contains all possible answers in the original Constellation with $k_{0}$ mismatches instance $(A,B)$ (with $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(n)$ probability). Note that by Item 2 above, $|C|\leq\frac{|A||B|}{|B|-(1+\eta_{0}/20)k_{0}}\leq 2\eta_{0}^{-1}|A|$ . Then, it remains to compute $(1_{A}\star 1_{-B})[c]$ for all $c\in C$ , and output all $c\in C$ satisfying $(1_{A}\star 1_{-B})[c]>|B|-k_{0}$ . This is the task of Problem 11.1 and satisfies the promise of Problem 11.1 for $k:=(1+\eta_{0}/20)k_{0}$ (by Item 2 above). This finishes the description of the reduction. ∎

Fischer [Fis24] already gave an algorithm solving Problem 11.1 which is efficient when $C$ is small:

#### Lemma 11.3 (follows from [Fis24]).

Problem 11.1 has a deterministic algorithm in $\widetilde{O}(|A|+|B|+k|C|)$ time.

#### Proof.

Note that

$$ |B+C|\leq|A|+\sum_{c\in C}|(c+B)\setminus A|\underset{\text{\lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{eqn:promisec}}}{\leq}|A|+k|C|. $$

Using Lemma 2.2, we can compute $(1_{A}\star 1_{-B})[c]$ for all $c\in C$ in $\widetilde{O}(|A|+|B+C|)\leq\widetilde{O}(|A|+|B|+k|C|)$ time. ∎

### 11.1 Algorithm for large $B$

The goal of this section is to prove the randomized version of Theorem 1.5 ( $k$ -mismatch Constellation for small $B$ ) as a warm-up. To do this, we will solve Problem 11.1. The algorithm for Problem 11.1 itself will be deterministic, but it only implies a randomized version of Theorem 1.5 due to the randomness in the reduction to Problem 11.1 in Proposition 11.2. We will modify this randomized algorithm into a deterministic one (hence fully proving Theorem 1.5) in the next subsection, using a standard scaling technique.

In Problem 11.1, we denote $L=|A|/|B|$ , and we think of $L$ as small.

Since we originally started with Constellation with $k\leq 0.3|B|$ mismatches (as stated in Theorem 1.5), after the reduction of Proposition 11.2 we still have

$$ k\leq 0.4|B|. $$

Let $1\leq R\leq k$ be a parameter to be determined later. If $|C|\leq|A|/R$ , then we can use Lemma 11.3 and solve Problem 11.1 in $\widetilde{O}(|A|+|B|+k\cdot|C|)\leq\widetilde{O}(k|A|/R)$ time deterministically, which is faster than $\widetilde{O}(k|A|)$ . Hence, in the following, we assume

$$ |C|\geq|A|/R. $$

#### Lemma 11.4.

$|C-C|\leq 5|A|L$ .

#### Proof.

Consider the bipartite graph $G=\{(b,c)\in B\times C:b+c\in A\}$ . The degree of a node $c\in C$ in $G$ is $\geq|B|-k$ by Eq. 28. For every $(c,c^{\prime})\in C\times C$ , since both $c,c^{\prime}$ have degree at least $|B|-k\geq 0.6|B|$ , they have at least $2\cdot(|B|-k)-|B|\geq 0.2|B|$ common neighbors in $G$ . Hence, $c-c^{\prime}$ can be represented as $(c+b)-(c^{\prime}+b)$ where $c+b,c^{\prime}+b\in A$ , for at least $0.2|B|$ many distinct $b$ . Therefore, $(1_{A}\star 1_{A})[c-c^{\prime}]\geq 0.2|B|$ for all $c-c^{\prime}\in C-C$ , and $|C-C|\leq\frac{|A|\cdot|A|}{0.2|B|}=5|A|L$ . ∎

We use Theorem 1.9 to deterministically compute a vector $f$ such that $\|f-1_{A}\star 1_{-C}\|_{\infty}\leq 0.25|C|$ , in $O((|A|+|B|+|C|)N^{o(1)})$ time, and let $B_{\mathrm{bad}}:=\{b\in B:f[b]\leq 0.5|C|\}$ . Then, we know

- • For all $b\in B_{\mathrm{bad}}$ , $(1_{A}\star 1_{-C})[b]\leq 0.75|C|$ .

- • For all $b\in B\setminus B_{\mathrm{bad}}$ , $(1_{A}\star 1_{-C})[b]\geq 0.25|C|$ .

Note that by Eq. 28, $\sum_{b\in B}(1_{A}\star 1_{-C})[b]=\sum_{c\in C}(1_{A}\star 1_{-B})[c]\geq|C|\cdot(|B|-k)$ . Hence,

$$ |B_{\mathrm{bad}}|\leq\frac{\sum_{b\in B}(|C|-(1_{A}\star 1_{-C})[b])}{|C|-0.75|C|}\leq\frac{|B||C|-|C|\cdot(|B|-k)}{0.25|C|}=4k. $$

Let $B^{\prime}=B\setminus B_{\mathrm{bad}}$ .

#### Lemma 11.5.

$|B^{\prime}+C|\leq 20|A|RL$ .

#### Proof.

Consider the bipartite graph $G=\{(b,c)\in B\times C:b+c\in A\}$ . For every $b\in B^{\prime}$ , the degree of $b$ in $G$ is $(1_{A}\star 1_{-C})[b]\geq 0.25|C|$ . Hence, for every $b\in B^{\prime},c\in C$ , $b+c$ can be represented as $(b+c^{\prime})+(c-c^{\prime})$ where $(b+c^{\prime})\in A,(c-c^{\prime})\in(C-C)$ by choosing $c^{\prime}\in C$ from the neighbors of $b$ in $G$ , which has $\geq 0.25|C|$ different possibilities. Therefore, $(1_{A}\star 1_{C-C})[b+c]\geq 0.25|C|$ for all $b+c\in B^{\prime}+C$ , and hence

$$ |B^{\prime}+C|\leq\frac{|A|\cdot|C-C|}{0.25|C|}\underset{\text{\lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{eqn:clb}}}{\leq}4R|C-C|\underset{\text{\lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{lem:cminusc}}}{\leq}20|A|RL. $$

∎

Then, the algorithm decomposes the answers into two parts,

$$ (1_{A}\star 1_{-B})[c]=(1_{A}\star 1_{-B^{\prime}})[c]+(1_{A}\star 1_{-B_{\mathrm{bad}}})[c], $$

which are separately computed as follows for all $c\in C$ :

- • Use Lemma 2.2 to compute $(1_{A}\star 1_{-B^{\prime}})[c]$ for all $c\in C$ , in $\widetilde{O}(|B^{\prime}+C|)\leq\widetilde{O}(|A|RL)$ time by Lemma 11.5 (this running time is dominated by the running time for the next part).

- • Use Theorem 4.1 (applied to $(A,B,C,S):=(C,B_{\mathrm{bad}},A,-C)$ ) to compute $(1_{A}\star 1_{B_{-\mathrm{bad}}})[c]$ for all $c\in C$ , in $\displaystyle\widetilde{O}\Big(\frac{|C-C|\sqrt{|A||B_{\mathrm{bad}}|}}{\sqrt{|-C|}}\Big)+(|C-C|+|A|)N^{o(1)}$ $\displaystyle\leq O\Big(\frac{|A|L\sqrt{|A|\cdot k}}{\sqrt{|A|/R}}N^{o(1)}\Big)$ (by Lemma 11.4, Eq. 29, Eq. 30) $\displaystyle=O(|A|L\sqrt{kR}N^{o(1)}).$

Combined with the running time $\widetilde{O}(|A|k/R)$ for the $|C|<|A|/R$ case, the total time for solving Problem 11.1 becomes

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{O}(|A|k/R)+O(|A|L\sqrt{kR}N^{o(1)}) \displaystyle\leq O(|A|k^{2/3}L^{2/3}N^{o(1)}) $$

by choosing $R=(k/L^{2})^{1/3}\geq 1$ (assuming $L\leq\sqrt{k}$ ; otherwise the $\widetilde{O}(|A|k)$ -time algorithm by [Fis24] already satisfies the claimed time bound).

### 11.2 Derandomization $B$ by scaling

In this section we will prove (the deterministic version of) Theorem 1.5, so we are not allowed to use the randomized reduction to Problem 11.1 any more. The main idea is basically the same as in the previous section, and we only need to apply the scaling trick (e.g., [BN21, BFN22]) on top of it, so we will be brief in the proof. We remark that Fischer’s deterministic algorithm for $k$ -mismatch Constellation [Fis24] also used scaling, but for a multiset (i.e., weighted) version of the problem. Here we avoid dealing with multisets in order to simplify some of the arguments.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.5.

Let $A,B\subseteq[N]$ be the input instance of the $k$ -mismatch Constellation problem, where $k\leq 0.3|B|$ .

At the very beginning, we use Lemma 4.2 to find a modulus $M\in[|B|/2,|B|\cdot N^{o(1)}]$ such that the set $B\bmod M$ has size $|B\bmod M|\geq 0.9|B|$ , in $O(|B|\cdot N^{o(1)})$ time.

We perform iterations $0\leq i\leq\lceil\log_{2}(2N/M)\rceil$ , where in iteration $i$ we define modulus $M_{i}=M\cdot 2^{i}$ , and define sets $A_{i}:=(A\bmod M_{i})+\{0,M_{i}\}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\cap[0,2M_{i}),B_{i}:=B\bmod M_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\cap[0,M_{i})$ . Note that $|B_{i}|\geq|B\bmod M|\geq 0.9|B|$ , so $k\leq 0.3|B|<0.4|B_{i}|$ for all $i$ . We have the following simple observation:

#### Observation 11.6.

For all $0\leq c<M_{i+1}$ , $|(c+B_{i+1})\setminus A_{i+1}|\geq|((c\bmod M_{i})+B_{i})\setminus A_{i}|$ .

#### Proof.

For any element $b_{i}\in B_{i}$ such that $(c\bmod M_{i})+b_{i}\in((c\bmod M_{i})+B_{i})\setminus A_{i}$ , let $b_{i+1}\in B_{i+1}$ be such that $b_{i+1}\in b_{i}+\{0,M_{i}\}$ . If $(c+b_{i+1})\in A_{i+1}$ , then we would have $(c+b_{i})\bmod M_{i}=(c+b_{i+1})\bmod M_{i}\in(A_{i+1})\bmod M_{i}=A\bmod M_{i}$ , so that $((c\bmod M_{i})+b_{i})\in(A\bmod M_{i})+\{0,M_{i}\}=A_{i}$ , a contradiction. Hence, $c+b_{i+1}\in(c+B_{i+1})\setminus A_{i+1}$ . This implies the desired size inequality. ∎

We will maintain the following invariant: at the end of iteration $i$ ( $i\geq 0$ ), we have computed the set

$$ C_{i}:=\{c\in[0,M_{i}):(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{-B_{i}})[c]\geq|B_{i}|-k\}, $$

which has size $|C_{i}|\leq\frac{|A_{i}||B_{i}|}{|B_{i}|-k}=O(|A_{i}|)=O(|A|)$ , and satisfies $|B_{i}+C_{i}|\leq|A_{i}|+k|C_{i}|$ .

This invariant at the end of iteration $0$ can be easily satisfied: we first use FFT to compute $1_{A_{0}}\star 1_{-B_{0}}$ in $\widetilde{O}(M_{0})=O(|B|N^{o(1)})$ time, and let $C_{0}:=\{c\in[0,M_{0}):(1_{A_{0}}\star 1_{-B_{0}})[c]\geq|B_{0}|-k\}$ .

Now we need to satisfy the invariant at the end of iteration $i$ ( $i\geq 1$ ). We already have $C_{i-1}$ from the previous iteration. We run the algorithm from Section 11.1 (in a whitebox manner) on $A_{i-1},B_{i-1},C_{i-1}$ , $k$ , which satisfy the promise of Problem 11.1 that $k\leq 0.4|B_{i-1}|$ and $(c+B_{i-1})\setminus A_{i-1}|\leq k$ for all $c\in C_{i-1}$ (due to the invariant). Now compute $C^{\prime}_{i}=C_{i-1}+\{0,M_{i-1}\}$ . We know $C_{i}\subseteq C^{\prime}_{i}$ . Recall that the algorithm from Section 11.1 has two cases:

- • Case $|C_{i-1}|<|A_{i-1}|/R$ . In this case we have $|B_{i}+C_{i}^{\prime}|\leq|B_{i-1}+\{0,M_{i-1}\}+C_{i-1}+\{0,M_{i-1}\}|\leq 3|B_{i-1}+C_{i-1}|\leq 3(|A_{i}|+k|C_{i-1}|)=O(|A|k/R)$ . So we can compute $(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{-B_{i}})[c]$ for all $c\in C^{\prime}_{i}$ in $\widetilde{O}(|A|k/R)$ time using Lemma 2.2 (similarly to Lemma 11.3).

- • Case $|C_{i-1}|<|A_{i-1}|/R$ . In this case, the algorithm from Section 11.1 computes the decomposition $B_{i-1}=B_{\mathrm{bad}}\cup B^{\prime}$ , such that $|B^{\prime}+C_{i-1}|=O(|A|RL)$ and $|C_{i-1}-C_{i-1}|=O(|A|L)$ , where $L=|A_{i-1}|/|B_{i-1}|\leq|A|/(0.9|B|)$ . We use this to obtain a decomposition $B_{i}=B_{\mathrm{bad},i}\cup B^{\prime}_{i}$ , such that $B_{\mathrm{bad},i}\subseteq B_{\mathrm{bad}}+\{0,M_{i-1}\}$ and $B^{\prime}_{i}\subseteq B^{\prime}+\{0,M_{i-1}\}$ . Then we still have $|B^{\prime}_{i}+C_{i}|\leq 3|B^{\prime}+C_{i-1}|=O(|A|RL)$ and $|C_{i}-C_{i}|\leq 3|C_{i-1}-C_{i-1}|=O(|A|L)$ , and $|B_{\mathrm{bad},i}|\leq 2|B_{\mathrm{bad}}|$ . So we can use the same procedure described at the end of Section 11.2 to compute $(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{-B_{i}})[c]=(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{-B_{i}^{\prime}})[c]+(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{-B_{\mathrm{bad},i}})[c]$ for all $c\in C_{i}^{\prime}$ , and the running time is the same as before up to a constant factor.

In both cases we have computed $(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{-B_{i}})[c]$ for all $c\in C^{\prime}_{i}$ . Since $C_{i}\subseteq C^{\prime}_{i}$ , we use this information to obtain the desired set $C_{i}$ .

When the last iteration $i^{*}$ finishes, since $M_{i^{*}}\geq 2N$ , the set $C_{i^{*}}$ gives the answer to the original $k$ -mismatch Constellation instance. ∎

### 11.3 Combinatorial lower bound

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.6, which we recall below: See 1.6

#### Proof.

For any $0<\alpha\leq 1$ , it was shown in [GU18] that, finding all shifts that result in $\leq k$ mismatches in a Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances instance with text $T$ and pattern $P$ where $|T|=n$ , $|P|=\Theta(n^{\alpha}),k=\Theta(n^{\alpha})$ requires $n^{1+\alpha/2-o(1)}$ time for combinatorial algorithms, under the BMM hypothesis.

We can then further reduce this instance to a $k$ -Mismatch Constellation instance with $\Theta(n)$ -size integer sets $A,B$ . Without loss of generality, we can assume all characters in the Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances instance are integers in $[n]$ . Let $M=10n$ be a sufficiently large integer. Then we let

$$ A:=\{1,\ldots,2n\}\cup\{i+M\cdot T[i]:1\leq i\leq|T|\} $$

and

$$ B:=\{1,\ldots,n\}\cup\{i+M\cdot P[i]:1\leq i\leq|P|\}. $$

For any $0\leq c\leq|T|-|P|$ , consider $\left|(c+B)\setminus A\right|$ . The $c+\{1,\ldots,n\}$ part of $c+B$ will lie in $A$ , so they will not contribute towards $\left|(c+B)\setminus A\right|$ . Hence,

$$ \left|(c+B)\setminus A\right|=\left|\left\{1\leq i\leq|P|:i+c+M\cdot P[i]\not\in A\right\}\right|. $$

For every $1\leq i\leq|P|$ , the only number in $A$ that can possibly be equal to $i+c+M\cdot P[i]$ is $i+c+M\cdot T[i+c]$ , by considering the numbers modulo $M$ (also, $i+c+M\cdot P[i]\geq M$ , so numbers in $\{1,\ldots,2n\}$ cannot be equal to it). Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\left|(c+B)\setminus A\right| \displaystyle=\left|\left\{1\leq i\leq|P|:i+c+M\cdot P[i]=i+c+M\cdot T[i+c]\right\}\right| \displaystyle=\left|\left\{1\leq i\leq|P|:P[i]=T[i+c]\right\}\right|, $$

which is exactly the number of mismatches between $T$ and $P$ with shift $c$ . Hence, if we can solve $k$ -Mismatch Constellation between $A$ and $B$ , we can determine the set of shifts $c$ for $P$ so that its number of mismatches with $T$ is bounded by $k$ . Therefore, by the lower bound from [GU18], $k$ -Mismatch Constellation requires $n^{1+\alpha/2-o(1)}=\sqrt{k}n^{1-o(1)}$ time for combinatorial algorithms, under the BMM hypothesis. ∎

### 11.4 Applications to $k$ -Mismatch String Matching with Wildcards

Given a text string $T[0\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}n)\in\Sigma^{n}$ and a pattern string $P[0\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}m)\in(\Sigma\cup\{\diamondsuit\})^{m}$ , our task is to find all occurrences of $P$ inside $T$ allowing up to $k$ Hamming mismatches (where wildcard $\diamondsuit$ can match any single character). We first present a simple reduction which yields an $\widetilde{O}(k^{2/3}n)$ -time algorithm for this task, and then describe how to improve it to $\widetilde{O}(k^{1/2}n)$ after some small modifications.

Assume $m\leq n\leq 2m$ via the standard trick of dividing $T$ into $\lfloor n/m\rfloor$ (overlapping) chunks each of length $\leq 2m$ .

#### Proof of Corollary 1.7.

View the alphabet $\Sigma$ as integers $\{1,2,\dots,|\Sigma|\}$ . Construct two point sets $A,B\subset\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ by $A:=\{(i,T[i]):0\leq i<n\}$ and $B:=\{(i,P[i]):0\leq i<m,P[i]\neq\diamondsuit\}$ . The key observation is that, for all $c\in\{0,1,\dots,n-m\}$ , $T[c\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}c+m)$ is a $k$ -mismatch occurrence of $P[0\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}m)$ if and only if $\big\lvert\big(B+(c,0)\big)\setminus A\big\rvert\leq k$ . (For every Hamming mismatch $P[i]\neq T[i+c]$ , the point $(c+i,P[i])\in B+(c,0)$ is not in $A$ , contributing one to the size of $(B+(c,0)\big)\setminus A$ . The wildcards do not make any contribution.)

Hence, we can apply our $k$ -mismatch Constellation algorithm (Theorem 1.5) to $A,B$ and obtain the set $C^{\prime}=\{c^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}:|(c^{\prime}+B)\setminus A|<k\}$ , and return $\{c\in\{0,1,\dots,n-m\}:(c,0)\in C^{\prime}\}$ as the answer.1010 10 To invoke Theorem 1.5 we need to first flatten each 2-dimensional point $(x,y)$ into $(yM+x)$ where $M$ is a large enough integer ( $M=10n$ suffices). Assuming $|B|\geq\Omega(m)$ , the (randomized) time complexity of Theorem 1.5 is $\widetilde{O}(|A|\cdot k^{2/3}\cdot(|A|/|B|)^{2/3})=\widetilde{O}(n\cdot k^{2/3}\cdot(n/m)^{2/3})=\widetilde{O}(n\cdot k^{2/3})$ as claimed.

Now we justify the $|B|\geq\Omega(m)$ assumption, as well as the $k<0.3|B|$ assumption required by Theorem 1.5. Note that $|B|$ equals the number of non-wildcard characters in the pattern. We add three non-wildcard characters $\spadesuit_{1}\spadesuit_{2}\spadesuit_{3}$ right after every character in the input pattern and every character in the input text. (The new text and pattern have lengths $4n$ and $4m$ respectively.) Then, when the shift is $4\cdot i$ , all the $\spadesuit_{(\cdot)}$ symbols are matched, and the number of Hamming mismatches is the same as in the original instance at shift $i$ . Now $|B|\geq 3m$ and $k\leq m<0.3|B|$ hold. ∎

Now we describe how to modify the proof of Theorem 1.5 to improve the time bound to $\widetilde{O}(k^{1/2}n)$ .

#### Proof sketch of Theorem 1.8.

Based on $P,T$ , construct the same point sets $A,B$ as in the first paragraph of the previous proof of Corollary 1.7. Now we run the $k$ -Mismatch Constellation algorithm described in Section 11.1 on input sets $A,B\subset\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ (for simplicity, here we directly work with $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ without flattening to 1-dimension), but with the following modifications:

- • Since we only care about shifts in $C^{\prime}:=\{(c,0):c\in\{0,1,\dots,n-m\}\}$ , we can discard all elements in the candidate set $C$ that are not in $C^{\prime}$ . Therefore, Lemma 11.4 can be trivially improved to $|C-C|\leq|C^{\prime}-C^{\prime}|<2(n-m+1)=O(n)$ .

- • Lemma 11.5 relies the estimate from Lemma 11.4, so it can be improved accordingly to $|B^{\prime}+C|=O(nR)$ . Hence, the step of using Lemma 2.2 to compute $(1_{A}\star 1_{-B^{\prime}})[c]$ for all $c\in C$ now runs in $\widetilde{O}(|B^{\prime}+C|)\leq\widetilde{O}(nR)$ time.

- • For the next step of computing $(1_{A}\star 1_{B_{-\mathrm{bad}}})[c]$ for all $c\in C\subseteq C^{\prime}$ , we apply Theorem 4.1 to $(A,B,C,S):=(C^{\prime},B_{\mathrm{bad}},A,-C^{\prime})$ , with time complexity $\displaystyle\widetilde{O}\Big(\frac{|C^{\prime}-C^{\prime}|}{\sqrt{|-C^{\prime}|}}\cdot\sqrt{|A||B_{\mathrm{bad}}|}\Big)+(|C^{\prime}-C^{\prime}|+|A|)N^{o(1)}$ $\displaystyle\leq O\Big(\sqrt{n}\cdot\sqrt{|A|\cdot k}+n^{1+o(1)}\Big)$ $\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{k}n^{1+o(1)}.$

- • Finally, combined with the running time $\widetilde{O}(|A|k/R)$ for the $|C|<|A|/R$ case, the total time for solving Problem 11.1 becomes $\widetilde{O}(|A|k/R)+\widetilde{O}(nR)+\sqrt{k}n^{1+o(1)}\leq\sqrt{k}n^{1+o(1)}$ by choosing $R=\Theta(\sqrt{k})$ .

Again, for the randomized algorithm the $n^{o(1)}$ factor in the time complexity can be replaced by $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(n)$ . For the deterministic algorithm, we use the same argument as in Section 11.2. ∎

# Approximation Algorithms for Min-Distance ProblemsThanks: minad@mit.edu, virgi@mit.edu, nvyas@mit.edu, nwein@mit.edu, xyzhan@mit.edu, ycyu@mit.edu, MIT EECS and CSAIL

**Authors:** Mina Dalirrooyfard Virginia Vassilevska Williams Nikhil Vyas Affiliation: Nicole Wein, Yinzhan Xu and Yuancheng Yu

## Abstract

We study fundamental graph parameters such as the Diameter and Radius in directed graphs, when distances are measured using a somewhat unorthodox but natural measure: the distance between $u$ and $v$ is the minimum of the shortest path distances from $u$ to $v$ and from $v$ to $u$ . The center node in a graph under this measure can for instance represent the optimal location for a hospital to ensure the fastest medical care for everyone, as one can either go to the hospital, or a doctor can be sent to help.

By computing All-Pairs Shortest Paths, all pairwise distances and thus the parameters we study can be computed exactly in $\tilde{O}(mn)$ time for directed graphs on $n$ vertices, $m$ edges and nonnegative edge weights. Furthermore, this time bound is tight under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis [Roditty-Vassilevska W.
